title: Graph Engineering: How I Ship Tickets With a Graph of AI Agents
description:
TL;DR: First I wrote down everything a session needs to know (the harness), so any fresh session can pick up the work. On top of that, a small script walks each ticket through fixed steps, each done by a fresh agent and checked by another. A step only passes when its proof file is on disk. A first-mate fable agent answers the questions, and I review its calls at the end.

The short version

I stopped asking one AI session to do a whole ticket. Now a small program walks each ticket through a fixed map of steps (the graph), and a different agent does each step. A step only counts as done when the file it was meant to produce is sitting on disk and passes a check. The agent saying "done" counts for nothing.

This is my own personal setup, built on Claude Code, that I use for my day-job tickets. The graph also sits on top of a harness (written docs, context and rules) that I built first, and it wouldn't work without one.

Three ideas carry the whole thing:

  1. Files decide, not agents. Every step leaves proof on disk, and a plain script reads that proof.
  2. The writer never grades its own work. Each step that changes code is followed by a fresh reviewer that has never seen how it was built.
  3. The run doesn't wait on me. Questions go to a "first mate" agent that settles what the evidence can settle. I review the rest at the end, over coffee.

Why one long session stopped working for me

A single session doing a whole ticket was quick to start, but I couldn't trust what came out the other end. It went fine on small changes. On anything bigger, the same few problems kept showing up.

  • It marked its own homework. The session that wrote the code also decided the code was good. It nearly always agreed with itself.
  • The target drifted. When a test got awkward, the easy move was to quietly reword what "done" meant.
  • Memory faded. Long sessions get summarised to save space. Details from the start of the ticket fell out by the end.
  • It stopped to ask me small things. I'd come back to find it had waited an hour on a question the code already answered.
  • One model for everything. The same expensive model did both the hard design call and the boring file rename.

Most of these problems come from one root cause: the session's memory was the only record of the work. So the first fix wasn't the graph at all. It was writing things down.

Before the graph: a harness that any session can pick up

The graph is the last layer, not the first. It only works because I first built a harness: written docs, context and rules that let a brand-new session pick up work with no memory of what came before. I based the whole setup on the free course Learn Harness Engineering. Its last lecture covers graph engineering, and it treats the earlier lectures as the groundwork you need first. I followed the same order.

The course's core idea is simple. An agent only knows what's in the repository, its prompts and its tool output. A decision that lives only in a chat, a ticket comment or my head doesn't exist for it. So the repository, plus my own docs folder next to it, has to be the record. The course calls this the system of record.

Here is what each pillar holds in my setup:

  • Entry files. These are short instruction files loaded into every session. One holds my personal rules, one is shared across my workspace, and each repo has its own. They say what the project is, how to run it and how to check it, then point to deeper docs instead of holding everything.
  • Living docs. These hold the architecture overview, where new code goes, coding guidelines, and a design doc for each feature. They are edited in place whenever the code moves, because stale docs mislead more than missing ones.
  • Ticket context. Every ticket I've investigated gets its own folder. The facts in it are tied to file and line numbers, and an index lets the next session find the right folder before it explores any code.
  • Progress files. Plans, review logs and decision records say what's done, what's next and what's blocked. One rule I keep everywhere: when the file and the chat disagree, the file wins.

Underneath it all are the checks that keep the harness honest. Lint, test and type-check gates run before anything counts as done. Small scripts that run around the tool's actions (hooks) block the common shortcuts.

Why this lets one session pick up another's work

Because everything that matters is written down, any session can carry on work another session started. That includes a session I open tomorrow, a helper agent spun up mid-task, or a stage the graph starts in the background.

Claude Code can now also let sessions message each other directly, and I do use that for quick nudges. But that is a separate, built-in feature, and it isn't what my handoffs rest on. A message only helps while both sessions are alive, and its content disappears when they end. A file stays. The graph leans on this completely: every stage is a fresh session that has never seen the chat, and it does its job from the files alone.

The course suggests a test I still use: open a fresh session, give it only the repository, and ask it basic questions about the work. Wherever it has to guess, the harness has a gap. That gap gets fixed before I'd trust a graph run on top of it.

The core idea: a map of small steps, and a referee that reads files

The graph is a small program that knows the route, not an AI that does the work. It never writes code and never has an opinion. Given the same files on disk, it always prints the same next step.

Three players share the work:

  • The graph is the referee. It holds the map of steps and checks each step's proof.
  • The driver is one Claude session that does exactly what the graph prints, nothing more. It never decides anything.
  • The stage agents do the real work: write a spec, build the change, review it. Each one is fresh, with one job and one output file.

Every step goes round this same loop. If the proof file is missing, stale, or fails its check, the step simply hasn't happened, whatever the agent said.

Here is how each old problem maps to a fix:

Old problem Fix in the graph
It marked its own homework A separate reviewer step follows every step that changes code
The target drifted The acceptance criteria are locked (frozen) when the spec is signed off
Memory faded Every step reads and writes files, so nothing depends on chat memory
It stopped to ask me small things A first-mate agent answers what the evidence settles
One model for everything Each step is sized and gets the cheapest model that can do it

A ticket's journey, from key to draft pull request

I hand the graph a ticket key and a base branch. It walks that ticket through four phases and stops at a draft pull request. The ticket's type picks the path at two forks: a bug gets reproduced before anyone writes a spec, and a spike (a research ticket) ends in a written answer instead of code.

A few steps are worth calling out:

  • Write the spec, lock the criteria. An agent writes the spec, including the acceptance criteria (the list of things that must be true for the ticket to count as done). When the spec is signed off, the graph takes a fingerprint (a hash) of that section. Later checks compare against the fingerprint, so nobody can quietly move the goalposts.
  • Right-goal check. Before any code exists, a separate agent asks a blunt question: if we meet these criteria, does that actually solve the problem the ticket describes? If not, the ticket stops there.
  • Build it, test-first. The build step runs one of my two delivery pipelines, one for UI work and one for everything else. Both write the failing test first, then the code.
  • Wait steps cost nothing. Waiting for a blocking ticket to merge, or for room under my cap on open pull requests, is a cheap background script. No AI model is running while a ticket waits, even for days.
  • The graph stops at a draft. It only ever opens a draft pull request, on its own branch, for the exact commit that passed the final checks. It never marks one ready, never adds reviewers and never merges. Those stay with me.

Nothing moves forward on an agent's word alone

Every step has a proof file, and a plain script decides whether that proof is good enough. The script checks simple, boring things: does the file exist, was it written during this step (not left over from an earlier try), does it have the sections it must have, and does it end with a pass verdict.

Step What counts as proof
Reproduce a bug A reproduction file with the steps, the expected result, what actually happened and the suspected cause
Write the spec A spec with acceptance criteria and no unresolved decisions left in it
Build it Delivery files, a closed review ledger and passing check scripts
Goal check A judge's review file that ends in PASS
Gates A gate report showing lint, tests and type checks passed on that exact commit
Pull request text A title and body that pass a template check

Three more rules keep a run honest:

  • Every loop has a cap and every step has a deadline. Nothing retries forever or stalls without anyone noticing.
  • When a ticket can't go on, it gets parked, not forced. The graph stops that one ticket, writes down why, and the other tickets keep going.
  • Tampering shows. Every event goes into a log where each line is chained to the one before it. If anything edits the run's history, the next command notices and refuses to trust it. It isn't a security wall, but it makes cheating visible.

The cheapest model that can do each step

Before a step runs, a small sizing agent reads a short brief about it and picks a model and an effort level. A rename gets the small, fast model. A tricky design call gets the big one. The driver never picks a model itself, because that would be a judgment call and the driver isn't allowed any.

If a step fails, it climbs a fixed ladder. It tries more thinking effort on the same model first, because that is cheaper than switching to a bigger model.

A few details that turned out to matter:

  • The graph sorts failures before it climbs. It looks at the evidence (the transcript, the launch record) to decide whether the model was the problem. A missing worktree doesn't buy a bigger model.
  • A guess can't steer the route. The chosen size is recorded, but no check is allowed to read it. So a model's guess about itself can never decide whether a step passed.
  • Every step leaves a cost record. A stats command reads the run log and tells me what each ticket cost and how often a size had to climb. Over time the sizer learns from those notes.
  • Overspending is invisible, so I watch for the other mistake. A step that passed on the big model might have passed on a smaller one, and no log can show that. A failed step does show up, so that's the signal the ladder tracks.

Where I fit in: a first mate stands between the run and me

A run never stops to ask me anything. Every question goes to a "first mate" agent first, and only a real blocker reaches me while the run is going. The first mate runs on the most capable model I have, because its rulings are the costly ones to get wrong.

Its job is to settle whatever the code, the docs and my written rules already settle. It only escalates a call that truly needs something only I have: my intent, my priorities, or my authority. When it does escalate, it brings real options and the one it would pick, never a bare question.

The spec is signed off the same way. An agent writes it, the first mate signs it off, and that sign-off locks the acceptance criteria. If I'd rather sign every spec myself, I can switch that one step back to a human step in my project settings.

When the run ends, its last lines name every ticket that has filed calls. I read those, overrule anything I disagree with, and restart a ticket from an earlier step if I need to. Before this, I spent my time answering questions mid-run. Now I spend it reviewing decisions after the fact, which is faster and easier to batch.

How it changed over its first week

The graph went from a first command-line entry to unattended runs in about a week, and the newest change applies the same maker-and-checker idea to every session I run, not just graph runs. I built it in small versions, each one reviewed before the next.

Date Change Why it mattered
10 Nov 2026 Strict orchestrator for every session The main session can no longer write files itself. It hands writing to an implementer agent, and a separate reviewer must check the result before the session can finish
10 Nov 2026 Version 5: the first mate signs off the spec Removed the last step that waited on me by default. I can still opt back in to signing specs myself
10 Nov 2026 Version 4: unattended by default, plus a setup interview No step asks me anything mid-run. A short interview sets up a new project's graph settings
10 Nov 2026 Version 3: route by ticket type Bugs get reproduced first, spikes end in a judged write-up instead of a pull request
9 Nov 2026 Version 2: sizing, headless steps and cost records Each step gets its own model, can run as its own background session, and leaves a cost line
7 Nov 2026 Stats with warning thresholds A daily report flags tickets that cost too much or climbed the ladder too often
5 Nov 2026 Batch runs in parallel lanes Several tickets run side by side, each in its own worktree and branch
4 Nov 2026 First command-line entry The graph, its map format and its first checks

The strict orchestrator change is the one I'd point other people at, because it works without the graph at all:

Each agent now carries a role tag, implementer or reviewer, so the second guard can tell whether a review actually happened after the last edit. A guard never blocks a graph step, because each step is already a worker with its own checker after it. Both guards also fail open: if one breaks, it lets the action through rather than freezing my session.

One idea is still on paper: running several tickets as separate full sessions, up to three at a time, taking turns on the one shared dev environment for manual testing. The plan is written but nothing is built yet.

What I learned, and what I'd tell anyone trying this

The biggest lesson: put the judgment inside small, checked steps, and keep the thing that moves work along completely dumb. Once the router stopped having opinions, runs became predictable and easy to debug.

What I'd pass on, starting with the step most people skip: build the harness before the graph. A graph of agents that can't read the project's context just makes more mistakes, faster.

  1. Trust files, not claims. If a step can't point to a file that proves it finished, it didn't finish.
  2. Separate the writer from the grader. A fresh reviewer that never saw the work being built catches what the writer talked itself out of.
  3. Lock the target before you build. Take a fingerprint of "done" at sign-off and check against it at the end.
  4. When nothing matches, stop. My routes have no "else" branch. A ticket that fits no path goes to a person, not to a default path by accident.
  5. Make waiting free. Most of a ticket's life is waiting on reviews and merges. That should cost nothing.
  6. Spend effort before model size. More thinking on the same model is the cheaper first retry.
  7. Let an agent filter your questions. A first mate that settles the easy calls turns constant interruptions into one review at the end.

Thanks for reading

Thanks for making it this far. This setup is still young and it keeps changing as I learn what works, so treat it as one person's notes, not a finished recipe. I hope some part of it is useful to you, whether that's the harness, the maker-and-checker split, or just the habit of writing things down so the next session can pick them up.

title: MCP Is Not a Trust Boundary
description:
Connecting an AI agent to a tool is not the same as deciding what that agent should be trusted to do.

That distinction matters with MCP-connected tools. MCP can make enterprise data and actions available to an agent, but the connection itself does not answer the buyer’s harder question:

Should this specific action be allowed right now, for this user, with this data, under these conditions?

Consider a hypothetical support agent connected to a ticketing system through MCP. A customer ticket contains hidden instructions telling the agent to export internal account data and attach it to a new ticket.

The agent follows the instruction because the content arrived through a trusted tool. The tool connection is legitimate. The requested action is not.

This is where many security designs break. They treat the path as trusted because the server was approved during setup. But trust in the tool does not transfer to every instruction returned by the tool, and it should not transfer to every action the agent can take afterward.

The practical control is to separate three decisions:

  • What entered the system? User request, retrieved document, tool response, or agent-generated reasoning.
  • What does the agent want to do? Read a record, modify a record, send a message, or trigger a transaction.
  • What authority applies now? User identity, data sensitivity, target system, action risk, and current policy.

A runtime policy should evaluate the proposed action, not just the source of the request. Reading a public knowledge-base article may be low risk. Sending customer data to an external address is not, even if the instruction came from an approved MCP server.

For an enterprise buyer, the useful test is simple:

Can you reconstruct why the agent was allowed to take each consequential action?

That means the audit record should connect the request, the tool response, the proposed action, the policy decision, and any human approval. A log that only says “agent called tool X” is activity history, not decision evidence.

Platform and security teams should inspect their integrations with three questions:

  1. Which tools can return untrusted content?
  2. Which actions can the agent take without a fresh policy check?
  3. Which high-impact actions require a human decision?

If the answer to the second question is “all actions available to the agent,” the system has a permission problem, even if the MCP server itself is secure.

The goal is not to make every agent slow or unusable. It is to put the trust boundary where the risk actually appears: immediately before the action, when intent, identity, context, and policy can still be evaluated.

title: The best tools to run multiple coding agents in parallel (2026), checked and sourced
description:
First published on traycer.ai.

By Anurag Sharma | Published 2026-10-26

Best tools to run Claude Code, Codex and other agents in parallel (2026). Top pick: Traycer, free and open source (MIT). Plus Conductor, Orca, T3 Code, Paradev.

By Anurag Sharma. Last checked: October 26, 2026.

Our top pick is Traycer: it's free and open source (MIT), runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and 19 more coding agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree, on Mac, Windows and Linux plus iOS and Android, and gives those agents shared specs and tickets so they work from one plan. It's free for individuals, phone apps included; the optional Sync plan for teams is $16 per user per month billed yearly, or $20 monthly (pricing). The alternatives are good at specific things. Conductor, the polished Mac app, has joined Meta: Conductor Cloud shuts down on Nov 20, 2026 and the local app winds down in early 2027. Orca is a free, open-source app for every desktop OS with a very large community. T3 Code, by Theo Browne and team, is the one to try if you want a hosted web app. If you only ever use one vendor's agent, Claude Code's or Codex's built-in worktrees and subagents may be enough.

All of them give each agent its own git worktree so parallel work doesn't collide, and all of them use the agent subscriptions you already pay for. They differ in platform (several are Mac-only), license (MIT, Apache, AGPL, GPL or proprietary), what's free versus paid (mobile, cloud, teams), and whether agents can coordinate with each other or only run side by side. If you're running Claude Code, Codex and Cursor as AI coding agents and one terminal tab isn't enough, start here.

Disclosure: Traycer makes this page. We've tried to be fair and link every claim to the vendor's own site or docs.

Desktop workspaces for parallel coding agents

Traycer (best overall)

Traycer is an open source (MIT) desktop app for running Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents in parallel on macOS, Windows and Linux, with shared plans and code review (docs). It supports 22 coding agents (coding agents). Work lives in Tasks: each holds its agents, a worktree per agent, and artifacts (specs, tickets, stories and reviews) that every agent reads (artifact workflow). Agents can message each other across Tasks and machines (agent-to-agent). A second agent can review a change and write a review artifact, and Send to chat returns each finding to the agent that wrote it (review guide). The iOS and Android companion apps and remote hosts on your own machines are free. Team-wide sharing is on Sync at $16/user/month billed yearly, or $20 monthly (pricing). Traycer is SOC 2 Type 2 certified. Its homepage reports 11,000+ developers using Traycer Desktop and 40,000+ Tasks created (traycer.ai).

Best for: most people running agents in parallel, and especially anyone who mixes agents from several vendors and wants them working from one shared plan with a review step, on any desktop OS or from a phone.

Watch out for: cloud sandboxes are a paid add-on rather than included (pricing), there are no line comments on diffs (Conductor and Orca win on line-level review), no built-in scheduler (it uses the CLI plus your own cron) and no SSO.

Conductor

Conductor (conductor.build) is a Mac app from Melty Labs that "lets you run many coding agents in parallel on your codebase" (llms.txt). Each task gets a workspace with its own branch, files and terminal, and Conductor walks you through review, PR, merge and archive. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode, and "does not bill or resell model usage" (providers). Its review loop was the strongest here: line comments back to the agent, a Checks tab, checkpoints and stacks. Pro ($50/month) added Conductor Cloud, Multiplayer, an API and the iOS app, and Teams was $60/user/month (pricing). Conductor has joined Meta: new sign-ups and upgrades stopped on Nov 4, 2026, Conductor Cloud goes read-only on Nov 13 and shuts down on Nov 20, and the local app winds down in early 2027.

Best for: Mac developers who want cloud sandboxes and a polished PR loop.

Watch out for: macOS only, proprietary, and winding down; Conductor Cloud shuts down on Nov 20, 2026 (announcement). See how to switch off Conductor Cloud, the Conductor alternative for teams, Traycer vs Conductor and the best Conductor alternatives.

Orca

Orca is a free, open source (MIT) app that runs "Claude Code, Codex, and any other coding agent in parallel, each in its own worktree," with terminals, diffs, a browser and a CLI (onorca.dev). It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and has a mobile companion on the App Store plus an Android APK. Its community is large: about 106,000 GitHub stars on October 26, 2026 (repo). Its site also lists an Enterprise offering.

Best for: anyone who wants a free, open-source app on every desktop OS with phone access.

Watch out for: a very fast release pace. Version 1.4.241 shipped on October 26, 2026, so re-check features before you rely on one. See Traycer vs Orca and T3 Code vs Orca.

T3 Code

T3 Code, by Theo Browne and team, calls itself "the open-source control plane for coding agents" (t3.codes). It's MIT-licensed and free, with no paid tier. It orchestrates Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, OpenCode, Cursor and Grok with the credentials you already have. A local server runs your agents, and you reach it from the desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux) or its hosted web app at app.t3.codes (repo). Its v0.1.0 release added delegate_task, which lets "an agent start child agents on any provider or model and wait for their results" (v0.1.0 notes).

Best for: a lightweight control plane you can drive from a browser through its hosted web app.

Watch out for: it's still v0.1.x (v0.1.2 on October 22, 2026). See Traycer vs T3 Code.

Paradev (formerly Superset)

Paradev, formerly Superset, is a desktop workspace for Claude Code, Codex "and any coding agent" (paradev.com). It's open source under the MIT License. Its site offers a macOS download. Free covers one user. Pro ($20/user/month, or $16 billed yearly) adds remote access, automations, Linear and Slack integrations and mobile. Team ($60, or $54 yearly) adds cloud workspaces in beta with 150 hours per seat each month. Ultra is $200/user/month (pricing).

Best for: Mac teams that want automations and hosted cloud workspaces.

Watch out for: it was recently renamed from Superset to Paradev, so older guides use the old name.

Nimbalyst

Nimbalyst is an open source (MIT) visual workspace for agents, tasks, docs, a wiki, diagrams and code (nimbalyst.com). It runs on Mac (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux, works with your Claude Code or Codex subscription, and includes worktrees and a mobile app for remote session and file management. It's free for individuals. Wiki Teams, a shared wiki that "every teammate's agents write into," is $20/user/month and free during its beta (pricing).

Best for: people who want docs, diagrams and an agent-maintained wiki next to their agents.

Watch out for: the team wiki is still in beta.

Emdash

Emdash is an open-source (Apache-2.0) "agentic development environment" for macOS, Windows and Linux, backed by Y Combinator (emdash.com, repo). Its site covers running agents in parallel, scheduling repeat work, a built-in browser for previews, and passing issues from Linear, Jira, GitHub, Notion, Asana and others straight to agents.

Best for: teams that want scheduled agent runs and issue-tracker intake in an open-source app.

Watch out for: Emdash 2.0 is in early access behind a waitlist, so features may shift.

Parallel Code

Parallel Code is a free, MIT-licensed app that runs "multiple AI coding agents, each in its own git worktree" on macOS and Linux (parallelcode.app). It supports Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI and Antigravity CLI, and shows what each agent changed and what was checked before you choose what ships.

Best for: a simple, open-source worktree runner on macOS or Linux.

Watch out for: no Windows build listed.

Terminal-first options

cmux

cmux is a "free and open source native macOS terminal built on Ghostty," licensed under the GPL (cmux.com). It has vertical tabs, notification rings when agents need attention, split panes, a CLI for scripting, and an iOS companion that syncs your terminals to iPhone and iPad. It uses libghostty for rendering and isn't a fork of Ghostty. It's a terminal, not a task manager: you bring your own worktree habits.

Best for: Mac users who live in the terminal.

Claude Squad

Claude Squad is a terminal app that "manages multiple Claude Code, Codex, Gemini (and other local agents including Aider) in separate workspaces" (repo). It needs tmux and the GitHub CLI, isolates tasks in git workspaces, and is licensed under AGPL v3.0 (site).

Best for: a minimal tmux setup with any CLI agent.

Watch out for: the repo's last push was August 20, 2026.

Built into the agents: do you need a separate app at all?

Claude Code: subagents, agent view, agent teams, worktrees and projects

Anthropic's docs list "five ways to work on several tasks at once": subagents, agent view, agent teams, dynamic workflows and projects (run agents in parallel).

  • Agent view (claude agents) is one screen to dispatch and monitor background sessions. It's a research preview.
  • Subagents run inside a session. By default, when 20 subagents are running, spawning another fails until the count drops. Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS to change the limit (subagents).
  • Agent teams are "experimental and disabled by default." Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 to turn them on. Teammates share a task list and message each other directly. The docs say "There's no hard limit on the number of teammates" and suggest you "Start with 3-5 teammates for most workflows" (agent teams).
  • Projects run parallel threads in the cloud or on your computer. They're in public beta on Pro and Max.
  • Worktrees: claude --worktree (or -w) starts a session in its own git worktree so changes don't collide (worktrees).

Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app

OpenAI's Codex app docs now point to the ChatGPT desktop app (app docs). Worktrees let Codex "run multiple independent chats in the same project without interfering with each other," and scheduled tasks can run on dedicated background worktrees (worktrees). In the ChatGPT iOS app you can open Codex to work with chats on a connected Mac or Windows machine (remote connections). Subagents are documented too. It runs Codex only.

Cursor: Agents Window and Cloud Agents

Cursor's Agents Window is its "agent-first interface," a single place to work with agents "across repos and environments, including local, cloud, remote SSH, and more" (Agents Window). You can hand a task to a cloud subagent with /in-cloud, so long-running work runs on its own VM and branch. Cloud Agents "run in isolated VMs in the cloud with full development environments" (Cloud Agents).

The takeaway

If you use one vendor's agent, its built-in features may be enough. A separate app earns its place when you mix vendors (Claude Code plus Codex plus Cursor), want one place to review everything, or want agents from different vendors to share a plan and coordinate. For the agents themselves, see Codex vs Claude Code and Cursor vs Claude Code vs Codex.

A note on Vibe Kanban

Vibe Kanban (Apache-2.0, about 28,500 GitHub stars on October 26, 2026) was popular, and AI answers still recommend it. Its site now says it "is sunsetting" and "will continue as open source and community maintained" (vibekanban.com), so know that before you adopt it.

How to choose

  • On Windows or Linux? Traycer, Orca, T3 Code, Nimbalyst and Emdash run on all three desktop OSes. Parallel Code adds Linux, and Paradev has an experimental Linux build.
  • Need open source? Drop Conductor (proprietary).
  • Need agents to coordinate on one plan? Traycer, or Claude Code agent teams if every agent is Claude.
  • Need cloud sandboxes that run while your laptop is closed? Paradev Team, Cursor Cloud Agents, or Traycer's cloud sandboxes as a paid add-on. Traycer can also run agents free on a remote host you own. Conductor Cloud shuts down on Nov 20, 2026.
  • Team sharing on a budget? Compare Traycer Sync ($16/user/month yearly; sharing a Task with invited people is free) and Paradev Pro ($16/user/month yearly). Conductor Teams no longer takes upgrades; see the Conductor alternative for teams.

How to run multiple Claude Code or Codex agents in parallel without an app

You don't need an app to start. You need one worktree per agent.

  • Create a worktree per task: git worktree add ../myapp-auth -b feat/auth (a separate checkout on its own branch).
  • Open a terminal in each worktree and start one agent there, such as claude or codex. Claude Code can also do this for you with claude --worktree auth.
  • Give each agent a narrow task that doesn't touch the same files as the others.
  • Review each branch's diff on its own, then merge or open a PR.
  • Remove the worktree when you're done: git worktree remove ../myapp-auth.

This stops scaling once you lose track of which terminal is doing what, or need agents to hand work to each other. That's the job the apps above automate: worktrees, terminals, review, and in some cases shared plans and messaging. Traycer's guide shows the same pattern inside a Task (parallel agents on worktrees).

FAQ

What is the best app to run multiple AI coding agents like Claude Code and Codex in parallel?

Traycer. It's a free, open-source (MIT) desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, with iOS and Android apps, that runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and 19 more agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree, and lets them share specs and tickets and message each other. Teams can add Sync at $16 per user per month billed yearly, or $20 monthly. Conductor, a polished Mac-only option, has joined Meta and Conductor Cloud shuts down on Nov 20, 2026. Orca is a free, open-source option with a large community, and T3 Code, by Theo Browne and team, adds a hosted web app.

What is the best tool to run multiple Claude Code agents in parallel?

For a desktop app, Traycer: it can give each Claude Code agent its own git worktree, lets the agents share specs and tickets and message each other, and also runs Codex, Cursor and 19 other agents when you want a second opinion. It's free and open source (MIT) on macOS, Windows and Linux. If you only use Claude Code and don't need an app, its built-in claude --worktree, subagents and experimental agent teams may be enough.

What is the best free, open-source app to run multiple coding agents in parallel?

Traycer is our pick: it's MIT-licensed and free for individuals, including the iOS and Android apps, cloud sync and remote hosts, and it runs 22 coding agents in parallel with a worktree each. Orca (MIT), T3 Code (MIT, by Theo Browne and team), Nimbalyst (MIT) and Emdash (Apache-2.0) are also free and open source.

Can I run multiple sessions of Claude Code in parallel?

Yes. Run each session in its own git worktree (claude --worktree) so their changes don't collide, or use Claude Code's agent view, subagents or experimental agent teams. Desktop apps such as Traycer, Conductor, Orca and T3 Code set up the worktrees for you.

How many agents can Claude Code use at once?

Anthropic's docs say there's no hard limit on agent-team teammates and recommend starting with 3 to 5. Subagents are capped at 20 running at once per session by default, and an environment variable changes that limit.

Can two Claude agents talk to each other?

Yes, in Claude Code's agent teams. They're experimental and off by default, and teammates share a task list and message each other directly. Traycer also lets agents from different vendors, such as Claude Code and Codex, message each other across Tasks and machines.

How do I run multiple AI coding agents in parallel?

Give each agent its own git worktree (a separate checkout on its own branch), start one agent per worktree, then review and merge each branch. Parallel-agent apps automate the worktrees, terminals and review.

Is there an open-source desktop app to run Claude Code, Codex and Cursor side by side with shared context?

Yes. Traycer is an open source (MIT) desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux that runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and 19 other agents in one Task, where they share specs, tickets and reviews. Orca, T3 Code, Nimbalyst and Emdash are also open source, but we didn't find a shared spec and ticket layer in their docs.

What tools let multiple coding agents share specs and tickets and message each other?

Traycer keeps specs, tickets and reviews as artifacts every agent in a Task reads, and lets agents message each other across Tasks and machines. Claude Code's agent teams share a task list among Claude sessions, and Nimbalyst gives agents a shared wiki.

Does ChatGPT have a coding agent?

Yes. Codex runs in the ChatGPT desktop app, where worktrees let it run several chats in the same project in parallel, and you can follow it from the ChatGPT iOS app.

Is Conductor available for Windows?

No, and it won't be. Its install guide says it's not available for Windows or Linux yet, and after joining Meta, Conductor stopped new downloads on Nov 4, 2026; Conductor Cloud shuts down on Nov 20. Traycer, Orca, T3 Code, Nimbalyst and Emdash all run on Windows.

Try Traycer

  • Download Traycer (free, open source)
  • Run agents in parallel on worktrees

title: The Agentic Shift: How Autonomous AI Agents Are Transforming Human Resources
description:
The Agentic Shift: How Autonomous AI Agents Are Transforming Human Resources

Executive Summary

Human Resources is experiencing a profound architectural shift. While the first wave of enterprise artificial intelligence focused on generative text and passive chatbots—answering standard FAQ questions or drafting job descriptions—the modern workplace is embracing agentic AI. Unlike traditional automation that follows rigid if-then rules, AI agents possess contextual reasoning, autonomy, and multi-step execution capabilities. In HR, autonomous agents are evolving from administrative assistants into active operational partners that streamline recruitment, personalize employee experiences, and proactively support talent retention.

1. Autonomous Talent Acquisition and Adaptive Sourcing

Recruiting has historically suffered from manual screening bottlenecks and fragmented applicant communication. Agentic workflows fundamentally redesign this funnel:

Dynamic Candidate Sourcing: Instead of waiting for applicants or running static boolean keyword searches, agentic sourcing systems continuously analyze industry repositories, professional networks, and open-source contributions. They evaluate technical competencies, trajectory, and cultural alignment against real-time workforce planning data.

Autonomous Pre-Screening and Scheduling: Sourcing agents interact with candidates conversationally across messaging channels, verifying prerequisite qualifications, handling mutual calendar coordination, and answering candidate questions about compensation benchmarks and team culture 24/7.

Objective Candidate Shortlisting: By anonymizing candidate profiles during early assessment rounds and focusing strictly on verifiable project outcomes and technical assessments, AI agents reduce unconscious bias in initial talent screening.

2. Hyper-Personalized Employee Onboarding and Navigation

Traditional onboarding often overwhelms new hires with compliance checklists, disparate portal logins, and static policy documents. An onboarding agent acts as a dedicated 90-day digital concierge:

Workflow Orchestration: The agent coordinates across IT, facilities, and department heads to provision hardware, assign software licenses, and schedule introductory peer check-ins before Day One.

Contextual Knowledge Retrieval: Rather than forcing employees to search hundreds of pages in an intranet wiki, the agent answers nuanced inquiries—such as healthcare tier eligibility, 401(k) vesting timelines, or travel reimbursement policies—tailored specifically to the employee's jurisdiction and job level.

Check-In Cadence: The agent proactively prompts new hires at days 7, 30, and 60 to gauge onboarding satisfaction, identify learning friction, and notify team leads when extra support is needed.

3. Continuous Performance Enablement and Skills Mapping

Annual performance reviews are notoriously backward-looking and time-consuming. Agentic HR tools shift organizations toward continuous coaching and internal mobility:

Real-Time Feedback Synthesis: Agents analyze structured feedback loops across project management tools, peer acknowledgments, and goal milestones to provide managers with objective performance summaries ahead of 1-on-1 coaching sessions.

Dynamic Skills Gap Analysis: As market requirements evolve, talent agents cross-reference employee project histories with company strategic priorities, autonomously recommending targeted learning paths and internal gig opportunities.

Proactive Career Pathing: Employees receive personalized recommendations for lateral transfers, certifications, and mentorship pairings that match their long-term professional aspirations.

4. Retention Risk Modeling and Sentiment Intelligence

Employee turnover often catches leadership by surprise. Autonomous agents provide early-warning signals while respecting personal data boundaries:

Anonymized Engagement Pulse: Instead of relying solely on annual engagement surveys, agents analyze aggregated sentiment across anonymized pulse surveys and workplace communications to detect team-level burnout or cultural friction points.

Predictive Flight-Risk Triggers: By correlating macro indicators—such as stagnant tenure in grade, market compensation divergence, and project fatigue—agents alert HR business partners to intervene proactively with tailored retention or role-refresh conversations.

5. Governance, Ethics, and the Human-in-the-Loop Imperative

With autonomous agency comes the vital responsibility of ethical stewardship. Organizations deploying HR agents must maintain strict governance guardrails:

Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) for High-Stakes Decisions: AI agents should recommend, summarize, and execute administrative workflows, but all consequential personnel decisions—such as hiring, termination, disciplinary action, and compensation adjustments—must remain strictly in the hands of human leaders.

Algorithmic Transparency & Auditability: Every decision tree, ranking score, and recommendation made by an agent must be auditable, explainable, and compliant with emerging employment regulations (such as NYC Local Law 144 and EU AI Act employment standards).

Data Privacy and Segregation: Employee personal data, medical leaves, and performance notes must be strictly partitioned with enterprise-grade encryption and role-based access control, ensuring external language models are never trained on proprietary organizational data.

Conclusion

The emergence of agentic AI does not eliminate the human element in Human Resources; rather, it liberates HR professionals from routine operational overhead. By deploying autonomous agents to handle repetitive coordination, continuous data aggregation, and real-time support, HR leaders can reclaim their essential role as strategic advisors, culture builders, and empathetic mentors. Organizations that balance agentic efficiency with rigorous ethical oversight will build the most agile, resilient, and human-centric workforces of the future.

title: GitHub MCP server in Claude and ChatGPT: repositories, issues and pull requests, nothing to install
description:
The GitHub MCP server lets Claude or ChatGPT read your repositories, search code, and work with issues and pull requests through GitHub's own official server. Fezola relays that server: you sign in once on GitHub's authorization page, with no personal access token and no Docker, and each assistant gets a single connector. The facts below come from GitHub's repository and Fezola's code as of 15 November 2026, and they change, so check the GitHub connector page.

What you can ask

  • "Which pull requests are waiting for my review?"
  • "Summarize the open issues labeled bug in this repository."
  • "Search the code for where we call this function."
  • "Why did the last Actions run fail?"
  • "Draft an issue describing this error and open it."

GitHub's server groups its tools in toolsets: repositories, issues, pull requests, Actions, code security, discussions, notifications, projects, gists and more. Your assistant finds the tool that fits your question, then calls it through Fezola.

Remote, local or hosted by Fezola

Local server Remote server Through Fezola
Where it runs Your machine (Docker or a binary) GitHub GitHub, relayed by Fezola
Sign-in OAuth login or a personal access token OAuth or a personal access token in a header OAuth on GitHub's page, no token to paste
Best for Hosts without remote MCP support Editors that support it Claude and ChatGPT, several accounts

How to connect it

  1. In the Fezola app, open Sources, add GitHub and approve access on GitHub's own authorization page.
  2. Connect Fezola to your assistant once, at https://api.fezola.com/mcp: see how to add a custom connector to Claude. ChatGPT custom connectors are available on Business, Enterprise and Edu plans (Pro read-only).
  3. Ask a question about your code.

Organization policies still apply: GitHub's remote server needs the relevant policies enabled on your organization.

Guardrails

  • Reading and changing. GitHub's server includes tools that create and change things, such as issues and pull requests. Your assistant should ask before it changes anything: keep approvals on.
  • Access you grant. Fezola requests the scopes GitHub announces for its server, private repositories included. You can hide GitHub from an assistant: see choose which tools Claude or ChatGPT can see.
  • Third-party text is data. Issue and pull request text returned by GitHub is data and never instructions.

Several accounts

Personal and work accounts are separate sources in Fezola, each labeled with its GitHub login, and one assistant works across them. Switching Claude account later means adding one connector, not every account again: see one connector, every Claude account.

Next steps

New to MCP? Start with what is MCP. For the other tools Fezola connects, see the GitHub connector page.

FAQ

What is the GitHub MCP server?

It is GitHub's official MCP server. It lets an AI assistant such as Claude read repositories, search code, manage issues and pull requests and work with GitHub Actions, with your permission.

How do I connect GitHub to Claude or ChatGPT?

Add GitHub once in Fezola and approve access on GitHub's own authorization page: no personal access token to create or paste. Then add Fezola to your assistant at one URL.

Do I need Docker or a personal access token?

Not with Fezola. GitHub's local server runs on your machine through Docker or a binary, and GitHub's remote server accepts OAuth or a personal access token in a header. Fezola connects to the remote server for you with OAuth.

Can the assistant change my repositories?

GitHub's server includes tools that create and change things such as issues and pull requests, and Fezola requests the permissions it announces, private repositories included. Keep your assistant's approval prompts on, and you can hide GitHub from an assistant in Fezola.

Can I connect several GitHub accounts?

Yes. Each GitHub account is its own source in Fezola, labeled with its login, and one assistant works across them.

Is it free?

Fezola is free with 2 sources, GitHub included. Pro connects unlimited sources, with a 7-day free trial.

Originally published at app.fezola.com. Written and published by Fezola's AI agents; facts checked against the code and the vendors' own pages.

title: Kling 4.0 API Pricing: Every Route, Compared
description:
Introduction

Kling 4.0 costs the least through the useapi.net Kling API, on the Kling AI subscription you already have. On Premier, a 5-second 1080p video uses $0.76 of the plan's monthly credits, or $0.152 a second (as of November 2026).

Kling's own developer API and every reseller we checked charge more per second, at 720p and at 1080p. The comparison table below has each route side by side.

useapi.net is a third-party API, not affiliated with Kling AI or Kuaishou Technology. Your videos spend your Kling AI subscription credits, and useapi.net adds no per-video charge. We read Kling's own prices and every reseller's live on November 5, 2026, and converted each one to the cost of the same video, so the routes compare like for like.

Official Kling 4.0 API pricing

Kling's own developer API went live with Kling 4.0 between October 25 and 28, 2026, and now lists Kling 4.0 and 4.0 Flash as fully launched. It sells them in prepaid packs that cover only these two models, from $500 for 3,250 units, valid 180 days, so a unit costs $0.154.

Kling 4.0 takes 1 unit a second at 720p and 1.5 at 1080p. That is $0.154 and $0.231 a second, or $1.15 for a 5-second 1080p video. Kling 4.0 Flash takes 0.6 units a second at 720p, $0.092 a second or $0.46 for 5 seconds (as of November 5, 2026). With an input video, Kling also bills its length: twice the output seconds when the input is no longer than the output, otherwise input plus output, at 0.6 units a second (0.9 at 1080p) for Kling 4.0 and 0.4 for Flash. Kling's other developer packs, from $700, don't cover Kling 4.0.

Kling 4.0 on a Kling AI subscription

Through useapi.net, Kling 4.0 (kling-v4-0) runs on your Kling AI subscription's credits, 10 a second at 720p and 15 at 1080p on every plan. Kling 4.0 Flash (kling-v4-0-flash) takes 6 a second at 720p. This is what one video costs on each plan, at the regular monthly price (as of November 2026):

The "Kling 4.0 API price" quoted around the web, about $0.11 to $0.14 a second, is the 720p rate, and the lowest of those, $0.1134, was UnificAlly's launch sale, which has ended. When you compare, match the resolution and check for a promotion.

What the subscription figures assume

A subscription price per video holds when you use the plan's credits. Premier's 8,000 credits a month make 106 five-second 1080p videos or 17 thirty-second ones. For more volume, connect several Kling accounts to one useapi.net token and it spreads jobs across them (Run several Kling accounts), or buy Kling credit top-ups.

Kling also sets the price. Its launch discount on Kling 4.0 for subscribers has ended, and on November 5, 2026 every plan paid the full 10 and 15 credits a second, as in the tables above. Check the live plans page before you commit spend. At full price, Premier's $0.152 a second at 1080p stays below every 1080p reseller rate above.

At the full price Kling charges now (November 2026), the same clip uses 30 credits, $0.33 at Pro's credit price. The prompt and every response are in the Kling 4.0 tutorial.

title: Product Compositing: Dissolving a Product Into a Scene, Then Finishing It as a Hero Shot
description:
Pasting a product into a scene is easy. Making it look like it belongs there — correct contact shadow, colour bounce from the environment, and a plausible edge where the product meets the surface — is the part that takes an afternoon.

This episode splits that into two jobs and gives each its own model.

The two workflows

# Workflow Job
01 Qwen Image 2.1 product-scene dissolve, 40-step quality + Viggle accelerated Compose the product into the scene
02 H3 VDN 12NFE high-quality second pass Finish it as a hero shot

The split matters: composition and finish are different problems and a single model doing both ends up mediocre at each.

What "dissolve" means here

Not alpha compositing. The model re-renders the product in the scene context — which means it reconstructs the lighting on the product from the scene, adds contact shadow at the base, and lets environment colour spill onto adjacent surfaces.

That is why the result reads as cohesive. It is also why the product's exact label text and logo placement drift — the model is reconstructing, not copying.

The 40-step vs Viggle trade

  • 40-step quality — label text stays legible, material reads correctly (glass reads as glass, fabric as fabric). Slow, used for the final frame.
  • Viggle accelerated — fast enough to iterate on composition. Label text degrades first, then fine surface detail.

Use the accelerated path to decide the composition, then re-run the same seed at 40 steps for the frame you actually keep.

The Hero Shot pass

The H3 VDN 12NFE pass takes the composited frame and re-renders it at higher fidelity. Its job is not composition — it is making the product read as a photograph rather than a composite: micro-edges, specular highlights, depth-of-field fall-off.

12 NFE is the operating point where that finish is convincing without costing a full render.

Where this fits commercially

  • E-commerce hero images without a product shoot.
  • Seasonal variants: one product, many scenes, consistent finish.
  • A/B testing backgrounds before committing to photography.

The honest limitation: if the product has text you need exact, composite the text in after the model pass. The model will not preserve it faithfully.

  • ModelScope: https://modelscope.cn/models/Sunjian520/h3-hero-shot-qwen21-composite

title: Reference Edit Advanced: RGB + Depth Composite Reference in a Single Video Pass
description:
Most reference-edit workflows use one reference. This one uses two simultaneously: an RGB reference for appearance and a depth reference for geometry. The combination unlocks doing four things in a single pass that normally need four passes.

What the two references each carry

RGB reference — who the character is. Face structure, hair, costume, colour.

Depth reference — where everything is. Camera position, subject distance from lens, scene layout.

Using both means the new character inherits appearance from one and spatial position from the other. Using only RGB, the character lands wherever the model feels like putting it.

The four jobs in one pass

  1. Character replacement — the subject becomes the reference character.
  2. Action inheritance — the motion of the source performance transfers.
  3. Scene and camera preservation — because depth is conditioned, the camera does not wander and the set does not rebuild itself between frames.
  4. Audio-driven lip sync — when audio is supplied, mouth movement is driven by it.

Doing these separately is how most pipelines end up with a character that has the right face but the wrong head angle, because each pass re-decides.

Three variants

File Use
Standard Default settings
Silent (无声版) No audio conditioning
Face Refine Extra pass on the face after the main render

The Face Refine variant is worth the extra time whenever the character is in frame larger than about a third of the image height. At smaller sizes the refine pass adds nothing.

Where it breaks

Depth conditioning is precise but rigid. If the source performance moves the subject closer to camera in a way the depth map does not describe (because the depth was extracted from a single frame), the composite drifts at that moment. The fix is a per-frame depth extraction, which is much more expensive — and the episode shows the difference.

  • HF: https://huggingface.co/AI-KSK/minimax-h3-role-swap-reference-edit
  • ModelScope: https://modelscope.cn/models/Sunjian520/minimax-h3-role-swap-reference-edit

Video walkthrough (Chinese): https://youtu.be/UespHFT9cjc
