title: Sticky Sessions Won't Save Your AI Chat: 6 Questions Before You Run a .NET Chat Backend on Two Nodes
description:
Scaling a normal API is a solved problem: make the servers stateless, put the state in a database, add nodes. An AI chat backend follows the same recipe and still goes wrong, because a chat turn is slow, costs money, depends on history, and gets retried by clients all the time.

When I moved a C# chat API from one node to three, nothing crashed. Every response was a 200. And the bill and the answers were both quietly wrong.

So instead of a tutorial, here are the six questions I now ask before a chat backend gets a second node, with the shape of the answer to each.

Tech Skill Builder is $5/month for a very limited time only (normally $10). Grab it now before it goes back to $10. The complete, tested project behind this post (a .NET 10 multi-node chat backend with Clean Architecture and 198 passing tests, running offline against a simulated model) plus a step-by-step PDF guide is inside. Join Tech Skill Builder

About the numbers: they come from my own local runs, with real Kestrel processes on one Linux box sharing one SQLite file and a simulated model at about 400 ms. They show how the backend behaves, not how fast any model is.

Question 1: "Can my server tell a retry from a new message?"

If the answer is "no", every timeout costs you a second model call. Phones lose signal, browsers time out, users tap Send twice, and the retry lands on whatever node the load balancer picks.

In my test, 60 messages each retried on another node produced 120 model calls and 60 duplicate messages in the history.

The shape of the answer: the client creates a clientMessageId when the user presses Send and repeats it on every retry. The server checks it in the shared store before anything else:

public sealed record SendMessage(
    Guid ConversationId,
    Guid ClientMessageId,   // created by the client, repeated on every retry
    string Text);

// In the admission rules, the retry check comes first:
// - same id, same text, already answered  -> return the stored reply
// - same id, same text, still running     -> 202, poll later
// - same id, DIFFERENT text               -> 422 (a client bug, not a retry)
// full implementation in the complete project

Storing a hash of the text matters more than it looks. Without it, a buggy client that reuses an id gets the answer to someone else's question.

Question 2: "What happens when the same user has two tabs open?"

Two tabs are two clients. If both send a message while an answer is being generated, both turns read the same history and one of them answers without seeing the other's question.

With two nodes and 240 two-tab messages, I got 115 replies built on stale history.

The shape of the answer: one running turn per conversation, enforced in the store. You still have to choose what the second message gets:

Option What the user sees Cost
Reject with 409 + Retry-After A short wait, then the message goes through Client must retry
Queue it behind the first Nothing, just slower You need a durable queue
Cancel the first, answer the newest The first answer disappears A paid call thrown away

I went with 409, and stale replies went from 115 to 0. The price was 120 extra 409 responses that the client retried. There's no free option here, only one you chose on purpose.

Question 3: "Why not sticky sessions, or a lock in memory?"

This is the one that catches most teams, because sticky sessions look like they fix everything above.

They don't. A retry after a crash or a deploy goes to another node anyway. Two tabs may land on different nodes. And a SemaphoreSlim or lock is one lock per process, so with three nodes you have three locks that don't know about each other.

The shape of the answer: correctness lives in the shared store, in one transaction that reads, decides and writes:

public async Task<BeginTurnResult> BeginTurnAsync(BeginTurn command, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // 1. open a write transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE in SQLite, SERIALIZABLE in Postgres)
    // 2. read: conversation, turn for this clientMessageId, active turn, tenant load
    // 3. decide with a pure Domain function (replay / busy / over cap / start)
    // 4. write the new turn + a fresh fencing token, then commit
    // full implementation in the complete project
}

The decision being a pure function is what makes it testable. In my concurrency test, 24 simultaneous begins from 4 store instances produce exactly one winner every time.

Question 4: "If a node loses its lease, can it still write?"

A lease stops two turns from running at once. It doesn't stop a late one from writing. A node pauses (GC, network blip, a slow model), its lease expires, another node takes over, and then the first one wakes up and saves its old answer on top.

The shape of the answer: every turn gets a fencing token that goes up by one each time ownership changes, and the commit refuses anything that isn't the current token:

public enum CommitStatus { Committed, StaleToken, VersionConflict }

// CompleteTurnAsync, in shape:
// if turn.FencingToken != command.FencingToken -> StaleToken (someone newer owns it)
// if conversation.Version != expected          -> VersionConflict (history moved)
// otherwise: save user message + reply together, free the conversation
// full implementation in the complete project

Saving the question and the answer in the same commit has a nice side effect: the history never contains a question without its answer. Any stale-token rejection is also worth an alert, because it means your nodes are pausing longer than the lease.

Question 5: "Who owns the answer when the client disconnects?"

If the model call uses HttpContext.RequestAborted, a client that disconnects cancels the generation. The answer is lost, and the retry pays for it again.

The shape of the answer: the turn runs on its own cancellation token, linked to things that should really stop it (the node shutting down, the lease being lost, a turn timeout), not to the HTTP request:

using var turnCts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(
    lifecycle.HardStop,   // node really stopping
    leaseLost.Token);     // another attempt took over
turnCts.CancelAfter(settings.TurnTimeout);
// model call + commit use turnCts.Token / CancellationToken.None, never RequestAborted
// full implementation in the complete project

Then the retry with the same clientMessageId (Question 1) gets the stored reply in milliseconds. These two ideas only work together.

Question 6: "What happens to in-flight answers during a deploy?"

Rolling deploys send SIGTERM, wait, then kill. Without a plan, every answer a node is generating at that moment is gone.

In my restart test, a hard kill kept 0 of 10 first requests, and the slowest user waited 18.6 seconds. With a graceful drain it kept 10 of 10, and the slowest waited 3.3 seconds.

The shape of the answer: IHostedLifecycleService.StoppingAsync runs before Kestrel stops, so the node can drain while it can still respond:

public async Task StoppingAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // 1. readiness -> 503, new turns -> 503 + Connection: close
    // 2. short delay so the load balancer notices
    // 3. wait for in-flight turns to commit, up to a drain timeout
    // 4. anything left becomes Interrupted (retryable), not stuck until lease expiry
    // full implementation in the complete project
}

Don't forget HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout: if it's shorter than your drain, the host cuts the drain short.

A bonus question: "Who owns retries to the model?"

The OpenAI SDK retries by itself. So does AddStandardResilienceHandler(). Stack them and one failure becomes several billed calls. Pick one layer, set the SDK's retries to zero if the handler owns them, and raise the default 10-second attempt timeout, which is too short for a long answer.

The checklist I use now

  • Every message carries a client-generated id, checked first in the shared store
  • One running turn per conversation, with a deliberate choice for the second tab
  • No correctness that depends on sticky sessions or in-memory locks
  • Leases plus fencing tokens on the commit
  • The turn's cancellation is detached from the HTTP request
  • Drain on SIGTERM, with a shutdown timeout longer than the drain
  • Exactly one retry layer for model calls

With all of it in place, 3 nodes handled the same load at 49.4 chats per second against 17.3 on one node, with 0 duplicates and 0 stale replies in my runs.

Get the complete version

The snippets above are the skeleton. The full project has the parts that took the longest to get right: the complete admission rules and store transactions, a lease heartbeat that cancels a model call the moment another node takes over, a reaper for turns left by crashed nodes, per-tenant token budgets, a bounded per-node gate that returns 503 instead of queueing forever, and a three-node docker-compose file as a starting point.

The complete, working, tested project (198 tests, Clean Architecture, .NET 10) and a step-by-step PDF guide are in Tech Skill Builder, $5/month for a very limited time only (normally $10). Grab it now before it goes back to $10: Join Tech Skill Builder

Which would you pick for the second tab: reject, queue, or cancel? I'm curious what others went with.

title: Understanding LLM Parameters and Context Memory for AI
description:
How Context Memory and Parameters Define the Intelligence of AI Models

Understanding the architectural foundations of Large Language Models (LLMs) is essential for students, educators, and technology partners who want to leverage artificial intelligence effectively. The interplay between context memory and parameters represents the two fundamental technical components that determine the information processing capacity and the underlying intelligence of these systems. By exploring these metrics, we can better understand how a model recalls immediate information versus how it utilizes its pre-trained knowledge base.

Key Highlights

  • Context memory acts as the active focus or short-term recall of an AI model during a single session.
  • Parameters represent the internal variables or weights that define the model's pre-trained knowledge and reasoning capabilities.
  • The number of parameters is a primary indicator of a model's complexity, often ranging from 7 billion to 70 billion or more.
  • Selecting the right AI tool requires balancing the need for long-document analysis (context) with sophisticated reasoning (parameters).

The Role of Context Memory in AI Interactions

Context memory, which is frequently referred to as the context window, is the maximum amount of data an AI model can process and remember during a single interaction. This capacity is typically measured in tokens, which are the basic units of text that a model reads. When a user interacts with an LLM, the context window dictates how much of the preceding conversation or uploaded data the model can keep in its active focus.

For technology partners evaluating models for business use cases, the context window is a critical factor. If a model has a small context window, it may forget the beginning of a long document or a lengthy conversation, leading to inconsistencies in its responses. A larger context window allows the system to hold more recent information, making it ideal for tasks such as analyzing long legal research documents, summarizing entire books, or maintaining context in complex coding projects.

Understanding LLM Parameters and Model Complexity

While context memory deals with immediate data, parameters are the internal variables or weights within a neural network that the model learns during its training phase. These parameters represent the stored knowledge and reasoning patterns the model has acquired. In the world of machine learning, the number of parameters is a primary indicator of a model's complexity and its ability to handle nuanced language tasks.

For example, models are often categorized by their parameter counts, such as 7 billion or 70 billion. A higher number of parameters generally suggests a more robust storage of knowledge and higher reasoning capabilities. Educators and students can think of parameters as the model's pre-trained intelligence. This is the information the model already knows before a user even types a single word into the prompt. It is the architectural depth that allows the model to understand grammar, facts, and logical relationships.

The Balance Between Short-Term Recall and Long-Term Intelligence

To choose the right AI tool, one must understand the relationship between these two metrics. Context memory can be viewed as the model's short-term recall, while parameters represent its long-term intelligence. A model might have high reasoning capabilities due to a massive parameter count but might be limited by a small context window, making it less effective for reading long files. Conversely, a model with a huge context window but few parameters might be able to read a lot of text but struggle to provide deep insights or complex analysis.

This balance is essential for various industry applications. In customer service, a model needs enough context to remember the user's current problem. In academic research, students need a model that combines a large context window for document review with enough parameters to synthesize that information into a coherent argument. At Bharath Lighthouse, we emphasize the importance of matching these technical specifications to the specific needs of the project or curriculum.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a token and a parameter?

A token is the unit used to measure the data within a context window, essentially representing the amount of text a model can process at one time. A parameter is an internal variable or weight within the neural network that the model learns during training to represent its knowledge base.

Why does the number of parameters matter for AI reasoning?

The number of parameters indicates the complexity and reasoning capabilities of a model. A model with more parameters, such as 70 billion, generally has a more sophisticated understanding of language and information than a model with fewer parameters.

How does context memory affect document analysis?

Context memory dictates how much of a document the model can hold in its active focus. If the document exceeds the context window, the model cannot process the entire file at once, which is why a larger context window is necessary for analyzing long reports or research papers.

Conclusion

Navigating the world of Artificial Intelligence requires a clear understanding of the technical pillars that drive performance. By distinguishing between context memory and parameters, students, educators, and technology partners can make informed decisions about which models best suit their educational and business goals. Whether you are focusing on high-level reasoning or large-scale data processing, these metrics will guide your AI journey. We invite institutions and partners to connect with Bharath Lighthouse to explore how these technologies can be integrated into your workflows.

title: Every test passed and the agent was still wrong
description:
The example is a fictional health plan's prior-authorization intake. A request comes in for an MRI, a CT scan or a spinal injection. The suite reads the request and the attached notes, finds the plan's policy for that service, checks each criterion against the notes and writes a packet for a nurse reviewer. It decides nothing. A person makes every decision, and the packet only has to be right about what the notes say.

I built it as the fifth worked example in a skill pack for coding assistants, and I tested it the way I'd been testing the others. Then I handed it to a reviewer that had written none of it, and the reviewer found three serious defects in a build where every test was green.

This post is about why that happened, what caught the defects in the end, and what I now think each kind of test can and can't show.

The test that said everything was fine

The pack has a test I call the removal run. Every safety rule the plan marks as met is written as a clause in the code. One example: "a rule set can't run until a named person approves it". Another: "provider text never reaches the packet". The removal run deletes each clause in turn and runs the test suite. If no test fails, the clause isn't really protected: you could delete it and nobody would notice.

On the prior-authorization build, the removal run deleted 36 clauses, one at a time. A test failed 36 times out of 36. Perfect score. By that measure, every control in the plan was held in place by a test.

What the reviewer found

The reviewer reported twenty findings. Three were high. Here they are.

First, the suite chose the service by word overlap. A request for "CT lumbar spine" shared enough words with the MRI policy that the suite applied the MRI policy to it, and a request for a lumbar spine injection got the same policy. In both cases the packet said the criteria were met. Wrong policy, confident packet.

Second, the static check that runs before a rule set is released skipped any market or month that had no rule at all. That is exactly the gap the check was supposed to catch: a market or a month where a service has no rule.

Third, the provider's free-text description of the service, and the sender's labels on attached documents, reached the packet, the intake record and the log. Anything typed into those fields, a patient's name included, went wherever the packet went.

All three were in the build. The removal run still passed 36 of 36. The run passed before the fixes and after them.

Why the green run meant less than it looked

The removal run answers one question: if this clause disappears, does some test notice? It doesn't ask whether the tests send the inputs that would break the clause in the first place.

The word-overlap defect is the clearest case. There was a clause that matched the service to a policy, and there were tests for it. Delete the clause and the tests failed. Nothing matched any more. But every test used a request whose wording matched its own policy. No test sent a CT request worded close to the MRI policy. The clause was protected against removal and wrong for a whole class of inputs at the same time.

This is the known limit of mutation testing, the older idea the removal run borrows from. A mutation score tells you how well the tests detect the changes you chose to make. It says nothing about inputs nobody wrote.

The tester that only changes one thing

What I added after that review is a tester whose whole job is near misses. I call it tester h in the pack. It reads the plan, the rule files and the function signatures. It never reads the existing tests. Then it writes twins of passing cases that differ in one field: a service code that is nearly right, a negation inside a clause, a name where a code belongs, a date one day past the last rule period.

Each twin asks one question. If a field changes in a way that should change the outcome, the outcome has to change, and if it changes in a way that shouldn't matter, the outcome has to stay where it was.

On the prior-authorization build it found three more defects, two of them high. A diagnosis code field printed whatever was typed into it, so a name typed there reached the packet. An unrecognized service code was printed the same way. The third was a negated claim: a note saying a treatment "is not supported after six weeks" was reported as confirming the six weeks.

The blind run

The obvious objection is that I wrote the near-miss tester's brief after seeing the review, so of course it found that kind of defect. To check that, I ran it blind: a fresh copy of the tester, with no access to the review, against a copy of the build with ten known defects put back in.

It caught seven of the ten, including all six high ones, and then it found eight more problems that nobody, me included, had listed anywhere. Four were high. A case ID was used as a folder name without checking, so an ID like "../../ESCAPE" wrote outside the cases folder. Placeholder names such as "TBD", "n/a" and "Unknown", and a role written out as "Medical Policy Owner", passed as the named approver on an override and on a rule-set release. The run-time gate checked only the release record's hash, so a record with no approver let cases run. And a negation inside a clause wasn't bound to what followed it: "and no foot drop" read as a red flag, and "did not complete 8 weeks" read as 8 weeks.

Every one of those now has a test that failed before the fix and passes after it. I keep the defects themselves as patches that put each one back, so I can check that a later version of the tester still catches them.

Across the other examples

I then ran the near-miss tester on the pack's other four worked examples, which had been through the same removal runs and review rounds. The task digest had 6 defects. The customs filing had 7. The insurance claims suite had 9. With the 3 and 8 in prior authorization, that's 33 defects across five example systems, each fixed with a test.

Some were small. Others matter a lot in a regulated workflow. In the customs filing, a job title was accepted as the approver's name. In the insurance claims suite, reworded prompt-injection lines got past the filter, and local phone numbers were stored.

None of these showed up as a failing test before the tester wrote its twins. Not one.

What each kind of test can and can't show

Here is how I read the three checks now, after five examples, two review rounds and one blind run that turned up eight problems nobody had written down.

A unit test shows the code does what its author expected on the inputs its author thought of. It can't show anything about inputs the author didn't think of, and on a rules system that is most of the risk.

The removal run shows each safety clause is held in place by at least one test. It can't show those tests reach the inputs that break the clause. A 100 percent removal score with three high defects standing is not a contradiction. It's what that score measures.

The near-miss tester shows how the decision behaves next to the cases you already have. It can't show anything far from them, and it is only as good as the fields it chooses to vary. It also isn't independent in any strong sense: the same model family wrote the build, the reviewer and the tester.

What changed in practice is the order. I now run the near-miss tester before I trust a green removal run. And a release report built on labels the builder wrote, or on a scorer that shares code with the step it measures, says self-consistent. It no longer says pass.

Where the approval check has to live

One more lesson. It's about the human in the loop. In every one of these examples a person approves before anything is paid, sent or released. Several of the defects above were not in the model at all. They were in the plumbing around the approval: a placeholder accepted as a name, a release record with no approver, a job title in the approver field.

A prompt can tell a model to wait for approval. It can't stop code from accepting "TBD" as an approver. Only code can. So the check belongs in code: an approval is a record with a real name and a date that isn't in the future, the gate refuses anything else, and each approval works once. In the insurance claims example a payment with no valid approval never reaches the payment system, and tests check that. Those tests passed long before the near-miss tester found the job-title gap in the customs example, which is the whole point of this post.

What this doesn't show

Every example here runs on fictional data. No run against a real health plan, insurer or customs broker is on record. One person built them, with one model family doing the building, reviewing and testing, so a defect that model family tends not to see may still be in there. The counts are small. And I wrote the near-miss tester's brief after the review that inspired it. So the blind run is the result to weigh.

The prior-authorization README says it directly: those defects are fixed and tested, and others like them may remain.

If you build agents that act on rules

Four things I'd do differently from the start:

  • Write near-miss cases for every key, threshold, scope field and selector the decision reads, one field at a time.
  • Have someone who didn't write the tests write them, from the plan and the rules rather than from the existing tests.
  • Treat a passing removal or mutation run as evidence that the controls exist. Whether they work is a separate question.
  • Put the approval check in code. Test it with bad approvers as well as missing ones: a placeholder, a job title, a future date.

I build and sell Agent Suite Builder, a skill pack for coding assistants that includes these five worked examples and the removal run and near-miss tester described here. The docs are free to read: design-upstrategy-az-llc.github.io/agent-suite-builder

title: Stop Trusting Your Cache Hit Rate. 7 Tests Show Why
description:
This article was originally published on the Actian blog.

In this post, you'll run seven tests against a semantic cache built on Actian VectorAI DB and measure how often a cache hit returns the wrong answer. You'll need Docker, Python 3.11 or 3.12, and uv. All the code is in the companion repo.

A semantic cache reuses an LLM response when a new query is similar enough to a stored one. Hit rate tells you how often that happens. It doesn't tell you whether the reused answer fits the new question. At a 0.80 similarity threshold, the test cache hit 79.2% of lookups, and 6.4% of those hits were wrong. Some of the wrong hits scored above 0.95.

The results at a glance

Test Failure mode Mitigation Result
1. Threshold sweep One threshold accepts too many wrong matches Calibrate against a 5% FPR target At 0.83, FPR was 4.8% and hit rate was 70.1% on held-out queries
2. Negation Negated questions score like paraphrases Check for negation differences Negated queries served fell from 98.7% to 4.0%, and the paraphrase rate stayed at 72.1%
3. Numbers and dates Changed values still match Require exact matches on numbers and date words Changed-value queries served fell from 100% to 0%, and the paraphrase rate stayed at 95.5%
4. Tenant and intent boundaries Matches cross partitions or intents MUST filters on tenant and predicted intent FPR fell to 4.7%, with a hit rate of 58.4%
5. Local verification Wrong hits pass the threshold and filters Check sampled hits with decider-0.8b FPR fell from 6.0% to 2.8% in a 100-hit sample, and the results are provisional
6. Query length Short queries produce more wrong hits Calibrate thresholds by query length FPR fell to 2.0%, with a hit rate of 64.2% on held-out queries
7. Stale answers Cached responses outlive their source data Mark stale entries and exclude them from lookup FPR fell from 24.9% to 11.4%, and the remainder needs refill or intent filtering

How the test cache works

The cache embeds each query, finds the closest stored question in VectorAI DB, and returns the stored response when the cosine similarity meets the threshold. Otherwise, the query goes to the model.

  • The cache stores 3,075 questions from Banking77, a public dataset of banking support queries labeled with 77 intents. That fits under the Community Edition's 5,000-vector limit.
  • Lookups use another 770 questions from the same dataset, embedded with sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
  • A wrong hit is one where the cached question has a different intent, belongs to another simulated tenant, or refers to a source that has changed.
  • The false-positive rate (FPR) is wrong hits divided by all hits, and the target is 5% or lower.
  • Thresholds are calibrated on one half of the lookup set and evaluated on the other half.

Tenants and source changes are simulated, and the negation and number pairs come from templates. The results show how each failure mode behaves under controlled conditions.

1. Set up the project

Clone the repo and move into the project folder.

git clone https://github.com/actian-devs/developer-content.git
cd developer-content/blog/semantic-cache-fp

Start VectorAI DB and install the dependencies.

docker-compose up -d

uv sync

Check that the container is up with docker ps before you run the tests. The first run downloads the dataset and embedding model, so it takes longer than later runs. Every script writes its measurements to the results/ directory.

2. Sweep the threshold

The sweep looks up all 770 questions at every threshold from 0.50 to 0.99 and records the hit rate and FPR at each step.

uv run python test1_threshold_sweep.py --threshold 0.80

At 0.80, the cache returned 39 wrong answers across 610 hits, an FPR of 6.4%. "Why was I unable to do a transfer?" matched "Why was I not able to complete my transfer?" at 0.921, even though Banking77 labels them declined_transfer and failed_transfer. Raising the threshold to 0.83 brought the FPR to 4.8% on held-out queries, and the hit rate fell to 70.1%.

Use 0.80 for the remaining tests to reproduce the article's numbers.

3. Test negation, numbers, and dates

Each test caches one question from a pair, asks the other, and checks whether the cache reuses the answer. Reworded questions with the same meaning check that good reuse still happens.

uv run python test2_negation.py --threshold 0.80
uv run python test3_numbers_dates.py --threshold 0.80

The cache served 74 of 75 negated questions (98.7%). "Should I not cancel my card?" matched "Should I cancel my card?" at 0.990. Negated pairs had a median similarity of 0.946, higher than the 0.936 median for true paraphrases, so no threshold up to 0.99 blocked 95% of negation errors. A check that rejects a match when only one query contains negation cut the served share to 4.0% and kept a paraphrase rate of 72.1%.

The cache also served all 38 changed-value queries. "Set my daily card limit to $2500" matched "Set my daily card limit to $250" at 0.962, and a charge on 21 June matched one on 21 July at 0.964. A threshold of 0.97 was needed to block 95% of them, which dropped the paraphrase rate from 95.5% to 13.6%. An exact-match check on numbers and date words blocked every changed value and kept the paraphrase rate at 95.5%.

Both checks are simple. The negation check can miss indirect changes in meaning, and the value check doesn't treat "fifty dollars" and "$50" as equal.

4. Enforce tenant and intent boundaries

This test spreads the cache across three simulated tenants, then repeats the lookups with VectorAI DB filters.

uv run python test4_partitions.py --threshold 0.80
Configuration FPR Hit rate
No filters 69.7% 79.2%
MUST filter on tenant 9.1% 61.4%
MUST filters on tenant and predicted intent 4.7% 58.4%
Tenant MUST plus top-two intents as SHOULD 7.9% 60.6%

Without filters, 409 of the 610 hits crossed tenant boundaries. A MUST filter on tenant removed every cross-tenant hit. The intent filter used a lightweight classifier that predicted the correct intent 88.4% of the time. Per-intent thresholds reached a 9.6% FPR, with only about five calibration questions per intent in this sample.

5. Verify hits with a local model

This test sends sampled hits to decider-0.8b, a small model that reads both questions and judges whether one answer serves both. It runs on a laptop, while larger models such as decider-4b need a GPU. Export the lookups first, then run the model on them.

uv run python test5_decider_verify.py \
  --threshold 0.80 \
  --export-hits data/test5_lookups.json

uv run --extra decider python test5_decider_verify.py \
  --threshold 0.80 \
  --model Mapika/decider-0.8b \
  --max-hits 100 \
  --hits-file data/test5_lookups.json

On an Apple Silicon M3 MacBook with a yes-probability cut-off of 0.5, the verifier caught four of the six wrong hits in a 100-hit sample. It also rejected 25 of 94 good hits (26.6%). Median latency was 106 ms per hit, with a 116 ms 95th percentile at batch size one. A cut-off of 0.3 rejected only two good hits and caught one wrong hit. With only six wrong hits in the sample, treat this as a preliminary result.

6. Compare short and long queries 

uv run python test6_query_length.py --threshold 0.80

Queries of eight words or fewer made up 43% of lookups and 27 of the 39 wrong hits. Their FPR was 9.4%, against 2.9% for queries of nine to eleven words and 4.6% for longer ones. Calibrated thresholds of 0.87 for short, 0.80 for medium, and 0.83 for long queries brought the FPR to 2.0% on held-out queries, with a hit rate of 64.2%.

7. Catch stale answers

Each Banking77 intent acts as a source, and the test changes 15 of the 77 sources after caching.

uv run python test7_stale_answers.py --threshold 0.80

Before invalidation, the FPR rose to 24.9%, with 113 hits returning the right intent and an outdated answer. One filtered set_payload call marked all 600 entries from the changed sources as stale, and a MUST NOT filter excluded them from lookups. The FPR fell to 11.4% with a 67.4% hit rate. The remaining errors matched a neighboring intent, so pair invalidation with a cache refill or intent filtering.

8. Build the results table 

uv run python make_table.py

These results depend on the embedding model, the Banking77 sample, and the experiment's definition of a wrong answer. Intent labels are an imperfect proxy for whether two questions can share a response.

Running a cache you can trust

  • Measure FPR on a labeled sample of your own traffic, sweep the threshold, and pick the lowest setting that meets your correctness target.
  • Report FPR beside hit rate on every dashboard, and use a stricter threshold for short queries.
  • Store tenant, intent, and source with every entry, and filter on them during the search.
  • Use a MUST NOT filter on a stale flag after a source changes.
  • Compare negation, amounts, and dates before serving a hit, and add local verification for high-stakes intents such as refunds and cancellations.

Wrapping up

Wrong hits concentrated in negated requests, changed amounts and dates, another tenant's data, and outdated policies. A threshold alone couldn't catch them. Set the threshold against a correctness target, partition the cache with VectorAI DB filters, and verify the hits you can't afford to get wrong.

What's next

  • Pull VectorAI DB Community Edition and run the same checks on a labeled sample of your own queries.
  • Join the Actian Discord community for help and discussion.
