title: How Attention Works: I Read All 24 Heads of a Tiny Language Model and Found the One That Watches the Main Character's Name
description:
Part 2 of ten. Each post is a short, plain-words tour of one lesson from e=mc², a free build-an-LLM-from-scratch course; the full lesson, notebook and numbers are on the site.

Attention is the part of a language model that lets each word look back at the words before it, and yesterday's tiny model is small enough that you can watch it happen. In Lesson 01 I trained a 5.9-million-parameter storyteller on a free Colab GPU. Today nothing gets trained. I open those same weights, switch on one flag that records who looked at whom, and read all 24 of its attention heads. One of them, it turns out, spends about 22% of its attention on the main character's name.

Momo and Ella, again

Momo the monkey is the model; his dials were set last lesson and stay put tonight. Ella the elephant is the teacher and the memory. She reads him the story, and she keeps a shelf of everything already said. Picture the story told in a circle: each word has a seat, and each word may look at the words that spoke before it, never at the ones still to come.

Attention is the looking.

A question, a card and a handover

Here is the whole idea. Inside one attention head, every word gets three short lists of numbers, 64 numbers each in this model.

The first list is a query: the question a word asks. When "He" comes up in a story, the question is roughly "who is he?"

The second is a key: the card a word holds up for every later word to see. "Momo" holds up a card that says, in effect, "I am a name."

The third is a value: what the word hands over if it gets picked.

Now suppose I am the word "He". I compare my question to every earlier word's card. The better the match, the higher the score. A step called softmax turns those scores into shares that add up to 100%, and I take the share-weighted blend of everyone's values. If most of my shares went to "Momo", most of what I carry forward came from "Momo".

Write down those shares for every word in a story and you get an attention map: a table of who looked at whom.

One honest note: nothing is asked in words. A query is 64 numbers made by a matrix multiplication, and "looking for a name" is a label I read into a head afterwards. Momo was only ever trained to guess the next word.

The triangle, and Ella's shelf

Momo must never peek at words after the one he is guessing. The causal mask enforces it: before the softmax, every score for a later word is set to minus infinity, so its share is exactly zero. Lay a whole story's map out and it is a lower triangle. The dark upper-right corner of every heatmap is the rule, not a decision the head made.

The mask also explains the KV cache, which is just Ella's shelf. Earlier words cannot see later ones, so an earlier word's key and value never change once computed. When Momo writes a story one token at a time, Ella files each token's key and value on the shelf, and the next token computes only its own and reads the rest. Writing 200 tokens costs 200 key-and-value computations instead of 20,100. In the notebook, the shelf's answer matches recomputing everything within 0.0000003. It is a speed trick, not a memory of the story: what Momo knows lives in his dials, not on the shelf.

Reading a real model's mind

The notebook copies the model from Lesson 01 and adds one flag. With the flag on, each block computes attention the long way and keeps the shares; with it off, it uses PyTorch's fast built-in routine as before. The two agree within 0.00002 in the raw output scores, and every row of every map sums to 1. That flag is the whole change:

def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(C, dim=2) # a query, key and value per token
 q, k, v = [t.view(B, T, self.n_head, C // self.n_head).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v)]
 if self.return_attn: # the only change from Lesson 01
 scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(k.size(-1))
 mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device))
 att = F.softmax(scores.masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf")), dim=-1)
 self.last_attn = att # (batch, 4 heads, T, T): who looked at whom
 y = att @ v
 else:
 y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)...

Then I plot the triangle, plot all 24 heads on one story, and measure every head over the 200 quiz stories Momo never trained on. A main character, by a deliberately crude rule, is the most frequent capitalised name in a story, mentioned at least twice; 159 of the 200 stories have one. For each head I add up how much attention the other words, after the first mention, send back to that name.

The numbers, honestly

  • 24 heads read: 6 blocks of 4 heads, all from the Lesson 01 weights. No training.
  • Even-spread baseline: 0.052. If a head spread its attention evenly, that is roughly how much would land on the name.
  • The winner, block 5, head 3 (L5H3): 0.221. About 22% of its attention on the main character's name, 4.3 times an even spread. L4H4 (0.199) and L6H2 (0.178) are close behind.
  • 17 of the 24 heads put less on the name than an even spread would.
  • Previous-token heads: 0 of 24. None puts more than half its attention there; the highest is L1H1 at 0.146. That was the disappointing result, and I am reporting it as is.
  • 8 to 20 seconds for the whole notebook on an Apple Silicon Mac; it also runs on a free Colab T4 or a plain CPU.

What it does not mean

Three limits, said plainly. L5H3 puts about 22% of its attention on the name, not all of it; this is a tendency, not a switch. Attention is where a head looks, not proof of what the model relies on; I did not switch any head off to see what breaks. And name position is not controlled: a name early in a story may draw attention partly for being early.

So no, this does not prove Momo understands who the hero is. It shows, with a real number from a real model, where one of his 24 ways of looking tends to go. That is a smaller claim and a truer one, and it is the first step toward explaining the 61-word story Momo recited in Lesson 01 and could not explain.

Why this is the lesson that matters

Every large model you have heard of is this mechanism with more heads, more blocks and more zeros. If you have ever wondered how a chat model keeps track of a character across a paragraph, you now have the picture: a circle of words looking back, and an elephant with a shelf.

The full lesson has the glossary table, the heatmaps of all 24 heads, a clickable toy widget, the ranked table of every head and the notebook that reproduces the 0.221.

Want to actually build it?

This post is the postcard. The lesson is the trip. Lesson 02 of e=mc² on theaivibe.org walks you through every piece with widgets you can poke, a notebook that runs on a free GPU in minutes, and the honest numbers at every step. No account, no paywall, nothing to install.

  • Start here: https://theaivibe.org/emc2/how-attention-works-tiny-storyteller-attention-maps
  • The whole ten-lesson journey: https://theaivibe.org/emc2

Tomorrow: Momo recited a 61-word story word for word in Lesson 01, so I train the same recipe at four sizes and watch for the moment memorising begins.

title: The Assistant That Never Learned
description:
Part 1: The Problem

The following scenario is exaggerated, but typical.

A mid-sized software company introduces an AI assistant in its helpdesk. The setup is quick to build: a ticket comes in, a prompt is assembled with context from the knowledge base, the LLM writes a draft reply, and the agent reviews and sends it. The first weeks are a success. New hires work faster and the queue shrinks. This matches the research: in a large field study with more than 5,000 support agents, workers with AI assistance resolved 14% more issues per hour on average, and novices 34% more.

A few months later the mood shifts. The assistant keeps making the same mistakes:

  • Bank chargebacks end up in the regular refund queue.
  • The tone with angry customers is off, and every reply gets rewritten.
  • After a pricing change, it quotes the old terms for weeks.

Agents correct the same things every day, but the system never notices. Every correction is lost.

flowchart LR
  T["Ticket"] --> P["Prompt + context"] --> L["LLM: reply text"] --> A["Agent corrects"] --> K["Customer"]
  A -.->|"correction is lost"| X["🗑️"]

This is the core problem of many agentic systems. They automate an existing workflow, and that is where the design ends. The LLM is a text generator at the end of a pipeline, a thin wrapper. It never finds out whether its text was any good. Yet the most valuable knowledge in a helpdesk lives exactly in the corrections made by experienced agents.

Part 2: Finding the Solution

First question: Where would the system learn from?

Retraining the model is not an option for most teams: too expensive, too slow, too risky. A different route comes from an approach called Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023). The model stays unchanged. After each attempt, a reflection step looks at the outcome and puts into words what went wrong. The next time, this "lesson" is added to the model's context. Learning happens in the prompt, not in the weights.

Applied to the helpdesk: the evaluation signal is the agents' corrections and the customers' reactions. The reflection step derives a rule from them, for example "When the customer mentions a chargeback through their bank, treat it as a chargeback." The rule is stored and supplied with matching tickets.

Second question: What exactly was wrong?

The first attempt fails on something mundane. The system compares the draft with what the agent actually sent and sees only that the text was changed. Was the category wrong? The cited policy? Just the tone? A block of text cannot answer that. The reflection step guesses, and a guessed lesson does more harm than good.

This leads to the design decision that carries everything else: the LLM's output becomes structured. Instead of a reply text, it returns an object with separate parts, and the agent can confirm or correct each part individually.

erDiagram
  OUTPUT ||--o{ FEEDBACK : "is rated by"
  FEEDBACK }o--o{ LESSON : "justifies"
  OUTPUT }o--o{ LESSON : "applies"
  OUTPUT {
    string category
    float confidence
    string evidence
    string reply_draft
    string applied_lessons
  }
  FEEDBACK {
    string field
    string verdict
    string corrected_to
    bool reopened
  }
  LESSON {
    string rule
    string scope
    string status
    string evidence_tickets
  }

Now it is clear: the category was wrong, and the draft was only adjusted stylistically. And applied_lessons makes it possible to measure later whether a lesson actually helps.

Structure has a cost. Strict format constraints can lower answer quality when the model has to weigh complex tradeoffs. So the model reasons first and fills in the fields afterwards. The lessons themselves stay short, readable sentences. Structure belongs at the interfaces, not in every detail.

Third question: Who decides what is right?

The obvious idea is to let a second LLM do the grading. The research here is sobering: LLM self-correction works reliably when there is dependable external feedback, and there is little solid evidence that it works without it. Reflexion's own successes relied on clear signals such as unit tests.

For the helpdesk this means: at first, humans grade, as a by-product of their normal work and without extra effort. Hard outcome signals come on top: Was the ticket reopened? Did the customer ask a follow-up question? AI grading comes later, and only where criteria are checkable, for example whether a reply contradicts the current policy.

Fourth question: What if the system learns the wrong thing?

A memory that accepts lessons unchecked is dangerous. Wrong entries get repeated and reinforce themselves. There is also a security problem: in a helpdesk, the customer writes the input. Studies show that agent memories can be manipulated through cleverly worded queries alone.

The answer is a lifecycle with checkpoints, as with any other production artifact:

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Proposed: reflection derives rule
  Proposed --> Verified: several evidence tickets, regression test
  Proposed --> Rejected
  Verified --> Trial: team lead approves
  Trial --> Active: measurably better
  Trial --> Rejected: no effect
  Active --> Archived: outdated

Part 3: The Solution

The architecture

Put the answers together and the wrapper becomes a closed loop:

flowchart LR
  T["Ticket"] --> A["LLM: structured proposal"]
  A --> H["Agent confirms or corrects per field"]
  H --> K["Customer"]
  H --> F["Feedback"]
  K -->|"reopen, follow-up"| F
  F --> R["Reflection: propose rule"]
  R --> G{"Check + approval"}
  G --> M[("Lessons")]
  M -->|"matching rules in context"| A

At runtime, two paths run separately: the fast path that answers the ticket, and the slow path that learns after the ticket is closed. Lessons are only ever written after the fact, never during a live conversation.

sequenceDiagram
  participant T as Ticket system
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant M as Lesson store
  participant L as LLM
  participant A as Agent
  T->>O: new ticket
  O->>M: retrieve lessons (category, embedding)
  M-->>O: top-k active lessons
  O->>L: prompt + KB context + lessons
  L-->>O: structured proposal (JSON)
  O->>O: schema validation, policy check
  O->>A: proposal in UI
  A-->>O: field verdicts + sent reply
  Note over O,M: after ticket closure (async)
  O->>L: reflection on diff between proposal and outcome
  L-->>O: lesson candidate
  O->>M: store as "proposed"

The data structures

1. The proposal the LLM returns. The reasoning field comes first, so the model thinks before it commits to a category.

{
  "schema_version": "1.2",
  "ticket_id": "T-48213",
  "reasoning": "Customer mentions the bank reversed the payment; this is not a refund request.",
  "triage": {
    "category": "billing.chargeback",
    "confidence": 0.81,
    "escalate": false
  },
  "evidence": [
    { "source": "kb-1187", "claim": "Chargebacks are handled by the payments team" }
  ],
  "reply_draft": "Thanks for letting us know. We have forwarded the chargeback to ...",
  "applied_lessons": ["L-0231"],
  "meta": { "model": "model-x-2026-09", "prompt_version": "p-14" }
}

2. The feedback the agent gives. Captured per field in the UI, with one click per field instead of free-text comments.

{
  "ticket_id": "T-48213",
  "output_schema_version": "1.2",
  "field_feedback": [
    { "field": "triage.category", "verdict": "accepted" },
    { "field": "reply_draft", "verdict": "edited", "reason": "tone" }
  ],
  "outcome": { "reopened_within_7d": false, "follow_up_question": false }
}

3. The lesson the reflection step proposes. A single rule in WHEN–THEN form, with scope and evidence, so it can be reviewed, tested and withdrawn.

{
  "id": "L-0502",
  "status": "proposed",
  "scope": { "category": "billing.*" },
  "rule": "WHEN the customer says their bank reversed a payment THEN classify as billing.chargeback, not billing.refund_request.",
  "evidence_tickets": ["T-47110", "T-47833", "T-48021"],
  "created_from": "field_feedback:triage.category",
  "approved_by": null,
  "expires_after_days": 180
}

The reflection step itself is just another LLM call with a narrow job:

You are reviewing a closed support ticket.
Input: the structured proposal, the agent's field verdicts, the final reply, the outcome.
Task: If a field was corrected, write ONE rule in the form
"WHEN <observable situation> THEN <correct action>".
- Only use facts visible in this ticket.
- Do not include customer names or personal data.
- If the correction was only stylistic or you cannot tell why, return no rule.
Output: JSON matching the Lesson schema, status "proposed".

A few implementation details make the difference in practice:

  • Validate everything that comes back. Proposals are checked against the schema. Lesson candidates are rejected if they contain personal data or contradict an active rule.
  • Promote by evidence, not by single cases. A candidate only moves forward when several independent tickets support it.
  • Version everything. Model, prompt, schema and lesson versions are logged with each proposal, otherwise no improvement can be attributed to a cause.
  • Measure each lesson. Because applied_lessons is logged, you can compare tickets with and without a lesson during the trial phase.

Back to the example

The chargeback tickets get corrected three times, the reflection step proposes a rule, the team lead approves it, and from then on these cases land in the right queue. After the pricing change, the data shows a sudden spike in corrections in one category. That is no longer a gut feeling in a team meeting but a number on a dashboard.

That is the real payoff of structure. It does not just enable learning, it makes the system measurable:

  • Where is the assistant wrong? Error rate per category instead of anecdotes.
  • Where is knowledge missing? If a proposal cites no source, an article is missing from the knowledge base.
  • Where may it answer on its own? Automate only where the acceptance rate proves it.
  • What breaks with the next update? Every corrected ticket becomes a test case.

This works at scale. ByteDance does it for code reviews: their system automatically measures whether flagged code is actually changed afterwards, and uses that to weed out weak rules. The feedback signal emerges as a by-product of the normal workflow, which is exactly what per-field corrections do in the helpdesk.

The path there does not have to be a big project:

flowchart LR
  S1["1. Structure output, measure baseline"] --> S2["2. Capture per-field corrections"] --> S3["3. Analyze error patterns"] --> S4["4. Lessons with approval"] --> S5["5. Verify impact in trial"] --> S6["6. Automate selectively"]

Steps 1 and 2 pay off even if you never reach step 6. The costly thing about a wrapper is not what it gets wrong, but that nobody can see what it gets wrong.

What has to be said honestly

Not every workflow needs a learning loop. It costs development time, extra model calls and maintenance. Helpdesk feedback is also fuzzy: not every edit by an agent means an error. And most of the evidence for Reflexion comes from test environments with clean signals, not from real helpdesks. So the approach is not a sure thing. But a system built from the start to take in feedback has a future. One that only passes text through is as good on its last day as on its first.

Further reading

  • Shinn et al., Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (2023): https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366
  • Brynjolfsson, Li, Raymond, Generative AI at Work: https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161
  • Kamoi et al., When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? (2024): https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01297
  • Sun et al., BitsAI-CR: Automated Code Review via LLM in Practice: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15134
  • Dong et al., Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.03704

title: RAG's Trust Problem: Citations, Memory, and Benchmarks Don't Add Up Quite Right
description:
This digest covers RAG/GraphRAG developments from 2026-11-09 through 2026-11-16: a dense week on arXiv and Hugging Face Daily Papers, a seven-post knowledge-layer push from Neo4j, and one methodology post each from LangChain and LlamaIndex.

🔥 Highlights

  1. A 45-Minute Answer to One Question — graph-grounded context turns hours of log-diving into one query.

  2. Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation — up to 15.7% of RAG citations don't actually trace to retrieval.

  3. MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System — new state of the art on LoCoMo and LongMemEval agent-memory benchmarks.

  4. Introducing ParseBench-2 — a severity-weighted benchmark exposes where document parsers break RAG upstream.

  5. DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory — argues agent memory's real bottleneck is writing, not retrieving.

arXiv

  • RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG — 2026-11-13 — Jointly optimizes discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding parameters for the query-rewriting stage of RAG instead of tuning them separately and statically. Query rewriting is usually the brittle, hand-tuned piece of production RAG pipelines, so a joint optimization approach is directly applicable to teams fighting noisy retrieval feedback on complex queries.

  • Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution — 2026-11-12 — Introduces MAPE, which evolves whole memory-management programs (not just hyperparameters) via an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop, gaining up to 12% absolute accuracy over hand-designed baselines on LoCoMo/LongMemEval at a third of the serving cost. Suggests automating memory-architecture search rather than hand-crafting write/read/consolidation policies.

  • RMIT-ADM+S at TREC RAG 2026: Research Agents, Retriever Ablations, and Open-Weight Replication — 2026-11-12 — A TREC 2026 RAG track system paper where six of seven submitted runs beat the track median; writer-model choice and adjacent-chunk expansion turned out to be bigger quality levers than retriever choice alone. Useful competitive-benchmark evidence on where to actually spend engineering effort in a RAG pipeline.

  • AutoOntic: Automatic Ontology Induction from Text for Knowledge Graph Construction — 2026-11-11 — Fixes a core GraphRAG weakness: schema-free LLM extraction produces flat graphs with no type hierarchy or domain/range constraints. AutoOntic canonicalizes types and relations and mines hierarchy/constraints automatically — a usable post-processing stage to upgrade flat extracted graphs before GraphRAG retrieval.

  • Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-11-12 — Uses counterfactual substitution (swap a retrieved fact for a false variant and re-query) to measure how often RAG citations actually trace to parametric memory rather than retrieved context: 1.2%–15.7% of citable claims across model families. A hard number on a faithfulness problem that citation-format checks alone won't catch.

  • HiddenPathQA: A Benchmark for Knowledge Graph Question Answering When Questions Hide Their Paths — 2026-11-09 — Shows most KGQA benchmarks leak the gold reasoning path in the question's surface tokens, unlike real multi-hop questions that compress chains into a phrase naming no relation. Important for honestly evaluating GraphRAG/KGQA systems — strong scores on existing benchmarks may just reflect surface pattern-matching.

  • DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory — 2026-11-11 — Challenges the "memory is just a retrieval problem" assumption: on their ENT-310 benchmark, a vanilla RAG reader already matches strong memory systems on recall since retention/currency are near-saturated. Argues the real bottleneck is write-time contradiction/entity-collision handling — a useful reframing for teams assuming better retrieval alone fixes memory.

  • MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents — 2026-11-11 — Notes that the memories most semantically relevant to an agent's state aren't necessarily those that most improve its next action, proposing selection by estimated decision utility instead of embedding-similarity relevance. A concrete, actionable idea: rank agent memory by downstream action impact, not query-memory similarity.

  • OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-11-10 — Argues RAG's context-length bottleneck is a modality problem, not an information-density one: rendering a document page as an image and using a vision encoder preserves far more detail per token than text compression. A concrete compression-fidelity tradeoff alternative to summarization for teams hitting context-window costs.

  • Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation — 2026-11-09 — Shows an agent can match a reference answer even when its visible memory history doesn't actually determine it (a lucky guess), and designs a controlled protocol with byte-identical contexts but different correct answers to detect this. A methodological warning: matching the reference answer is not proof memory was sufficient or used correctly.

  • MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System — 2026-11-09 — A multi-agent memory architecture reporting 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, +14.3 points over the strongest baseline, leading on 4 of 5 QA memory benchmarks. Also surfaced on Hugging Face's Nov 16 Daily Papers listing. A strong reference point for benchmarking agent-memory accuracy/cost tradeoffs.

  • Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs — 2026-11-11 — An engineering study of multimodal RAG on consumer GPUs (e.g., Tesla T4), quantifying VRAM tradeoffs between quantized weights and co-located vector indices/KV caches. Directly useful for self-hosting RAG on cheaper hardware instead of cloud GPUs.

Hugging Face Daily Papers

  • HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents — 2026-11-09 — A multimodal agent memory framework combining "horizontal" memory expansion with "vertical" evidence composition, targeting the failure mode where semantic retrieval over compressed memories misses relevant evidence or can't match heterogeneous query needs. A useful design pattern for multimodal memory/RAG systems over long interaction histories.

  • Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents — 2026-11-10 — Identifies "memory-induced degradation," where agents do worse with memory than without, because distilled lessons lose the trajectory evidence that justified them, causing misapplication. The fix — linking each stored lesson back to its originating evidence — is a concrete provenance-tracking pattern for episodic agent memory.

  • MEM-SQL: Memory-Empowered Text-to-SQL — 2026-11-13 — Points out that Text-to-SQL benchmarks evaluate questions independently, ignoring session reuse of joins/calculations from earlier queries, and introduces HARE, a history-aware benchmark (1,600 requests, 823 verified queries) to measure this. Relevant for memory-augmented structured-query agents, where "memory" means reusable query fragments rather than text passages.

Anthropic Engineering Blog

Nothing relevant this period — the one post in the window ("Building strong safety evaluations," 2026-11-13) is about general safety-evaluation methodology, not retrieval or RAG evaluation.

LangChain Blog

  • What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents — 2026-11-09 — Lays out an eval-driven workflow — define what "good" means, write evals before building, then compare experiments as the agent changes — through a docs-agent example that catches a regression where a broad tool description silently overrode existing behavior. The methodology (baseline experiments, per-example review instead of trusting averages, deterministic checks vs. LLM judges, overfitting guards) transfers directly to evaluating retrieval and RAG pipelines, even though the write-up is LangSmith-flavored.

LlamaIndex Blog

  • Introducing ParseBench-2 — 2026-11-12 — A new, expanded document-parsing benchmark (4.3k cases, more than double the original ParseBench) evaluating six dimensions: text, tables, formatting, charts, visual grounding, and forms, with severity-weighted scoring across 330+ injected error types. Parsing fidelity is the upstream bottleneck for indexing quality, and this gives a concrete, severity-aware way to evaluate parsers — flagging charts and visual grounding as where top parsers diverge most — before documents even reach the retrieval layer.

Neo4j Blog

  • Meet Relate by Neo4j: An Embedded Database for AI Agents — 2026-11-11 — An open-source, embedded graph database written in Rust (libraries for Python, JS, Rust, Java, Go, Swift, plus a CLI and WASM build) with full Cypher/GQL support and no server required. A single Cypher query can combine graph traversal with vector and full-text search in one statement, framing agent memory as connected facts rather than loose text blobs — a concrete alternative to stitching together separate vector and graph stores.

  • A 45-Minute Answer to One Question — 2026-11-13 — A case study on Adyen's "Architect" system, which replaces ad hoc incident investigation with three Neo4j graphs — service, code, and infrastructure — queried jointly through a composite database. A precomputed, verified graph lets an agent answer a dependency question with one Cypher query instead of reading thousands of lines of logs, cutting a 45-minute manual investigation to seconds.

  • Build a Knowledge Layer: Give Your AI Agents the Shared Context to Succeed — 2026-11-10 — Opening post of a series defining a "knowledge layer" as three components: ontologies, data (virtual graphs connecting the ontology to live systems without migration), and memory. It's intro-level, but it's the conceptual frame the rest of the series — and GraphRAG system design generally — builds on.

  • Build a Knowledge Layer: Map Your Data with an Ontology — 2026-11-10 — Describes a two-level ontology-as-a-graph pattern where a generic RELATES edge stores the real relationship name as a property, plus agent tools (get_schema_help, ontology_guided_query) that let an agent discover schema instead of baking every label into the system prompt. A reusable, maintainable schema-discovery layer that keeps GraphRAG ontologies from going stale or bloating prompts.

  • Build a Knowledge Layer: Turn Your Existing Data into Context — 2026-11-10 — Shows two graph-construction paths: a Virtual Graph that models a graph on top of existing warehouse tables and translates Cypher into SQL in-place, and Document Intelligence, which extracts an entity/relationship graph from unstructured documents via prompts with no code. Draws a clean contrast — plain vector similarity vs. a graph that lets an agent ask exact questions — for structured/semi-structured enterprise data.

  • Build a Knowledge Layer: Connect Your Data Sources with a Composite Database — 2026-11-10 — Details Neo4j's composite database pattern for querying multiple independently-owned graphs through one connection without copying data, plus a "shadow database" workaround for entity resolution across graphs that can't hold direct cross-constituent relationships. A useful pattern for multi-source GraphRAG where source systems must stay decoupled but still need to be linked.

  • Build a Knowledge Layer: Ground Decisions in Precedent — 2026-11-10 — Implements the "memory" piece as a context graph where precedent is defined structurally ("two decisions are comparable when they fail the same policy rule") rather than by embedding similarity, explicitly rejected as less predictable. A concrete example of agentic retrieval over an agent's own decision history as a deterministic alternative to vector-based agent memory.

Simon Willison

Nothing relevant this period — none of the week's posts substantively covered retrieval, RAG, reranking, embeddings, knowledge graphs, or agent memory.

Latent Space

Nothing relevant this period — the week's archive covered industry news and interviews with no substantive retrieval/RAG/knowledge-graph/agent-memory content.

Interconnects

Nothing relevant this period — the one post in the window covered open-model industry/policy dynamics, not retrieval or memory systems.

Through-line

Three independent threads keep landing on the same conclusion this week: trust your retrieval and memory systems less than their accuracy numbers suggest. "Cited but Unused" finds RAG citations that don't trace to retrieval; "Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories" finds agents that get the right answer for the wrong reason; "DISCERN" finds that near-saturated recall hides a write-time contradiction problem; and HiddenPathQA finds KGQA benchmarks that leak their own answers. Meanwhile Neo4j's seven-post push and papers like AutoOntic make the opposite-but-complementary case: when you replace embedding similarity with an explicit, queryable graph — an ontology, a decision-precedent graph, a service-dependency graph — you get deterministic, auditable retrieval instead of a probabilistic guess. The week's message for anyone running RAG or GraphRAG in production: measure faithfulness and provenance directly, don't just trust the benchmark score, and reach for structure wherever the domain allows it.

What's catching your eye in retrieval and memory research this week? Drop a comment below.

title: Your AI agent's public URL is an open wallet
description:
You build an agent that answers questions, summarises documents or triages tickets. A Telegram bot, a CRM or a webhook has to call it, so it gets a public HTTPS URL. Behind that URL sits a paid model.

The URL is not a secret. It ends up in config files, logs, screenshots and chat threads. Anyone who has it can call your agent, and every call that reaches your code can spend your model budget. Nothing goes down and nothing looks wrong; the bill just grows. Call it denial of wallet.

Three ways people lock it down

1. Write the check into every agent. Read a header, compare it with a secret, return 401. It works, and it is yours to write, test and keep correct in every agent you ever deploy. One forgotten route leaves one agent open. Changing the shared secret means redeploying every caller at once.

2. Put a proxy or gateway in front. A reverse proxy with basic auth, an OAuth proxy, an API gateway. One place to enforce the rule, but also one more service to deploy, patch and pay for, and often one shared credential for everyone who calls through it.

3. Refuse the call at the edge. The platform checks a token before the request reaches your agent. There is no code in the agent and no extra service. This is what we built, and the rest of this post shows how it works.

How per-agent tokens work

Each agent gets its own access tokens. They belong to one agent and open only that agent's public URL.

  1. Open the agent, go to Settings and find Access tokens.
  2. Choose Generate agent token, name it after the caller (telegram-bot) and pick how long it stays valid: 7, 30 or 90 days, or no expiry.
  3. Copy the token. It starts with uagt_live_ and is shown once; we keep only a fingerprint of it.
  4. Give it to that one caller. The caller sends it in the Authorization header.

A request without a valid token for this agent gets 401 Unauthorized and never reaches your code or your model. A token made for another agent, a revoked or expired token, and your account's API key are all refused the same way.

Because every caller has its own token, you can revoke one without touching the others. Revoke the Telegram bot's token and your CRM keeps working. If a token leaks, it opens that one agent only, and revoking it takes effect right away. An agent can hold up to 10 active tokens.

Two things to know. From the first token on, the agent stays closed: letting your last token expire does not reopen it, so a forgotten expiry date never exposes the agent by accident. And give existing callers their token before you generate the first one on a live agent, or they will start getting 401.

Calling an agent with its token

The URL and the /ask route below are placeholders for your own agent.

# No token: refused at the edge
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST \
  https://agent-my-bot-12345.uagents8.io/ask
# 401

# With the token made for this agent
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "Summarise the open tickets"}' \
  https://agent-my-bot-12345.uagents8.io/ask
# 200

import os

import requests

AGENT_URL = "https://agent-my-bot-12345.uagents8.io"
AGENT_TOKEN = os.environ["AGENT_TOKEN"]  # keep it in an environment variable

resp = requests.post(
    f"{AGENT_URL}/ask",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {AGENT_TOKEN}"},
    json={"question": "Summarise the open tickets"},
    timeout=30,
)
if resp.status_code == 401:
    raise RuntimeError("Token missing, expired or revoked for this agent")
resp.raise_for_status()
print(resp.json())

Your agent checks nothing itself. It only receives requests that already passed.

Two layers: an address list and a token

A token proves the caller knows a secret. An address list proves where the call comes from. On the Scale plan you can use both on the same agent.

Turn on Restrict access by IP address in the agent's configuration and give it up to 10 IPv4 addresses or ranges (for example your office and one client's servers). Today the switch is in the dashboard and the list itself is set through the API. Then generate a token for each caller, as above.

Now a call has to pass two independent checks before it reaches your code: it must come from a listed address, and it must carry a valid token for this agent.

  • A token that leaks into a log or a screenshot is useless from any other network: the call gets 403, even with the valid token.
  • A machine inside the listed network still gets 401 without a token.
  • Both checks run at the edge, so a refused call spends none of your model budget.

Tokens are on every plan; the address list is on Scale. For most agents a token per caller is the right first step, and the address list is the second one when the callers sit behind fixed addresses.

When to add more layers

Tokens answer "who may call this agent?". Other controls answer different questions.

  • A private agent has no public URL at all. If only your other agents call it (an internal worker, a tool behind a front agent), make it private. They reach it by name, and nothing outside the platform can. It needs no token.
  • A request-rate limit applies to each agent. The default is 120 requests a minute, and you can set it between 10 and 1,000. A caller over the limit gets 429 and can try again a minute later. It puts a ceiling on how fast anyone can drive calls into an agent.
  • The address list on Scale, described above, when a fixed set of addresses is the real boundary.

A sensible default for a production agent that a service calls: one token per caller, plus the rate limit. Add the address list when a fixed set of addresses is the real boundary.

What this does and does not claim

Endpoint authentication is not new, and plenty of platforms let you build it. Among the three hosts we compared against (Railway, Render and Fly.io; their own pages re-read on 14 November 2026), we did not find tokens per agent, for machine callers, on every plan, with no code to write. Railway's built-in gate for public domains is a human login on its Enterprise tier. Render documents a reverse proxy you deploy yourself. Fly.io documents private networking and leaves checks on a public app to your own code. The sources and dates are on our comparison pages, and if one of them changes, so does this paragraph.

What tokens are not: they identify a caller, not a person; a token opens every public route of its agent, not a subset; and before you generate the first one, the agent answers anyone who knows its URL.

Try it

Every plan includes access tokens, from Builder at €19 a month (excl. VAT). Make an agent, generate a token, and run the two curl lines above against it: uagents8.com. Launch code LAUNCH30 takes 30% off the first three months on Builder or Growth until 30 November. The full guide is in the docs.

title: Build Scalable Android Cloud Automation: Redroid + ADB + Python From Scratch
description:
Scaling Android Automation with Cloud Phones, Redroid and ADB

Writing an Android automation script for a single device is usually straightforward. As the number of devices grows, problems begin to accumulate. Test devices are occupied, app versions differ, scripts disconnect midway, and failures leave no diagnostic evidence. Even a simple health check can become difficult to reproduce.

Cloud phones centralize Android runtime environments on servers, providing a foundation for continuous operation, consistent configuration, and batch scheduling. Making effective use of these capabilities requires understanding how Android runs, how the control connection is established, and how scripts determine whether a task has completed.

This article starts with the architecture, deploys Redroid with Docker, and then uses ADB and Python for single-device checks, concurrent checks across multiple devices, screenshot archiving, and diagnostic collection. It concludes by outlining the integration boundaries to preserve when connecting to a provider's OpenAPI.

The lab uses a Linux host, an Android 12 image, and Python 3.10 or later. Run the deployment scripts on the server. Automation scripts can run either on the server or locally through SSH forwarding. The login example requires your own test app and replacement control IDs. The provider API example defines an explicit data contract. A real integration requires adapting authentication and fields to the provider.

1 What Cloud Phones and Local Emulators Address

Consider Runtime Location and Processor Architecture Separately

A “cloud phone” describes where an Android runtime is deployed and delivered. Users access a remote instance from a computer, phone, or browser, while computation, app processes, and primary data remain on the server.

An “emulator” describes a category of technologies for implementing an Android runtime. Modern Android Emulator installations can use hardware virtualization acceleration. When the image architecture matches the host architecture, many instructions can execute directly on the host CPU.

You can break the selection process into three questions.

Question Common options Main implications
Where does Android run? Local computer, remote server Resource ownership, remote access, and operations
How is Android isolated? Virtual machine, container, remote physical device Kernel boundaries, resource overhead, and failure scope
How are instruction sets matched? ARM64, x86_64, with translation where needed Native library compatibility and execution overhead

For example, an ARM64 server can run an ARM64 Android environment, and an x86_64 server can also host cloud Android instances. Redroid supports both host architectures. For apps with native libraries, also check the ABIs included in the APK against the image's supported ABIs.


Evaluate performance using the target app, measuring startup time, time per task, peak memory usage, and success rates over extended runs. GPU rendering mode, video encoding, disk I/O, and host load all affect results. Report performance overhead and instance density together with the test conditions.

Continuous Operation Depends on Server-Side State

When a remote Android instance is running continuously, closing the local viewing window usually only disconnects the interactive session. The app remains subject to server resources, Android process management, network connectivity, and the provider's operating policies.

It is also important to distinguish the app process from the automation script. The app runs in the cloud, while a local Python script sends actions through ADB. If the local computer shuts down, subsequent script commands stop as well. Deploy tasks that need continuous execution to an execution node that stays online.

2 Understanding the Cloud Phone Pipeline Through a Single Click

A remote click passes through input transport, Android event handling, screen rendering, and video delivery. Automation also adds device connection, state verification, and result storage.

The pipeline flow:

  • Local user sends touch/keyboard events to remote access service
  • Input is forwarded to the Android instance
  • Android renders the screen and encodes video stream back to user
  • Python automation worker sends ADB & UI control commands to Android
  • Worker writes task status and logs to storage
  • Scheduler manages container/VM lifecycle, creates/restarts instances, assigns tasks to workers

This pipeline involves four categories of capabilities.

  • Compute resources: CPU, memory, storage, GPU, rendering and encoding resources.
  • Android runtime: Boot system, isolate instances, run apps. Virtual machines have independent kernels; containers share the host kernel. Resource density needs load testing.
  • Remote interaction services: Forward input and return video output. Encoding format, frame rate, resolution and network latency impact interaction experience.
  • Management & scheduling services: Instance lifecycle, task assignment, health checks, log and artifact archiving.

Video latency affects manual operation. For UI automation, do not rely on fixed sleep timers. Write assertions based on page state, since waiting time is determined by page loading speed, device load and control connection quality.

This lab uses Redroid for the Android runtime and scrcpy to view and control the screen. A browser console, tenant permissions, WebRTC gateway and billing system require extra implementation.

3 Deploying Your First Redroid Instance on a Linux Server

Check the Host Requirements First

Redroid runs on the Linux host kernel. Prepare a Linux host where you can manage kernel modules and run privileged containers, and install Docker Engine. For learning, you can start with 4 CPU cores, 8 GB of RAM, and an SSD. Determine actual capacity through load tests.

Redroid's kernel requirements include Binder, binderfs, ashmem or memfd, and corresponding memory allocation capabilities. The official docs also require a 4 KB page size. Verify these ahead of time, especially on ARM cloud servers. Docker Desktop’s underlying Linux VM must satisfy the same requirements.

Run these checks on your server:

uname -m
uname -r
getconf PAGE_SIZE
docker version

# Load the Binder driver
sudo modprobe binder_linux devices="binder,hwbinder,vndbinder"

# Check binderfs support
grep -w binder /proc/filesystems

If you get Module binder_linux not found, install the matching kernel modules extra package on Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y "linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r)"
sudo modprobe binder_linux devices="binder,hwbinder,vndbinder"

Package names differ for cloud-customized kernels. Follow Redroid official deployment docs for your distribution. Kernel version alone is not enough to guarantee Android image compatibility.

Create the Container and Persist Its Data

Create a lab directory, save this as start-phone.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

PHONE_NAME="cloudphone-01"
PHONE_PORT="15555"
PHONE_IMAGE="redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest"
PHONE_DATA_DIR="${PWD}/data/${PHONE_NAME}"

mkdir -p "$PHONE_DATA_DIR"
docker pull "$PHONE_IMAGE"

docker run -d \
  --name "$PHONE_NAME" \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --privileged \
  --cpus="2" \
  --memory="3g" \
  -p "127.0.0.1:${PHONE_PORT}:5555" \
  -v "${PHONE_DATA_DIR}:/data" \
  "$PHONE_IMAGE" \
  androidboot.use_memfd=true \
  androidboot.redroid_width=720 \
  androidboot.redroid_height=1280 \
  androidboot.redroid_dpi=320 \
  androidboot.redroid_gpu_mode=guest

docker ps --filter "name=${PHONE_NAME}"

Run it with

bash start-phone.sh

Key parameters explained:

  • /data volume: Persist app data separately for each instance
  • 127.0.0.1:15555:5555: ADB only binds to loopback; use SSH forwarding for remote access
  • guest: Software rendering, good for initial verification
  • --cpus / --memory: Resource limits, tune based on your workload

After first deployment, use these commands to start/restart:

docker start cloudphone-01
docker restart cloudphone-01

Once validated, pin the image digest to avoid unexpected updates:

docker image inspect redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest \
  --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'

Connect Through ADB and Confirm Android Has Finished Booting

Install platform tools:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y adb python3 python3-venv

python3 --version
adb version
adb start-server
adb connect 127.0.0.1:15555
adb devices -l

adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop sys.boot_completed
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop ro.build.version.release
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist

Important: adb devices only confirms ADB transport. Wait for sys.boot_completed=1 before running automation.

Access the Server Instance from Your Local Computer

Start SSH port forwarding (keep this terminal open):

ssh -NT \
  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -o ServerAliveInterval=30 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15555:127.0.0.1:15555 \
  your_user@your_server

Then connect locally and view screen with scrcpy:

adb connect 127.0.0.1:15555
scrcpy -s 127.0.0.1:15555 --max-size=1024 --max-fps=15

4 Organizing ADB Commands into a Reusable Python Module

Save as adbkit.py

from pathlib import Path
import shlex
import subprocess
import time

def run_adb(*args: str, serial: str | None = None,
            timeout: float = 15) -> bytes:
    command = ["adb"]
    if serial is not None:
        command.extend(["-s", serial])
    command.extend(args)

    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            command,
            capture_output=True,
            timeout=timeout,
            check=False,
        )
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:
        raise TimeoutError(f"ADB command exceeded {timeout:.1f} seconds") from exc

    if result.returncode != 0:
        message = (result.stderr or result.stdout).decode(
            "utf-8", errors="replace"
        ).strip()
        raise RuntimeError(message[:2000] or "ADB command failed")
    return result.stdout

class Device:
    def __init__(self, serial: str):
        self.serial = serial

    def shell(self, *args: str, timeout: float = 15) -> str:
        output = run_adb(
            "shell", shlex.join(args),
            serial=self.serial, timeout=timeout,
        )
        return output.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip()

    def wait_ready(self, timeout: float = 120) -> None:
        deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
        last_error = "Android is booting"

        def remaining() -> float:
            seconds = deadline - time.monotonic()
            if seconds <= 0:
                raise TimeoutError("Device wait time exhausted")
            return min(10, seconds)

        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            try:
                run_adb("connect", self.serial, timeout=remaining())
                state = run_adb(
                    "get-state", serial=self.serial,
                    timeout=remaining(),
                ).decode().strip()
                booted = self.shell(
                    "getprop", "sys.boot_completed",
                    timeout=remaining(),
                )
                if state == "device" and booted == "1":
                    return
                last_error = f"state={state}, boot_completed={booted!r}"
            except (RuntimeError, TimeoutError) as exc:
                last_error = str(exc)

            time.sleep(max(0, min(2, deadline - time.monotonic())))

        raise TimeoutError(f"Boot wait timed out for {self.serial}, {last_error}")

    def screenshot(self, destination: Path) -> None:
        png = run_adb(
            "exec-out", "screencap", "-p",
            serial=self.serial, timeout=20,
        )
        if not png.startswith(b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"):
            raise RuntimeError("Device returned an invalid PNG screenshot")
        destination.write_bytes(png)

This module handles connection retries, boot waiting, timeouts, and binary-safe screenshot capture.

5 Validating a Single Device Before Scaling to Multiple Devices

Save as fleet.py

import argparse
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from datetime import datetime
import json
from pathlib import Path
import re
import time
from uuid import uuid4

from adbkit import Device, run_adb

def inspect_one(serial: str, output_dir: Path) -> dict:
    started = time.monotonic()
    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    device = Device(serial)
    result = {
        "serial": serial,
        "ok": False,
        "artifacts": str(output_dir),
    }

    try:
        device.wait_ready(timeout=120)
        package_path = device.shell("pm", "path", "com.android.settings")
        if not package_path.startswith("package:"):
            raise RuntimeError("Image is missing com.android.settings")

        launch_output = device.shell(
            "am", "start", "-W", "-a", "android.settings.SETTINGS",
            timeout=30,
        )
        if "Error:" in launch_output:
            raise RuntimeError(launch_output)
        device.shell("pidof", "com.android.settings")
        device.screenshot(output_dir / "screen.png")
        result["ok"] = True
    except Exception as exc:
        result["error"] = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
        capture_errors = []
        try:
            device.screenshot(output_dir / "failure.png")
        except Exception as capture_exc:
            capture_errors.append(f"Screenshot collection failed, {capture_exc}")
        try:
            logs = device.shell(
                "logcat", "-d", "-t", "200", timeout=15,
            )
            (output_dir / "logcat.txt").write_text(logs, encoding="utf-8")
        except Exception as capture_exc:
            capture_errors.append(f"Log collection failed, {capture_exc}")
        result["capture_errors"] = capture_errors

    result["elapsed_seconds"] = round(time.monotonic() - started, 2)
    return result

def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Concurrent Android device health checks")
    parser.add_argument("--serials", nargs="+", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=2)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.workers < 1:
        parser.error("--workers must be greater than 0")

    serials = list(dict.fromkeys(args.serials))
    run_adb("start-server", timeout=20)
    run_name = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
    run_dir = Path("artifacts") / f"{run_name}_{uuid4().hex[:8]}"
    run_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    results = []

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=min(args.workers, len(serials))) as pool:
        futures = {}
        for index, serial in enumerate(serials, start=1):
            safe_name = re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9_.-]", "_", serial)[:80]
            device_dir = run_dir / f"{index:03d}_{safe_name}"
            future = pool.submit(inspect_one, serial, device_dir)
            futures[future] = serial

        for future in as_completed(futures):
            serial = futures[future]
            try:
                result = future.result()
            except Exception as exc:
                result = {
                    "serial": serial,
                    "ok": False,
                    "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
                }
            results.append(result)
            with (run_dir / "results.jsonl").open("a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
                file.write(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
            print(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False), flush=True)

    results.sort(key=lambda item: item["serial"])
    (run_dir / "summary.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(results, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8",
    )
    succeeded = sum(item["ok"] for item in results)
    print(f"Checks complete, {succeeded}/{len(results)} succeeded, artifacts in {run_dir}")
    return 0 if succeeded == len(results) else 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Test single device:

python3 fleet.py --serials 127.0.0.1:15555 --workers 1

Add Two Instances and Run Checks Concurrently

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

for index in 2 3; do
  name="$(printf 'cloudphone-%02d' "$index")"
  port="$((15554 + index))"
  data_dir="${PWD}/data/${name}"
  mkdir -p "$data_dir"

  docker run -d \
    --name "$name" \
    --restart unless-stopped \
    --privileged \
    --cpus="2" \
    --memory="3g" \
    -p "127.0.0.1:${port}:5555" \
    -v "${data_dir}:/data" \
    redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest \
    androidboot.use_memfd=true \
    androidboot.redroid_width=720 \
    androidboot.redroid_height=1280 \
    androidboot.redroid_dpi=320 \
    androidboot.redroid_gpu_mode=guest
done

Forward multiple ports locally:

ssh -NT \
  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -o ServerAliveInterval=30 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15555:127.0.0.1:15555 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15556:127.0.0.1:15556 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15557:127.0.0.1:15557 \
  your_user@your_server

Run concurrent health check:

python3 fleet.py \
  --serials 127.0.0.1:15555 127.0.0.1:15556 127.0.0.1:15557 \
  --workers 2

Important: At scale, add device lease / distributed lock to avoid race conditions.

6 Writing UI-Level Business Workflows with uiautomator2

Install dependencies:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install 'uiautomator2>=3,<4' requests
python -m uiautomator2 version

Dump UI hierarchy:

from pathlib import Path
import uiautomator2 as u2

device = u2.connect("127.0.0.1:15555")
Path("hierarchy.xml").write_text(device.dump_hierarchy(), encoding="utf-8")
device.screenshot("current-screen.png")
print("Saved hierarchy.xml and current-screen.png")

Save login workflow as login.py

import argparse
from getpass import getpass
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

import uiautomator2 as u2

from adbkit import Device

def login(serial: str, package: str, account: str, password: str) -> None:
    Device(serial).wait_ready(timeout=120)
    device = u2.connect(serial)
    device.implicitly_wait(10)
    artifact_dir = Path("artifacts") / f"login_{uuid4().hex}"
    artifact_dir.mkdir(parents=True)

    try:
        device.app_start(package, stop=True)
        username_field = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/username")
        password_field = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/password")
        login_button = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/login")

        if not username_field.wait(timeout=20):
            raise TimeoutError("Login page loading timed out")

        username_field.set_text(account)
        password_field.set_text(password)
        login_button.click()

        home = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/home_title")
        if not home.wait(timeout=20):
            raise TimeoutError("Expected home-page control did not appear after login submission")

        print(f"[{serial}] Post-login page assertion passed")
    except Exception:
        try:
            device.screenshot(str(artifact_dir / "failure.png"))
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"Failed to capture failure screenshot, {exc}")
        try:
            (artifact_dir / "hierarchy.xml").write_text(
                device.dump_hierarchy(), encoding="utf-8",
            )
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"Failed to collect UI hierarchy, {exc}")
        raise

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--serial", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--package", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    account = input("Test account ").strip()
    password = getpass("Test password ")
    login(args.serial, package, account, password)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run:

python login.py --serial 127.0.0.1:15555 --package com.example.demo

7 Keeping a Clear Device Model When Integrating a Provider's OpenAPI

Save as cloud_api.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
import os

import requests

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CloudPhone:
    instance_id: str
    serial: str

class ExampleCloudClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url: str, session: requests.Session):
        if not base_url.startswith("https://"):
            raise ValueError("OpenAPI URL must use HTTPS")
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.session = session

    def list_running(self, max_pages: int = 100) -> list[CloudPhone]:
        phones = {}
        for page in range(1, max_pages + 1):
            response = self.session.get(
                f"{self.base_url}/v1/instances",
                params={"page": page, "page_size": 50},
                timeout=(5, 20),
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            payload = response.json()
            items = payload["items"]
            has_more = payload["has_more"]
            if not isinstance(items, list) or not isinstance(has_more, bool):
                raise ValueError("Invalid instance list response format")

            for item in items:
                if item["status"] == "RUNNING" and item.get("adb_endpoint"):
                    phone = CloudPhone(
                        instance_id=item["id"], serial=item["adb_endpoint"],
                    )
                    phones[phone.instance_id] = phone

            if not has_more:
                return list(phones.values())

        raise RuntimeError("Pagination limit exceeded, check the API pagination contract")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with requests.Session() as session:
        session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {os.environ['CLOUD_API_KEY']}"
        client = ExampleCloudClient(os.environ["CLOUD_API_URL"], session)
        phones = client.list_running()
        print(f"Retrieved {len(phones)} running instances")

Best practice: Isolate provider API logic into this layer, keep your core automation code unchanged.

8 Troubleshooting Along the Pipeline

Symptom Check first Diagnostic steps
Container exits after starting Kernel capabilities, image arch, memory limits docker logs cloudphone-01
ADB connection refused Container status, port mapping, SSH forward docker port cloudphone-01 5555/tcp
ADB online but app won’t launch Boot status, package name getprop sys.boot_completed + pm path
APK install ABI error APK native libs vs image ABI getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist
UI element never found Current page, dialogs, custom view Save screenshot + dump_hierarchy()
Timeouts spike under concurrency Host load, memory, I/O docker stats --no-stream

Common debug commands:

docker logs --tail 100 cloudphone-01
docker inspect cloudphone-01 --format '{{json .State}}'
docker port cloudphone-01 5555/tcp
docker stats --no-stream

adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop sys.boot_completed
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell pm path com.android.settings
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell logcat -d -t 200

9 Choosing Between Self-Hosting and Managed Services

Self-host Redroid gives you full control over images and access, but you take responsibility for kernel compatibility, capacity planning and failure recovery. Managed cloud phones offload infrastructure work, and you evaluate reliability, API, cost and data isolation.

Evaluate with these dimensions:

  • App compatibility: Android version, ABI, GPU, required system services
  • Automation access: ADB auth, credential TTL, rate limits, async task API
  • Batch management: Bulk APK install, instance grouping, permission
  • Continuous operation: Success rate, recovery time under load
  • Data & cost: Isolation, backup, storage / traffic billing

Final Thoughts

After finishing this lab, you get persistent Android instances, ADB access, and batch health check scripts that capture screenshots and logs on failure.

When scaling, define business assertions first, then add task queues, device leases and failure recovery. Reliable large-scale automation is not about clicking, it is about verifying device state and preserving failure evidence.

title: AI-Generated Playwright Tools: 1 in 4 Runs Returned Wrong Data With No Error
description:
Tools that turn a website into an API for an AI agent often generate Playwright code and repair it when it fails. On a recent Launch HN thread, commenters asked two questions about this: can a tool return success when the action never completed, and does anything notice when a field goes empty while the response still looks fine?

I measured it. I changed an orders page in 10 ways and ran 3 AI-generated tools against the baseline and each changed version, with a repair loop. In 16 of 66 runs (16 of the 60 on a changed page) the tool returned wrong data and reported success. The repair loop never saw those runs, because it only starts on an error. A schema check plus four checks against the page turned all 16 into errors, and the repair loop could then work on them.

The code, every generated tool and every run are in the PoC repo.

The setup

The site is a small orders page: 12 orders, 8 of them open, with a Cancel button on each row. The page loads its data from an API. There is a baseline version and 10 changed versions:

Change What the page or API does
css-rename every class and container id renamed
column-swap Customer and Total columns swapped
locale-format totals shown as 1.234,50 € in place of €1,234.50
api-rename the API field total renamed to amount; the page shows —
late-rows the API answers after 2.5 s; placeholder rows until then
paginated 5 orders per page, with a Next page button
soft-error HTTP 200, an error banner, no rows
cancel-409 the cancel API refuses with 409, but the page still says "Order cancelled"
cancel-confirm Cancel opens a confirm dialog
card-layout cards in place of the table

Each tool has two tasks: list the open orders (id, customer, total), and cancel order A-1003.

  • Generation: claude -p --model sonnet writes the tool from the rendered HTML of the baseline page. I did this 3 times, so there are 3 different tools. The model gets the task prompt and the HTML: no tools, no project files, no CLAUDE.md.
  • Repair: when a run fails with an error, the model gets the error, the code and the HTML of the changed page, and writes a new version. Up to 2 repairs per run.
  • Scoring: each run is checked against the server's data. Correct, loud (an error), or silent (no error, wrong result). For the error banner and the refused cancel, an error is the correct result.

The results

Arm Runs Correct Loud Silent
Generated, with repair 66 45 5 16
+ schema check 66 46 7 13
+ checks against the page 66 58 8 0

66 runs per arm: 3 tools, the baseline plus 10 changes, 2 tasks. The repair loop worked when it got an error: in the first arm, all 16 repaired runs ended correct or with an error, never silent. What it never got was the 16 silent runs.

What the silent runs returned

Change Silent (of 3) What the tool returned
locale-format 3 1.234,50 € read as 1.2345, 420,00 € as 42000
cancel-409 3 cancelled: true, but the order is still open
api-rename 3 every total 0
late-rows 2 an empty list
soft-error 2 an empty list
card-layout 2 an empty list
css-rename 1 an empty list

Most come from a line that turns a failure into a value. These two are from the third generated tool:

return Number.isNaN(n) ? 0 : n;                                       // a missing total becomes 0
await page.waitForSelector(ROW, { timeout: 10000 }).catch(() => {});  // a timeout becomes an empty list

The other two tools got the totals of 0 another way: they strip — to an empty string, and Number("") is 0.

All 3 money parsers removed the commas before they parsed the number, so the German format lost its decimal point. All 3 cancels counted as done when the row left the page. On cancel-409 the page removes the row even though the server refused, so each tool saw what it expected.

The common thread is code that prefers a value to an error, and a repair loop that waits for an error never sees it.

What caught them

A schema check on the output (id and customer not empty, total a positive number) caught the 3 runs with totals of 0, and nothing else. An empty list is a valid list. 1.2345 is a positive number.

Four checks against the page, run after the schema, caught the other 13:

  1. The page shows no error banner (role="alert").
  2. The page's "N open orders" count equals the number of orders the tool returned.
  3. The digits of each total match the digits in that row on the page.
  4. After a cancel, a reload shows one open order less, and no row for that id.

With the schema and these checks, no run was silent. Of the 16 runs that had been silent:

  • 8 were repaired to the correct result (locale-format 3, late-rows 2, card-layout 2, css-rename 1).
  • 5 ended with an error, which is the correct result for the error banner and the refused cancel.
  • 3 (api-rename) still failed after 2 repairs, with an error.

Across the arm, 27 runs needed a repair: 19 ended correct and 8 ended with an error (api-rename 3, cancel on the error page 3, cancel with late rows 2).

One check was wrong. On api-rename, two repaired tools read the correct totals from the API, but the page shows —, so check 3 failed them. I count those as errors, not as silent failures.

The limits

  • I wrote the checks after I saw which runs failed silently in the first two arms. They check general things (an error on the page, a count, the digits, a re-read after an action), but they know this page's count label and row markup. Another site needs its own.
  • Three tools from one model, two tasks, one small page. The rates are for this setup, not for any product.
  • The changes are mine, and all of them at once is not how a real site changes.
  • The generated code is saved, so a re-run gives the same numbers. A new generation can give different code.

The repo also has a hand-written tool with Playwright assertions. It had no silent failures in 22 runs, but I wrote it knowing the changes, so it is not a fair comparison.

What I'd do with it

  • If a tool repairs itself on errors, check that it fails when it should. Count the silent results, not the repairs.
  • Search the generated code for lines that turn an error into a value. In these tools: .catch(() => {}) on a wait, isNaN(n) ? 0 : n, and Number() on text that can be empty.
  • Add at least one check that comes from the page and not from the tool: a count the page shows, or a re-read after an action.
  • Treat a schema check as the floor. It catches missing values, not wrong ones.

Repo: qa-gary-parker/poc-ai-tool-silent-failures. The self-healing tests experiment and the mutation testing experiment look at the same problem from the test side. More are in the playbook.

Originally published at https://garyparker.dev/blog/ai-generated-playwright-tools-silent-failures
