The Nolte, Rateike and Finck analysis is a good starting point for how those requirements apply, and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is now a common reference in security reviews. Detailed traces with version information give your compliance owners real material to work from.

To be clear about scope, tracing supports compliance work but doesn't certify it. It can't tell you which laws apply to you or replace legal review.

Start with one agent

Pick the agent that takes real actions. Add a trace around its retrieval, model calls and tool calls. Put the model and prompt version on every record. Make it searchable by run ID. That alone makes the next "why did it do that?" take minutes.

If you'd rather not build and maintain this yourself, BotGauge records the full trace behind every run, including prompts, tool calls, retrieved context and the execution path, in a shared workspace. There's a free tier to try on your own agent.

What do you capture today when an agent does something unexpected? Do you keep the retrieved context and tool arguments, or just the final reply? Tell us in the comments.

title: AI Agent Infrastructure: A Beginner's Guide to the Stack, Tools, and Architecture Behind Autonomous Agents
description:
HustleToAI | Beginner-friendly guide | Research and fact-check cut-off: November 16, 2026

AI agent infrastructure is everything that sits around an AI model so it can do real work: the tools it calls, the memory it keeps, the system that coordinates its steps, and the controls that stop it from breaking things. A chatbot answers. An agent acts. That gap is why agents need their own plumbing, and this guide walks you through it in plain English, with a starter stack near the end.
What Is AI Agent Infrastructure (and Why Does It Matter)?
Think of an AI model as an engine. The infrastructure is the rest of the car. Without it, you have a loud thing sitting on a workbench.
AI Agents vs. Chatbots vs. Generative AI: The Key Differences
Generative AI makes content, like text, images, or code. A chatbot wraps a conversation around it: you ask, it answers, done. An agent takes a goal, breaks it into steps, uses tools, checks the result, and keeps going until it finishes or gets stuck.
Ask a chatbot how to book a flight and you get instructions. Ask an agent and it books the flight, if you've given it permission to.
Why Agents Need Their Own Infrastructure
A normal app does the same thing every time. An agent decides what to do next, and it might decide differently on Tuesday than it did on Monday. So you need ways to limit what it can touch, remember what it did, and see why it did it. Regular app hosting doesn't give you that.
Illustrative scenario: Imagine an agent asked to organize a support inbox. If its permissions are too broad, it might archive or forward messages when it was only supposed to summarize them. This is a hypothetical example, not a report of a real incident. It shows why tool permissions, approval steps, and activity logs matter.
Who Needs to Understand This (Developers, IT Teams, Business Leaders)
Developers build agents. IT teams decide what access those agents get. Business leaders pay for them and own the risk. If you're signing off on an agent that can touch customer data, you should know what's underneath it.
The Core Layers of an AI Agent Infrastructure Stack
Names vary from article to article, but most stacks have the same five layers.
Model Layer: The "Brain" (LLMs and Reasoning)
The large language model handles reasoning and decision-making. Common options include Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, and Mistral. Choose a model based on the complexity of the task, response quality, speed, and cost. A simple information lookup may not need an expensive reasoning model. Before estimating your operating budget, check the provider's current API pricing because input tokens, output tokens, caching, and additional features can have different charges.
Tools Layer: How Agents Take Action (APIs, Browsers, Code Execution)
Tools are how an agent touches the outside world: an API, a browser, a code runner, a database. Without tools, an agent can only talk. With them, it can file a ticket, read a spreadsheet, or restart a server.
Data and Memory Layer: Short-Term, Long-Term, and Vector Storage
Short-term memory is the conversation so far, held in the model's context window. Long-term memory lives outside the model, often in a vector database that finds information by meaning instead of exact words. That's how an agent can recall last week's customer issue. The pattern is called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.
Orchestration Layer: Coordinating Steps, Agents, and Workflows
The orchestrator decides what happens next: call this tool, wait for that result, retry, hand off to another agent. LangGraph, LlamaIndex, and the OpenAI Agents SDK are common options. It's the project manager. It doesn't do the work, it makes sure the work happens in the right order.
Observability and Governance Layer: Monitoring What Agents Do
You want a log of every step: what the agent saw, what it decided, what it called. Tools like Langfuse, LangSmith, and OpenTelemetry-based setups handle this. Governance sits on top, with rules about who approved what. Without this layer you can't explain a mistake afterward, which gets awkward fast.
Types of AI Agents and Where Each Fits in Your Infrastructure
The textbook list of agent types sounds abstract. It comes from Russell and Norvig's AI textbook, and here's what it means in practice.
Reactive and Task-Specific Agents
These respond to an input with no memory of the past. A spam filter is one. They're fast, cheap, and predictable, which makes them a good fit when the job is narrow and the rules are clear.
Stateful, Model-Based, and Goal-Based Agents
These remember what's happened and work toward an outcome. A support agent that knows you already tried restarting your router is stateful. A goal-based agent picks its actions to reach something specific, like "resolve this ticket."
Planning and Learning Agents
Planning agents organize actions into steps before or during execution. Learning agents use experience or feedback to modify their future behavior. These are different capabilities: an agent can plan without learning, and an agent can learn without following a fixed planning process. In production systems, feedback-based improvements may involve updating memory, refining instructions, or retraining a model. These approaches should not be treated as interchangeable.
Multi-Agent Systems: When One Agent Isn't Enough
Several agents, each with one job: one researches, one writes, one reviews. That helps when a task is too big for one context window or needs a second pair of eyes. It also multiplies cost and the number of places things can fail. Start with one agent. Add more when you hit a wall.
Key Components Explained Simply
Five pieces come up in almost every project.
Tool Discovery and Integration (APIs, MCP, Function Calling)
Function calling allows an AI model to request specific functions, such as looking up an order or retrieving information from a database. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for AI applications to connect with external tools and data sources. Anthropic introduced MCP as an open-source project on November 25, 2024. In December 2025, Anthropic donated the protocol to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, supporting its development as an open industry standard. For a small project, ordinary function calling may be enough. MCP becomes useful when you need standardized connections across multiple tools and applications.
Browser Automation and UI Interaction
Some systems have no API. In that case an agent can drive a browser with a tool like Playwright and click through pages like a person would. It works, but it's slower and breaks when a site changes its layout. Use an API when you can.
Authentication, Identity, and Secrets Management for Agents
Give the agent its own identity. Don't hand it your login. Use narrow permissions (least privilege), keep keys in a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault or your cloud's built-in one, and rotate them. Never paste an API key into a prompt.
Memory Systems and Vector Databases
Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Chroma, and pgvector all do this job. If you already run Postgres, pgvector is the easy first step. A dedicated vector database makes more sense once your data gets big. You may not need one at all for a first agent.
Compute, Hosting, and Sandboxed Execution Environments
If your agent writes and runs code, run it in a sandbox: a locked-down container that can't reach your real systems. Docker works for the basics, and services like E2B and Modal exist for this. Hosting itself can be a plain cloud server or serverless functions. GPUs only matter if you host your own model.
Designing Infrastructure for Machine-Speed Operations
Agents work faster than people and don't sleep. Your systems might not be ready for that.
Why Human-Centric Systems Become Bottlenecks
Approval emails, ticket queues, and manual logins were built for people. An agent can send hundreds of requests in the time a person opens one ticket, then sit there waiting for a human to click Approve.
API-First and Agent-Native Architecture
Agent-native means every action has a clean API, clear error messages, and predictable responses. If a task can only be done by clicking around a dashboard, agents struggle with it. Platform teams are starting to treat agents as a new kind of user, with their own needs.
Scalability, Latency, and Concurrency Considerations
Three things bite first: rate limits on the services you call, slow model responses, and many agents running at once. Use queues and retries, and make actions idempotent, so repeating a request doesn't repeat the side effect (like charging a card twice). Tools like Temporal handle long-running workflows.
From "Self-Healing" Systems to Self-Architecting Ones
Self-healing means a system can respond to known problems automatically, such as restarting a failed service. Self-architecting describes a more ambitious idea: agents design or modify infrastructure itself. These capabilities should not be treated as interchangeable, and autonomous infrastructure changes require strong testing, permissions, and rollback controls. For beginners, treat self-architecting systems as an emerging direction rather than a capability to assume is production-ready.
Real-World Use Cases of AI Agent Infrastructure
The real uses today are boring, in a good way.
IT and Network Operations (Provisioning, Configuration, Capacity Planning)
Agents provision servers, push config changes, check backups, and forecast capacity. Tools like Terraform and Ansible make the actual changes, and the agent decides when. Network teams worry most about blast radius here, since one bad config can take down a whole site.
Illustrative scenario: An IT operations agent could review server alerts, summarize the likely cause of a problem, and prepare a configuration change for an engineer to approve. This is a hypothetical workflow; it should not be presented as a task the author has personally automated.
Security Operations and Compliance
Agents can help triage security alerts, gather relevant evidence, and draft incident reports. A human should review consequential actions, such as disabling an account or changing access permissions. Avoid claiming a specific time saving unless you have a reliable study or measured result for the exact workflow.
Customer Support and Business Workflows
A support agent looks up an order, checks the refund policy, issues a refund under a set limit, and escalates the rest. ServiceNow, Salesforce, and Zendesk all ship agent features now. Set the limit in code, not in the prompt.
Software Development and DevOps
Coding agents like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code write and test code. DevOps agents read logs when a deploy fails and suggest a fix or open a pull request for review.
Build vs. Buy: Choosing Platforms, Frameworks, and Tools
Short answer: use managed pieces first, and build only the parts that make your work different.
Popular Frameworks and Orchestration Options (Open Source vs. Managed)
Open source options like LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, and AutoGen give you control and cost engineering time. Managed platforms give you speed and cost more per use, with some lock-in.
Cloud Provider Options (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud)
AWS provides Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft offers Microsoft Foundry (formerly Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry)), and Google Cloud provides Vertex AI. These platforms offer different combinations of model access, agent development, deployment, and enterprise infrastructure. If your organization already uses a particular cloud provider, starting with its existing AI platform can simplify identity management, billing, and security integration.
Evaluation Checklist: Features, Cost, Lock-In, and Support
Before you pick anything, ask:
Does it log every step the agent takes?
Can you set permissions per agent?
What happens to your data? Is it used for training?
What does it cost at ten times your expected usage?
How hard is it to leave?
Does support answer in hours or in weeks?
A Sample Starter Stack for Beginners
Here's a setup that keeps things small.
Layer
Starter choice
Why
Model
One hosted LLM through an API
No servers to run
Tools
Function calling to two or three APIs
Simple to debug
Memory
Postgres with pgvector
One database to manage
Orchestration
LangGraph or plain code
Plain code is fine at first
Observability
Langfuse
Hosting
One small cloud container
Cheap and easy to restart
Before publishing, you can add an original screenshot of a starter stack you have personally configured. If you have not built one, keep the example table above and do not imply that it is your own deployed setup.
Security, Safety, and Risk Management for AI Agents
An agent with broad access and bad instructions is a real problem. Here's how it usually goes wrong.
Key Risks: Prompt Injection, Over-Permissioned Agents, and Data Leakage
Prompt injection occurs when malicious or misleading instructions in user input or external content influence an AI model to behave in unintended ways. For example, an agent reading an email or website might encounter hidden instructions designed to make it reveal sensitive information or perform an unauthorized action. OWASP ranks Prompt Injection as LLM01:2025, the first category in its 2025 Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications. Over-permissioned agents have access beyond what their tasks require, while data leakage occurs when private information is exposed to an unauthorized destination.
Containment and Recovery: Planning for When Agents Fail
Assume it will fail eventually. Limit what the agent can reach, set spending caps, keep a kill switch, and make actions reversible where you can. Take a snapshot before any change, and test the rollback before you need it.
Human-in-the-Loop: Putting People at the Right Decision Points
Don't approve every step. You'll get tired and start clicking yes without reading. Require approval for actions that are expensive, hard to undo, or visible to customers. Let low-risk reads run on their own.
Compliance and Regulation Basics for U.S. Businesses
The United States does not have one comprehensive federal statute specifically regulating every type of AI agent. However, this does not mean AI agents operate without legal requirements. Existing laws can apply depending on the industry, data involved, and actions an agent performs. For example, HIPAA applies to covered healthcare entities and their business associates, while Section 5 of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive practices in commerce. Colorado enacted Senate Bill 26-189 in May 2026, with provisions scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027; the state also enacted a separate Chatbot Safety Act with the same scheduled effective date. SOC 2 is an independent attestation framework, not a law. Businesses should review applicable federal and state requirements with qualified legal counsel. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework can help organize AI risk-management practices.
How to Adopt AI Agent Infrastructure Step by Step
Don't start with full autonomy. Earn it.
Phase 1: AI-Assisted (Humans Decide, AI Suggests)
The AI drafts, summarizes, or recommends. A person does the actual work. Risk is low, and you learn where the agent is wrong before it can hurt anything.
Phase 2: Supervised Execution (AI Acts, Humans Approve)
Now the agent takes the action, but only after a person says yes. This is where you tune permissions and find the gaps in your guardrails.
Phase 3: Autonomous Operations (AI Acts Within Guardrails)
The agent acts alone, inside tight limits, on tasks with clear rules where a mistake is cheap. Keep logging on. Review a sample of its work every so often.
How to Choose the Right Starting Problem (Risk, Clarity, Consequences)
Ask three questions. Does the task need action, or just advice? Is it well defined? What happens if the agent gets it wrong? Good first picks are things like summarizing support tickets or drafting config changes for review. Bad first picks are anything that moves money or touches production with no review.
Costs, Metrics, and Future Trends in AI Agent Infrastructure
Most beginners underestimate the cost and skip the measuring. Don't.
What AI Agent Infrastructure Really Costs (Compute, Tokens, Tooling, Staffing)
Four buckets: model tokens, compute and hosting, tool subscriptions, and people. People are usually the biggest. AI agent infrastructure costs can increase as an agent performs more reasoning steps and makes additional model calls. Each call may involve input and output tokens, and some implementations pass previous conversation context into subsequent requests. This can increase input-token consumption, particularly in long-running workflows. However, the exact cost depends on the API, conversation-state design, prompt caching, and model selected. To control spending, monitor token usage per task, limit unnecessary reasoning loops, and check your provider's current pricing.
How to Measure Success: Reliability, Cost Per Task, and ROI
Track task success rate, cost per completed task, time saved, and how often humans override the agent. Compare against doing the work by hand. Start tracking before launch, or you'll have no baseline to compare with.
Emerging Trends to Watch (Agent Interoperability Standards, Agent-to-Agent Communication, Operational Invisibility)
AI agent interoperability is an important area of development. Two notable protocols are the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A). MCP standardizes connections between AI applications and external tools or data sources. A2A focuses on communication and collaboration between different AI agents. Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025, while the Linux Foundation launched the A2A project in June 2025. Both initiatives aim to improve interoperability, but their long-term adoption and implementation will continue to evolve. Operational invisibility describes the goal of infrastructure running reliably in the background; it is an aspiration, not a formal technical standard.
Frequently Asked Questions About AI Agent Infrastructure
What is AI agent infrastructure in simple terms?
It's the set of systems that lets an AI model do tasks instead of just chatting: tools to act, memory to remember, orchestration to coordinate, and controls to keep it safe.
What are the main components of an AI agent infrastructure stack?
A model, tools, data and memory, orchestration, and observability with governance. Add hosting underneath and security across all of it.
How is AI agent infrastructure different from traditional IT or MLOps infrastructure?
Traditional apps follow fixed code paths. MLOps focuses on training and serving models. Agent infrastructure has to handle software that makes its own decisions at run time, so permissions, logging, and rollback matter a lot more.
Do I need to build my own infrastructure, or can I use a managed platform?
Most beginners should use a managed platform or a framework on top of a hosted model. Build custom pieces later, once you know where the managed options fall short.
Is AI agent infrastructure safe for business use?
It can be, with limits. Give agents narrow permissions, require approval for risky actions, log everything, and plan for failure. Safe depends on how you set it up, not on the tool.
What is the difference between the Big Four accounting firms' AI platforms?
The Big Four accounting firms have introduced separate enterprise AI initiatives: Deloitte announced Zora AI, PwC launched agent OS, EY introduced the EY.ai Agentic Platform, and KPMG launched KPMG Workbench. These products have different capabilities and deployment status, so they should not be treated as identical.
Is there an official list of the Big Four AI companies?
No. The phrase does not have a universally accepted definition. Some discussions refer to companies, while others refer to products. Compare companies with companies and products with products rather than treating them as one official ranking.
What are the five components of an AI agent?
One useful teaching model includes perception, reasoning, memory, planning, and action. This is a conceptual framework, not a universal technical standard. Some architectures combine these functions or include additional components.
Is there a 30% rule of AI?
There is no established rule that divides work into 70% AI and 30% human effort. A May 2024 McKinsey Global Institute report estimated that, under its midpoint adoption scenario, up to 30% of current working hours in the United States and Europe could be automated by 2030. This is a scenario-based forecast, not a guaranteed outcome or a recommended work split.
Which five jobs will survive AI?
No reliable source can guarantee that five specific occupations will survive AI unchanged. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projections show expected employment growth in several occupations, including electricians, plumbers, registered nurses, and mental health counselors, but these are labor-market projections—not guarantees of protection from AI.
Your Next Step
Choose one small, low-risk task, such as summarizing support tickets. Begin with an AI-assisted workflow in which the agent makes suggestions and a person decides what to do. Record errors and review the results before granting the agent permission to take actions.

title: Sizing an add to a position your agent already holds
description:
Most sizing code answers one question: how many shares can I buy so a stop-out costs 1% of the account. That works for a new position. It goes wrong when the agent already owns the stock, because the formula doesn't know about the shares you have.

Here is a test account I used. Margin account, $50,000 equity, $21,340 cash.

MSFT  18 @ 420   Technology
NVDA  40 @ 185   Technology
JNJ   60 @ 155   Health Care
XOM   40 @ 110   Energy

The agent wants more NVDA at $185 with a stop at $170.

Step 1: size by risk 

import requests
AFA = "https://agent-financial-advisor.agent-financial-advisor.workers.dev/v1/tools/"

positions = [
    {"symbol": "MSFT", "quantity": 18, "market_price": 420, "sector": "Technology"},
    {"symbol": "NVDA", "quantity": 40, "market_price": 185, "sector": "Technology"},
    {"symbol": "JNJ",  "quantity": 60, "market_price": 155, "sector": "Health Care"},
    {"symbol": "XOM",  "quantity": 40, "market_price": 110, "sector": "Energy"},
]

size = requests.post(AFA + "position_size", json={
    "equity": 50000, "entry_price": 185, "stop_price": 170,
    "method": "fixed_fractional", "risk_pct": 0.01, "max_position_pct": 0.2,
}).json()
print(size["quantity"], size["position_pct_of_equity"], size["binding_constraint"])

33 0.1221 fixed_fractional

33 shares, $495 at risk, 12.2% of equity. Looks fine. The 20% cap didn't bind because the sizer only sees this order. It has no idea there are already 40 shares in the account.

Step 2: check the order against the account

pre_trade_check gets the positions, so it can do the math on the total.

body = {
    "account": {"type": "margin", "equity": 50000, "cash": 21340, "positions": positions},
    "order": {"symbol": "NVDA", "side": "buy", "quantity": 33,
              "order_type": "market", "stop_loss_price": 170},
    "market": {"last_price": 185, "avg_daily_volume": 180000000},
}
r = requests.post(AFA + "pre_trade_check", json=body).json()
print(r["decision"], r["suggested_quantity"])
for c in r["checks"]:
    if c["status"] != "pass":
        print(c["id"], c["message"])

approve_with_warnings 14
concentration NVDA would be 27% of equity (limit 20%). Max additional quantity: 14.

40 + 33 = 73 shares, $13,505, 27% of the account. The max you can add and stay at 20% is 14. Risk per trade passed (0.99%), so the risk rule was never the problem. The position cap was.

The default cap is 20%. You can change it with "policy": {"max_position_pct": 0.15} if you want a tighter book.

Step 3: sectors

The single-name check doesn't look at sectors. MSFT and NVDA are both Technology. Before the trade that is $14,960, about 29.9%. I let the agent cap sectors at 35%, so I ran the post-trade book through portfolio_review:

holdings = [{"symbol": p["symbol"], "quantity": p["quantity"], "price": p["market_price"],
             "sector": p["sector"], "asset_class": "equity"} for p in positions_after]
review = requests.post(AFA + "portfolio_review", json={
    "holdings": holdings, "cash": 18750,
    "limits": {"max_single_weight": 0.2, "max_sector_weight": 0.35},
}).json()
print(review["sector_weights"])
for f in review["findings"]:
    print(f["severity"], f["issue"])

positions_after is the same list with NVDA at 54 shares (14 added), and cash is $21,340 minus 14 × $185. Output:

{'Technology': 0.351, 'Health Care': 0.186, 'Energy': 0.088}
medium Technology sector is 35.1% (limit 35%).
medium Effective number of holdings is 4.1; the portfolio behaves like a concentrated book.

Just over. The sector room is easy to work out yourself, so I do that locally and use the review as a second look:

def sector_room(positions, equity, sector, price, max_sector_pct=0.35):
    held = sum(p["quantity"] * p["market_price"] for p in positions if p["sector"] == sector)
    return max(0, int((max_sector_pct * equity - held) // price))

print(sector_room(positions, 50000, "Technology", 185))  # 13

Putting it together 

qty = min(size["quantity"], r["suggested_quantity"] or size["quantity"],
          sector_room(positions, 50000, "Technology", 185))

33 by risk, 14 by the position cap, 13 by the sector cap. The agent buys 13. Whatever limit is smallest wins, and the agent should log which one it was so you can see later why the order was smaller than it asked for.

Limits

  • Positions need current prices. If the agent passes avg cost instead of market price, every percentage is off. This one is alot easier to get wrong than it sounds when positions come from a cache.
  • Equity has to match the positions plus cash. My first run had them out of sync and the review flagged JNJ over 20% when it wasn't.
  • The first 5 calls a day need no signup. POST /v1/keys gives a free key with 25 calls a day.
  • It's rule-based analysis for software, not investment advice.

The API is the Agent Financial Advisor API. The same tools are on the MCP server at /mcp.

Disclosure: I built this. If your agent caps something else before it adds to a position, like correlation or beta, I'd like to hear how you do it.

title: DeepMind Proved Signal's Code Is Secure — Demand the Same Standard From Your AI Vendors
description:
On November 10, 2026, Google DeepMind published a result that quietly resets the standard of evidence for every software vendor you buy from.

AI agents generated over six million lines of machine-checked proof demonstrating that the actual deployed code behind the Signal protocol — the encryption protecting billions of conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages — delivers the security properties it claims. Not the design on paper. The compiled code running on devices. Human experts specified what to prove and reviewed every specification; agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proving; the Lean proof language checked every line mechanically. Four weeks, for a task DeepMind says historically took expert teams years — and which, by their account, no widely deployed protocol implementation had ever been formally verified before, by any method.

Notice what's missing from that claim: "we tested it a lot."

No badge. No attestation. No "trusted by thousands of teams." A proof is different in kind, not degree — it's an artifact you can check, not an assurance you're asked to believe. DeepMind even open-sourced the verification artifacts so others can.

Your AI vendors will not hand you Lean proofs. But the frontier of evidence just moved, and there is a business-owner-sized version of it you can start demanding tomorrow.

Assurance vs. artifact

Almost every AI buying decision a small business makes today rests on assurance: a demo, a security page, a logo wall, a compliance badge. Assurance is a vendor telling you something is true. An artifact is something you can inspect, re-run, or audit yourself — a checkable claim.

The difference matters most exactly where small businesses spend money: tools and agents that touch customer data, send outbound communication, or act on your behalf in systems you don't watch all day. When the tool is wrong quietly, assurance is what you had. When you need to find out what happened, an artifact is what you need.

You don't need a research lab to close that gap. You need three things from the vendor, in writing, before you sign.

The three artifacts to demand from every AI vendor

1. A written scope — what it can and cannot touch

DeepMind's proof started with humans vetting a specification: exactly what was being claimed, and nothing more. That's not a formality — a proof is only as strong as its stated scope, and that's the part worth stealing. Demand one page from the vendor that names the data categories the tool reads, the systems it can touch, and the actions it can take — plus, just as important, what it explicitly cannot.

"The agent only works inside your CRM sandbox and cannot send emails" is a scope. "Enterprise-grade security" is not. If the vendor can't produce the page, the tool's boundaries are undocumented — which means unknown, to both of you.

2. A planted-failure test you can re-run

How did DeepMind convince themselves the system could tell secure code from buggy code? They reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated copy of the Signal code — and in both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. Known answers, deliberately broken.

That's the shape of question to put to any vendor: "Show me a failure your product catches." A support agent should catch a ticket linked to the wrong customer account. An invoice tool should catch a refund for the wrong amount. If the vendor can't show you a single failure their system detects, they haven't instrumented for failure — which means you'll be the one discovering it, in production, with your customers.

A claim you can't test is marketing. This question turns marketing back into a claim.

3. An action log you can read after the fact

The DeepMind agents flagged roughly one percent of the proof for a second look by a human; a machine checked the rest. Volume handled by automation, judgment reserved for people. That division of labor is the right model for any AI tool acting inside your business — but it only works if the tool records what it did.

Demand a log of every action the tool takes on your behalf, in a form you can read without the vendor's help. A log converts trust into verification: when something looks wrong next month, you can see what actually happened instead of filing a support ticket and hoping. If the vendor's answer is "we can pull that for you," that's not a log — that's still assurance, with a delay.

Honest boundaries

  • Scope is the proof's strength, not its weakness. The Signal result covers the core protocol library; reporting on the work (The Next Web) notes the guarantees cover one-to-one chats, not the entire Signal apps. An artifact covers exactly what it says it covers — so the closing question in any vendor conversation is always "what does this cover?" Never let a certificate be waved at a question it doesn't answer.
  • You won't get formal verification at SMB prices. The standard being imported is the class of evidence — checkable artifacts — not Lean machinery. Scope, test, and log are the small-business translation, and they're achievable now.
  • Demanding all three on day one will slow some purchases. Fine. Prioritize: anything that touches money, customer data, or outbound communication gets all three, no exceptions. Everything else, the written scope alone is a reasonable start. A vendor who resists even the scope is telling you something.

The step that comes before all of this

You can't demand artifacts from vendors you don't know you have. Most small businesses are in exactly that position: AI features embedded in software you already pay for, subscriptions nobody opens, and tools the team adopted that never went through anyone's approval. Evaluating evidence requires knowing who your vendors actually are — start with a complete inventory.

That's what SMB Scale Up's AI Clarity Sprint is for: two weeks, one fixed fee ($1,495 CAD), and you get the complete inventory of every AI touchpoint in your business, an own-vs-use analysis (what you pay for versus what gets used), three quick wins ranked by ROI, and one first-project plan with an honest build / buy / don't-automate verdict. title: Check Point Patches a Root Daemon That Accepts Commands From Any Local Process
description:
TL;DR

  • CVE-2026-123039 is a local privilege escalation in Gaia OS, the operating system that runs on Check Point security appliances, where a daemon named dynamic_server executes commands as root.
  • The daemon listens on a Unix socket, /tmp/dynamic_socket, and on affected builds that socket is world-writable with no authentication of the process connecting to it, so any local user can ask the appliance to run a command as root.
  • Check Point published emergency hotfixes and records an active exploit against a couple of dozen customers, in a single region, with a CVSS score of 7.8 for the flaw itself.
  • The socket sits second in a chain: PHP2Shell in the Mobile Access portal reached the appliance first, and the DynamicCLI escalation turned that foothold into root between 30 October and 4 November 2026.
  • The activity arrived in two waves, the second one broader and spread across several countries, and Check Point Research records the scanning concentrated between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC.
  • The fix ships in four jumbo hotfix takes, and an operator confirms it with two commands: the socket mode reads 0660 after the patch, and the log lists rejected connections from an unauthorized uid.
  • A root shell on a security appliance reaches the management plane, the policy, and whatever the gateway can route to, which is why the next steps in this intrusion went to a hypervisor and a wiper.

Netics visual, 13 November 2026: the score, the socket mode on each side of the fix, and the four Gaia branches that received a jumbo hotfix take.

What the DynamicCLI daemon accepts on a Gaia appliance

Gaia OS carries two command interfaces. The Clish shell is the documented one, and behind it sits an extended CLI served by a process called dynamic_server that runs as root. The advisory describes the interface plainly: the daemon listens on a local Inter-Process Communication socket at /tmp/dynamic_socket, and that socket is created with mode 0777 on affected products, with no authentication of the connecting process.

Read that combination as a permissions statement. A socket with mode 0777 accepts a connection from any account on the box, the daemon runs as root, and it executes whatever command string it receives. Check Point's own wording is that any authenticated local user can run arbitrary commands as root by writing a single request to the socket. The precondition is real and worth stating: the attacker needs local code execution on the appliance first. This flaw converts a limited foothold into full control.

The official advisory (created 8 November 2026, last modified 12 November 2026) where the socket permissions, the affected products and the jumbo hotfix takes are listed in that order. Page from https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk1000362.

The affected list covers Check Point Force Firewalls, Management and Log Servers, Multi-Domain Security Management and Multi-Domain Log Server, and Maestro Orchestrator, across R81, R81.10, R81.20, R82, R82.10 and R82.20. Spark Firewalls and Smart-1 Cloud sit outside the exposure.

The chain that reached root: PHP2Shell first, then the socket

The intrusion Check Point Research documented started from the network. Initial access came through PHP2Shell in the Mobile Access portal, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 at 9.2, which gave code execution in the portal. The DynamicCLI escalation supplied the root.

Figure 1 from Check Point Research, 12 November 2026: the infection chain from the portal to privilege escalation and the destructive stage. Image from https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/php2shell-exploitation-on-check-point-gateway/.

What happened with root reads as a study in persistence. The researchers describe PHP webshells written into the templates directory the portal uses to build its login pages, launched so a file named zz.tpl carries a command shell that later accepts a hardcoded key and supports operating-system commands, PHP evaluation and file uploads. Then came a standalone backdoor: TSGA, deployed as /tmp/CPconfigdaemon and relaunched as slot_CPconfigdaemon from the boot persistence directory, with an embedded shared library called TSProxy written to /lib/libcpfwcommon.so so selected appliance processes carry the attacker's traffic inside ordinary connections.

Figure 3 from Check Point Research: the webshell the attackers dropped once they held root, with the key gate, the base64 XOR path and the fixed upload location. Image from https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/php2shell-exploitation-on-check-point-gateway/.

The detail that matters for anyone running a gateway is the third stage. With root on the appliance, the attackers ran the gogo scanner to map the internal network, then moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host using the vpxuser service account and executed a wiper named destroy_v6.

Two waves, several countries, and the hours they ran in

Check Point's blog advisory dates the exploitation activity from 30 October to 4 November 2026. The research write-up splits it: a first wave on 30 October against Israeli organisations, including destructive activity against some of them, and a broader second wave on 2 November across multiple countries and sectors with no destructive activity observed.

Figure 4 from Check Point Research: requests per hour of day in UTC during the campaign, concentrated between 00:00 and 09:00. Chart from https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/php2shell-exploitation-on-check-point-gateway/.

The hour chart is the part a small security team can act on. Requests cluster in a nine-hour window, with the two largest bars at 00:00 and 01:00 UTC, and the research links that window to working hours in one region. An internet-facing management portal that receives authenticated and unauthenticated traffic at 2 a.m. local time is worth a look in the web server log, whatever the vendor's attribution concludes.

The hotfix takes that carry the fix, and how to confirm it landed

The fix is inside the jumbo hotfix accumulators: R82.20 from Take 14, R82.10 from Take 52, R82 from Take 132, and R81.20 from Take 174. NVD lists the vulnerable side of those same branches as Take 10 or below, 50 or below, 130 or below and 173 or below.

Confirmation is mechanical, and this is where an operator earns the patch ticket. The advisory says the fixed build creates the socket as srw-rw---- root config, mode 0660. A build that still shows srwxrwxrwx is still in the affected world-writable state. The second check reads the daemon log: grep "Rejected connection from unauthorized uid" /var/log/dynamicCli.log returns entries such as uid 99 (pid 123456), and a burst of them correlates with authentication events on the portal.

Netics visual, 13 November 2026: the six dates that frame the episode, from the available fix to the exploited-vulnerability listing.

Where a maintenance window is days away, Check Point offers a harder stop: disable the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting. The trade-off is stated in the advisory itself, because Dynamic CLI commands simply stop working, so the mitigation buys time at the cost of a documented capability.

What a root shell on an appliance reaches next

A firewall or a management server is the wrong place for a root shell to land. Both hold policy, both hold credentials for the estate they manage, and both sit on a network path that other systems trust. Root on a gateway means the attacker reads the rulebase, changes it, and uses the appliance's own trust relationships to reach hypervisors and management networks.

Netics visual, 13 November 2026: what changes on the appliance once the jumbo hotfix is installed, as the advisory describes it.

The remediation that follows from this incident has three parts. Patch the appliance branches in the estate, starting with anything internet-facing. Verify the socket mode and the log entries on each box, because a hotfix take number in a report is a claim and a 0660 socket is evidence. Then check what the appliance could reach from where it stood, including hypervisor service accounts, since that is the path this intrusion took. Fleet-level checks of that kind belong in infrastructure monitoring with plain-language alerts, where a changed socket mode or an unexpected log burst is visible without a nightly manual sweep.

Two numbers from this episode deserve to stay in view. A 9.2 unauthenticated portal flaw and a 7.8 local escalation were enough together to reach root on a security appliance, and the chart of when those requests arrived shows a nine-hour working day. The advisory is strong on product scope and appliance-level patch evidence; its count of a couple dozen unpatched systems covers the observed incidents in one region, leaving the wider installed-base exposure unmeasured.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: My Agent Got a Credit Card. I Still Have to Face-ID the Sweater.
description:
Originally published on Hlinor.

OpenAI's new ChatGPT Wallet lets AI agents pay. Today, every purchase goes through your thumb. Later, OpenAI says, you might set limits in advance and let the agent shop without asking every time. A stand-up reading of the fine print.

Photo: Syced, "LaCuCa card reader – payment terminal at supermarket register", via Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0

Your agent got a credit card.

You still have to Face-ID the sweater.

That's the whole product in two lines. Honestly, I've seen looser governance from humans with corporate cards.

On Friday, 13 November 2026 (yes, Friday the 13th, the day you'd naturally pick to hand a robot your money), OpenAI announced ChatGPT Wallet. In OpenAI's words, it's a wallet that "lets agents pay without access to users' actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase." It was "built in partnership with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa," and it "will initially be available through dots for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US." Dots, as Reuters puts it, are the company's always-on AI agents.

For years, the scariest slide in any AI-agent safety deck was the one where the agent clicks Buy. Now there's a wallet for it. And a fingerprint.


Wallets used to hold paper. Now they hold an agent, a token and a fingerprint. Photo: "Wallet (AM 613844)", Auckland Museum, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. No changes made.

Act 1. The permission slip

Here's how it works today, according to OpenAI. You add a card once. Before each purchase you review the items, the total and the card, then approve with a security check "such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan." After that, "the payment network provides a payment token — a substitute for the user's actual card details — with a card number, security code, and expiration date." The merchant gets paid, and neither the merchant nor the agent gets your real card number.

So my agent has a card it can't see, on an account it can't charge without my thumb.

That's not a credit card. That's a permission slip with a chip.

Picture the scene:

Agent: I found the sweater. Merino. Your size. Twenty percent off.
Me: Great.
Agent: Please place your thumb on the glass.
Me: Are we buying a sweater or opening a bank vault?
Agent: Yes.

My thumb is now the most senior employee in the household. It does nothing all day, and nothing ships without it.

And here's the part I want to praise, sincerely, before I go back to being rude. OpenAI says "each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make." That's the rarest sentence in agent marketing: a feature that already sounds like an audit log. Most launch posts promise the agent will understand you. This one promises a receipt. I'll take the receipt.

Act 2. The bouncer at the door

Now the guest list. I'm not a US Pro subscriber, so I read OpenAI's help center the way you read the menu in the window of a restaurant you won't get into.

To get in, you must be 18 or older, live in the United States, and have a US billing address for the card. The card must be a US-issued credit card from American Express, Chase, Mastercard or Visa. Debit cards are not supported. Virtual cards are "not supported at launch." And it only works in conversations with a dot, not in regular Chat, Work or standalone Codex threads.

My favorite rule is about Chase. To add a Chase card, you must be the primary cardholder, not an authorized user. So an AI agent gets to spend on that card, with the cardholder's thumb every time. A human authorized user can't even add it. The robot got the promotion you didn't.

And even if you tick every box, the rollout is gradual, so an eligible user may still not have it. To sum up, you need to be an adult, an American, and lucky.

Then there's the most honest sentence ever written about delegation. The help center says: "Ready to check out means your approval is complete. It does not confirm that the merchant has placed your order."

Every manager knows this feeling. "I sent it." Sent where? Did it arrive? Approval is complete, and the sweater is now in a superposition. OpenAI's advice is to check for the merchant's confirmation before you try again, which is exactly how you avoid owning two identical sweaters.

One more small surprise: the card number used at checkout may not match the one on your physical card, because it's a token. If the numbers don't match, that's not a bug. That's the whole point of the product.

Act 3. Three desks, one sweater

Something went wrong. Who do you call? The help center splits it three ways. The merchant handles order status, cancellations, returns and refunds. Your card issuer handles declined, pending, disputed or unrecognized charges and bank verification. OpenAI Support handles Wallet errors, suspected unauthorized access to your ChatGPT account, and a purchase that's different from the one you approved.

That's a clear routing table. It's also the plot of a short, entirely made-up play:

Me, to the store: The sweater's the wrong color.
Store: Returns? That's our desk.
Me, to the bank: There's a charge I don't recognize.
Bank: Unrecognized charges? That's our desk.
Me, to OpenAI: I approved a different sweater.
OpenAI: Not what you approved? That's our desk.
Me, to myself: And who handles the fact that I now know three help desks by heart because of one sweater?

The comedy isn't a scandal. It's the hand-off.

OpenAI also asks you never to share your full card number, security code, password or bank verification codes in the chat or in a support message. Card details go only into the secure form. I love this moment: the product built so your agent never sees your card number has to remind you not to show it to the agent.

Then the trapdoor that isn't new at all. If you agree to a recurring payment plan, "the merchant may store the payment credential and charge it again under the terms you agreed to," and canceling is between you and the merchant. The agent buys once. The subscription buys forever. That isn't an AI problem. Gyms have run on it since the invention of January.

Now the other side of the counter. OpenAI says "1.2B people use ChatGPT each week" (its own figure), and that many of them already use it to research and compare what to buy. The missing piece was never taste. It was the till.


The till: the last place in commerce that still checks who's actually paying. Photo: Patrick OTER, "Cash register NCR", via Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0

The till has opinions, though. OpenAI says websites need to make sure agents aren't blocked by accident, and "payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents." Along with the wallet, it published a Commerce Partner Playbook. It covers product information and feeds, signed requests via Web Bot Auth so CDNs and firewalls don't block ChatGPT agents, and working with payment and risk providers to cut unnecessary declines. OpenAI says it's also working with fraud-prevention partners including Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd, and payment providers including Adyen, Checkout.com and Stripe. And the help center says plainly: "Wallet may not be able to complete checkout at every store."

For twenty years, a store firewall had one job: if it walks like a bot, block it. Now the bot walks in with a tokenized card and a signed note from its human. If your risk engine treats every agent checkout as fraud, you don't have a security posture. You have a CLOSED sign.

Act 4. The sentence after the sentence

Everything so far is a careful, human-in-the-loop checkout. Then comes the next sentence in OpenAI's announcement:

"Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters — such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods — and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today's protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization."

That's a plan, not a feature. There's no date and no promised scope. But it's where OpenAI says this is heading, and that's the day my thumb retires. We'll throw it a party. The agent will order the cake, within limits.

Here's the joke, and it's also the serious part: the roadmap is the risk register. Every phrase in that sentence is a question someone will have to answer. Spending limits: whose, and how big? Purchase categories: is a sweater "clothing" or "a gift for Mom"? Time periods: what does the agent do at 23:59 on the last day of the budget?

Finale. Who owns the sweater

At Hlinor we ask the same question about any agent that can take a real-world action. Who can spend, up to how much, with whose approval, and where is the record next Tuesday?

If your team is about to let any agent near money, not just this one, write these down first:

  1. Where it may buy: allowed merchants and categories.
  2. How much: hard limits per purchase and per period.
  3. Who says yes: which person approves, and how.
  4. What gets recorded: what's logged, where it lives, and who can read it.
  5. What happens on a bad charge: who calls the merchant, who calls the bank, and who calls the platform. Those are the three desks, and a name next to each one.

OpenAI says users keep their card's existing rewards and protections "for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective." Note the word eligible. Merchants, it says, keep control over pricing, fulfillment, returns and customer service. In other words, the agent got the card, but the relationship stayed with people.

Wallets used to hold paper. Now they hold an agent, a token and a fingerprint.

Your agent got a credit card. Somebody still has to own the sweater.

This piece is commentary on OpenAI's public announcement and help pages, and on coverage by Reuters and The Verge. The dialogues are made up. Hlinor hasn't tested ChatGPT Wallet, and this isn't financial, legal or security advice, or a recommendation to use it or to avoid it.

Sources

  • OpenAI: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet (13 November 2026)
  • OpenAI Help Center: Making purchases with ChatGPT Wallet (checked 15 November 2026)
  • ChatGPT Wallet Privacy Notice (effective 12 November 2026)
  • ChatGPT Wallet Terms (effective 12 November 2026)
  • Reuters via Investing.com (13 November 2026)
  • The Verge (13 November 2026)

Hlinor works on governance for AI agent systems: approvals, audit trails and control planes. This article was first published at hlinor.com.

title: How to Write a Prompt That Actually Helps
description:
A good prompt is not a magic phrase. It is a clear request. I write software, automation and electronics projects for a living, and I use assistants almost every day. The pattern that helps me is simple: say what you want, say how it should look, give the context the model cannot see, and then correct the first draft instead of starting over.

Official prompting guides say much the same thing. OpenAI's prompting documentation is built around clear instructions, examples, and giving the model enough structure to finish the job. Anthropic's prompt-engineering overview makes the same point in slightly different words: be explicit about the goal, the constraints, and the output format. You do not need a secret prefix.

A practical framework I actually use

I keep a short checklist next to the chat box. If a task matters, I fill it in before I press Enter.

  1. Goal. What should I have in my hands when this is done, and who is it for?
  2. Format. A list, a table, a commit message, a polite email, a JSON object, a 200-word explanation?
  3. Constraints. Length, language, tone, libraries I am allowed to use, things to leave out.
  4. Context. The facts the assistant cannot see: the error message, the file names, the battery voltage, the audience, the deadline.
  5. Example. One short sample of a good answer, if I have one.
  6. Check. If the first reply is almost right, I say what to change. I do not throw the whole prompt away.

That is the whole method. The rest of this article is just how those six lines look in practice.

A weak prompt, then a better one

Here is a request I used to write, and still catch myself writing when I am in a hurry:

Write a Python script that reads a CSV and sends emails.

It is not wrong. It is just unfinished. The assistant has to invent a library, a column layout, a mail server, an error policy, and a tone. You will spend the next ten messages unsaying things it guessed.

Here is the same task, written as a prompt I would actually send:

Goal: a small Python 3 script I can run from the command line to send
a reminder email to people listed in a CSV file.

Format:
- one .py file
- use the standard library only (csv, smtplib, argparse, pathlib)
- print a one-line summary at the end: sent / skipped / failed

Constraints:
- do not send anything when --dry-run is set; only print what would be sent
- skip rows with an empty email field and count them as skipped
- do not invent SMTP credentials; read host, port, user and password
  from environment variables
- keep comments to a minimum
- I will review the message body before I ever run this without --dry-run

CSV columns: name, email, due_date
Email subject: "Reminder: your item is due on {due_date}"
Body: short, polite, plain text, in English.

Please show the script first, then a short example of how to run it.

The second prompt is longer, but it removes most of the guessing. The first answer is usually close enough that I only have to adjust a few lines.

Put the goal in the first line

Models pay attention to the beginning of a prompt. I start with the outcome, not the backstory.

  • Weak: "I have been thinking about rewriting our onboarding email and maybe you can help."
  • Better: "Write a 120-word onboarding email for a new freelance client. Tone: calm, direct, no marketing slogans. Include: what happens this week, when I will send the first draft, and how to reach me."

If the task has a reader, I name the reader. "Explain this circuit to a computer science student who has not done much analogue work" produces a different answer than "Write this up for a hardware engineer who already knows the parts."

Say the format, or you will get an essay

If I need a table, I say "a markdown table with these columns." If I need a git commit message, I say "one subject line under 72 characters, then a short body." If I need code, I say which language and which libraries are allowed.

This is also where I stop the model from padding. "No preamble. No 'hope this helps'." is a dull instruction, but it saves me a cleanup pass.

OpenAI's own guidance has said for years that you should be specific about length, format and style, and that examples help more than adjectives. I have found that to be true.

Give context the model cannot see

An assistant does not see your desk, your repository, or your last email. If you leave those out, it will fill the gaps with something typical, which is often wrong for your case.

For code, I paste the error, the function, and the versions. For electronics, I state the supply voltage, the load, and whether this is a prototype or a device that has to run for months on a battery. For writing, I state what must not be claimed — no invented clients, no invented benchmarks, no private details.

I also say what to do when the context is missing: "If a fact is not in the text I pasted, say you do not know. Do not invent a citation."

Use an example when the shape matters

One short example is worth a paragraph of style notes. If I want a changelog written a certain way, I paste two real lines from an old changelog and say "match this shape." That is few-shot prompting, and it is ordinary engineering, not a trick.

Keep the example small. A huge example buries the actual task.

For a hard task, ask for steps, then the answer

If the job is a refactor, a diagnosis, or a design choice, I ask the assistant to work through the problem in short steps and only then give the final answer. OpenAI has long recommended giving the model time to work out a solution instead of jumping to a conclusion. Anthropic's guides similarly suggest breaking complex work into stages.

I do not always need to see the reasoning in the final document. Sometimes I say: "Think the options through first. In the final answer, give me the recommendation and the two main risks."

Correct the draft. Do not start from zero

The first reply is a draft. If it is 80 percent right, I reply with the 20 percent that is wrong: "Keep the function, but drop the extra class. Use argparse instead of hard-coded paths. The CSV has a header."

Starting a brand-new chat is useful when the thread has become messy. It is not useful when you only need a small correction.

What I do not bother with

I ignore lists of "secret codes," magic roles, and copied jailbreaks. They age badly, they often do not do what the post claims, and they teach the wrong habit: looking for a hidden switch instead of stating the task. If a product has a useful feature — custom instructions, projects, temporary chats, a system prompt in an API — use the official feature. I will write about those separately.

I also do not pretend that a perfect prompt removes the need to check the result. Assistants still invent function names, paper titles and confident explanations. A clear prompt reduces the mess. It does not replace a review.

A short template you can copy 

Goal: [what I need, and who it is for]

Format: [list / table / code / email / length / language]

Constraints:
- [must include]
- [must avoid]
- [tools or libraries allowed]

Context:
- [the facts, errors, or files the model cannot see]

Example (optional):
[one short sample of a good answer]

Process: if the task is complex, work through it in steps.
If something is unknown, say so instead of guessing.

Now do the task.

Fill it in, send it, and then edit the reply. That is enough. Clear instructions still beat clever phrasing.

I'm Saulius, an independent full-stack, automation and electronics developer in Kaunas, Lithuania. You can also find me on Dev.to and LinkedIn.

title: Your Agent Now Checks Every Page It Builds
description:
You let your agent move a client's website. Thirty pages, rebuilt as editable sections, done in an afternoon. The agent reports "all pages created". Then someone on the team clicks through before the handover and finds a link to a page that's still a draft, a team photo without alt text, and a heading structure that jumps all over the place.

None of that is the agent being careless. In most AI-and-CMS setups, a write ends with "saved". Whether the page works for a visitor is something the agent never hears about.

Back in August I wrote about the three ways an agent can check its own work in Neleto. The last of them, opening the live page and looking at it, only worked if your agent had a browser. Since version 1.22, released on 12 November, the most common checks don't need one anymore. Neleto runs them itself and hands the result back with every write.

What happens now when your agent writes a page

When your agent creates or changes a page (page_create or page_update on Neleto's MCP server), Neleto renders the page the way a visitor gets it, with its layout. It checks the result and returns it in the same answer, under check. There's no extra step and no second tool to call.

A real example: find, fix, check again

On our demo site, we had Claude build an "About us" page with three mistakes in it on purpose:

  • an image without alt text,
  • a button linking to a services page that was still a draft,
  • a heading that jumps from <h1> straight to <h3>.

This is the check Neleto returned with the page (shortened):

"check": {
  "route": "/about",
  "summary": { "errors": 2, "warnings": 1, "notices": 4, "linksChecked": 2 },
  "issues": [
    { "severity": "error", "rule": "img-missing-alt",
      "element": { "component": "Text-element", "id": 22 }, "field": "content",
      "message": "Image https://uiblocks.neleto.app/image/user-upload/3b67a79c-… has no alt attribute (use alt=\"\" only for decoration)." },
    { "severity": "error", "rule": "broken-link",
      "element": { "component": "Hero", "id": 20 }, "field": "primaryHref",
      "message": "Link to /services answers 404: visitors get an error page (missing page, draft or typo)." },
    { "severity": "warning", "rule": "heading-skip",
      "element": { "component": "Text-element", "id": 22 }, "field": "content",
      "message": "<h3> \"Our team\" follows <h1> and skips a level." },
    { "severity": "notice", "rule": "title-too-short",
      "message": "The title \"About us\" is shorter than 10 characters." }
  ]
}

(Three more notices are cut here: no preview image, no preview description and no canonical link.)

Every finding names the section and the field. So the agent didn't have to search for anything. It did three things:

  1. Published the services page, so the button no longer leads to an error.
  2. Fixed the content field of the text section: the heading became an <h2>, and the image got an alt text.
  3. Gave the page a longer title.

The next write came back with a fresh check:

"check": {
  "route": "/about",
  "summary": { "errors": 0, "warnings": 0, "notices": 3, "linksChecked": 2 }
}

What's left are the three notices about link previews and the canonical link, which the agent wasn't asked to fix.

One more thing happened along the way. Publishing the services page ran the check on that page too, and it reported that the page has no <h1> and no meta description. You don't only hear about the page you're working on, but also about the one you just put live.

What it checks, and what it doesn't

Checked on every write Not checked
SEO basics: page title, meta description (missing or wrong length), og:image, og:description, canonical link, exactly one <h1> External links. Only links within the site are requested
Accessibility basics: page language, alt texts, link and button text (including vague "here" or "more"), form labels, skipped heading levels, iframe titles Colour contrast and layout. Those need a browser: an agent with one, or you
Links within the site: every internal link is requested. A link to a missing page or to a draft is an error Duplicate titles and descriptions across pages. The Site Health plugin covers that

And one thing no check covers: whether the page is right. Tone, facts, prices, a claim that isn't true. The check confirms the page works, not that it says the right thing. That review stays with you. It's a check of the basics, not an accessibility audit, but the basics are exactly what nobody looks at on page 27 of 30.

When the problem is in the template

In the example, every finding named a field, so the fix went into the page's content (page_update, or layout_update for the header and footer). Sometimes a finding names only a component. Then the problem sits in the component's template, for example a hard-coded heading level. The agent fixes the component once with component_update, and every page that uses it is fixed with it.

To re-check a page without changing it, for example after adjusting a layout, there's a new tool, page_check.

We've also updated the prompt for moving a website with your agent. The agent now fixes each page's findings before moving on, and re-checks every page through Neleto at the end. A migration that used to end with "all pages created" now ends with "all pages created and checked".

Why this matters if you run client sites

For an agency, the expensive moment isn't building a page. It's the email two weeks after handover: "the link on the services page goes nowhere". Each one costs an apology and an hour nobody pays for.

With the check coming back on every write, the mechanical mistakes are caught while the agent is still on the page, not by your client. Your review before handover can be about whether the site is right for the client, not about clicking through thirty pages looking for broken links.

Try it

The live check ships with Neleto 1.22 on every plan, the free plan included. Existing sites get it when they update to 1.22. Connect your agent, let it build or change a page, and look at the check in its answer. The MCP tools reference lists everything it checks.

Start free on neleto.io, no credit card needed.

— Martin

title: Speculative decoding: how LLMs get 2-3x faster with identical outputs (and when it won't help you)
description:
Tuesday AI Deep Dive. Most of the time you wait on an LLM, you're not waiting on math. You're waiting on memory. Generating each token means one full forward pass of the model, and those passes have to happen one after another. Speculative decoding is the trick behind a lot of "why is this model suddenly so fast" announcements: it lets a big model emit several tokens per forward pass without changing what it would have output.

Here's how it works, the one formula worth remembering, the variants you'll see in serving stacks, and when it won't help.

Why decoding is slow in the first place

From the Google paper that introduced the idea (Leviathan, Kalman, Matias, 2022): "decoding K tokens takes K serial runs of the model." Token 5 depends on token 4, so you can't parallelize across the output.

DeepMind's speculative sampling paper (Chen et al., 2023) adds the key hardware fact: transformer sampling is typically memory-bandwidth bound. For each new token, the accelerator streams the model's weights from memory, does relatively little arithmetic with them, and moves on. The Medusa paper puts it the same way: each step "necessitates moving the full model parameters from High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to the accelerator's cache."

The consequence: scoring several tokens in one forward pass costs about the same wall time as scoring one. Chen et al. build the whole method on that observation: the latency of scoring a short continuation in parallel "is comparable to that of sampling a single token from the larger target model."

So if someone could hand the big model a good guess of the next few tokens, it could check them all at once.

The algorithm: draft, verify, accept

You need two models:

  • a target model (the big one whose outputs you actually want), and
  • a draft model (small and fast, ideally similar in behavior).

Each iteration:

  1. Draft. The small model generates 纬 tokens autoregressively (cheap, because it's small).
  2. Verify. The target model runs one forward pass over the prefix plus all 纬 drafted tokens, getting its own probability for every position in parallel.
  3. Accept or reject, left to right. For each drafted token x, the target accepts it with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p is the target's probability and q the draft's. At the first rejection, it stops and samples a corrected token from the normalized residual max(0, p - q).
  4. If all 纬 are accepted, the target's pass already gives you the distribution for one more token, so you get a bonus token for free.

Every iteration produces at least one token from the target model, and up to 纬+1.

The important part is step 3. This modified rejection sampling is what makes the method exact: the paper proves the output follows the target model's distribution. With greedy decoding that means the same tokens you'd have gotten without the draft. Leviathan et al. show 2X-3X acceleration on T5-XXL "with identical outputs." Chen et al. report 2-2.5x decoding speedup on Chinchilla 70B in a distributed setup, preserving the target distribution "within hardware numerics."

That's the difference from just using a smaller model: the small model only proposes. The big model always has the final say.

The one formula: acceptance rate decides everything

Leviathan et al. define 伪, the expected acceptance rate, as a measure of how well the draft approximates the target (formally 伪 = E[min(p, q)] summed over tokens). Under a simplifying i.i.d. assumption, the expected number of tokens per target call is:

E[tokens per target pass] = (1 - 伪^(纬+1)) / (1 - 伪)

Plugging numbers into that formula (my arithmetic, not benchmark results), with 纬 = 4 drafted tokens:

Acceptance rate 伪 Expected tokens per target pass
0.6 ~2.31
0.8 ~3.36

Two practical reads:

  • 伪 matters more than 纬. Drafting more tokens has diminishing returns, because every extra token must survive all the earlier ones. A bad draft model with a big 纬 just burns compute on tokens that get thrown away.
  • Tokens per pass isn't wall-clock speedup. You also pay for running the draft model. The paper's walltime analysis assumes you have spare compute for the extra concurrency.

The variants you'll actually meet

The classic two-model setup has a practical problem the Medusa authors call out: "acquiring and maintaining a separate draft model." It needs the same tokenizer, should behave like the target, and must be served alongside it. Newer methods attack exactly that:

  • Medusa (Cai et al., 2024). No separate model. Extra decoding heads on top of the target predict several future tokens, and tree-based attention verifies multiple candidate continuations in one step. Medusa-1 (heads trained on a frozen backbone) is lossless and reports over 2.2x speedup. Medusa-2 trains heads together with the backbone for higher speedup, but needs a careful training recipe.
  • EAGLE (Li et al., 2024). Drafts at the feature level (the second-to-top layer) instead of the token level, feeding in the token sequence advanced by one step to resolve uncertainty. For LLaMA2-Chat 70B it reports 2.7x-3.5x latency speedup and doubled throughput "while maintaining the distribution of the generated text."
  • Prompt lookup / n-gram drafting. The "draft model" is just string matching: propose the continuation that follows a matching n-gram in the prompt. It costs almost nothing and shines when outputs copy from inputs (summarizing a document, editing code, RAG answers quoting sources). The reference implementation describes itself as a simple speculative decoding technique integrated in vLLM and Hugging Face transformers.

When it won't help (or will hurt)

Speculative decoding sells spare compute for lower latency. That trade isn't always available:

  • High-batch, throughput-bound serving. The whole trick relies on decoding being memory-bound with idle compute. When you're already batching many requests, the GPU's compute is busier and verifying rejected draft tokens is real waste. Benchmark at your actual batch sizes and concurrency, not with one request.
  • Low acceptance. Creative, high-temperature output, or a draft model trained on different data, means low 伪 and small gains. Code, structured output and text that copies from the prompt tend to be more predictable.
  • Operational cost. A separate draft model means more GPU memory, matching tokenizers, and one more thing to upgrade when the target changes. Heads (Medusa/EAGLE) need training per target model.
  • "Lossless" depends on the implementation. The math is exact, but some variants trade exactness for speed. Medusa's paper, for example, proposes a "typical acceptance" scheme to boost acceptance while maintaining generation quality, which is a quality claim, not a distribution guarantee. Know which mode you've turned on.

What I'd do as an AI engineer

  1. Measure first. Log time to first token and inter-token latency per request. If your users are waiting on long generations at low concurrency, speculative decoding is a strong candidate.
  2. Start with the cheapest draft. For RAG, summarization and code edits, try n-gram/prompt lookup drafting before training anything.
  3. Track acceptance rate in production. It's the number that tells you whether the draft still fits your traffic. A drop after a prompt change or model upgrade explains a latency regression.
  4. Benchmark at real load. Compare p50 and p95 latency and tokens/sec with and without speculation at your typical and peak batch sizes.
  5. Verify outputs, don't assume. With greedy decoding, run a fixed eval set with speculation on and off and diff the outputs. They should match; if they don't, find out why before shipping.
  6. If you use hosted APIs, you can't control this, but it helps explain why output speed varies by provider for the same open model.

The takeaway

Speculative decoding works because a big model can check several guesses in the time it takes to write one token, and a clever acceptance rule makes those guesses invisible in the output. The speedup lives or dies on one number, the acceptance rate, and on whether your hardware has idle compute to spend.

What are you serving where latency per token matters most, chat, code, or agents?

References

  • Leviathan, Kalman, Matias (2022), Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding: https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192
  • Chen et al. (2023), Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling (DeepMind): https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318
  • Cai et al. (2024), Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774
  • Li et al. (2024), EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15077
  • Prompt lookup decoding: https://github.com/apoorvumang/prompt-lookup-decoding

title: Your prompt contract should fail a test before your agent does
description:
A refund agent has one rule in its prompt: never approve an amount above 200 without manager sign-off. In March the limit is raised to 500 for a VIP pilot. Nobody lowers it again. In June a 340 refund is approved with no sign-off, and the only record the system keeps is the final answer.

The postmortem usually produces a new sentence in the prompt. That makes the rule more emphatic, not more testable. Nothing in the run record says which version of the rule was in force. Nothing asserts that the rule was consulted on this input. And no test would have failed when someone changed 200 to 500, because the rule was prose and prose does not have a diff you can assert on.

This is a contract problem. The spec that governs a semantic node deserves the same treatment as an API schema: versioned, validated before use, and covered by cases that fail when it changes. The phrase for that here is a structured prompt contract: a versionable spec of role, hard constraints, I/O contract and fallback rules, testable and portable, rather than free-form prompting.

Four fields, each with a checkable criterion

A contract has four fields. Each one has a characteristic way of being wrong, and each way can be tested without running the whole agent.

Role sets the scope of the spec, not a character to perform. Written as a field, it says which node this contract governs: applies_to: classify_refund_request. A spec that quietly starts applying to the escalation node as well is a scope bug, and the criterion is simple: list the nodes a contract is allowed to bind, and assert that no other node loaded it.

Hard constraints are predicates over declared inputs, each with an id and a destination when it fails:

constraints:
  - id: approve_limit
    predicate: amount <= 200
    on_fail: manager_review
    reason: approve_limit_exceeded
  - id: currency_known
    predicate: currency in ["USD", "EUR"]
    on_fail: blocked
    reason: unsupported_currency

The predicate reads declared fields, not generated text. If approve_limit has to parse the amount out of a sentence the model wrote, the same component is producing the value and checking it, and the check will pass as often as the model happens to agree with itself.

I/O contract types the boundary. status is an enum, answer is null unless status is answered, and evidence_ids is a list of ids that came from retrieval. Every field names its source: declared input, declared constant, or model output. A model may only write fields marked as model output. That constraint is enforceable at the boundary, and it is what stops a fallback decision from leaking back through a free-text answer field.

Fallback rules map each constraint's on_fail to a reason and a state transition. They belong in the contract and in the orchestrator. Under hybrid orchestration the deterministic backbone owns the transition, while the contract declares which reason should accompany it. If a reason exists only in the spec, the model has to remember to emit it, which returns the system to a sentence in a prompt with better formatting. If it exists only in code, an operator cannot see which fallback the node is meant to have. Both copies are checked against each other at load time.

Version the spec, then diff the constraints
