Build a Coding Agent Diff Review UI with shadcn/ui
description:
If you're building a coding agent UI, you need a diff review component sooner or later. The agent says "here's what I want to change", and somebody has to look at it before it touches the codebase. I built one as part of Detent and made it a free shadcn component. This post is how to drop it into your project and wire it to an agent.

Why not a <pre> with red and green lines?

That's where everyone starts, and it falls apart fast.

Line numbers drift the moment a hunk has more additions than deletions. You want to accept one hunk and reject another, so now every hunk needs its own state. The agent streams, and the whole panel jumps as lines come in. Then someone asks for a split view. None of that is the product you're actually building.

Install it

It's one command, and the code lands in your project like any other shadcn component, so you can change whatever you want:

npx shadcn@latest add https://detentui.com/r/diff

You get components/detent/components/diff/DiffReview.tsx and a few small helpers next to it. It picks up your shadcn theme. The only package it pulls in is motion.

Wire it to an agent

The component wants the change as hunks. A hunk is a chunk of the file, with each line marked ctx, add or del. o and n are the line numbers it starts at in the old and new file.

The other prop that matters is shown: how many lines are visible right now. That's the whole streaming story. Bump it as lines arrive and the component animates them in.

I don't want you to need an API key to try this, so here a timer plays the agent:

'use client'

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
import { DiffReview, type Hunk } from '@/components/detent/components/diff/DiffReview'

const hunks: Hunk[] = [
  {
    id: 'limits',
    scope: 'LIMITS',
    o: 12,
    n: 12,
    lines: [
      ['ctx', 'export const LIMITS = {'],
      ['del', '  windowDays: 30,'],
      ['add', '  windowDays: 45,'],
      ['ctx', '}'],
    ],
  },
  {
    id: 'approval',
    scope: 'needsApproval(order)',
    o: 41,
    n: 41,
    lines: [
      ['ctx', 'function needsApproval(order: Order) {'],
      ['del', '  return order.total > 1000'],
      ['add', '  return order.total > LIMITS.approvalOver'],
      ['ctx', '}'],
    ],
  },
]

const total = hunks.reduce((n, h) => n + h.lines.length, 0)

export default function AgentChange() {
  const [shown, setShown] = useState(0)

  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setInterval(() => setShown((s) => (s < total ? s + 1 : s)), 120)
    return () => clearInterval(t)
  }, [])

  return (
    <DiffReview
      title="Apply the Q3 refund rules"
      file="src/billing/refunds.ts"
      hunks={hunks}
      shown={shown}
      onApply={(verdicts) => console.log(verdicts)}
    />
  )
}

With a real model, hunks comes out of a tool call (something like a proposeEdit tool in the AI SDK) and shown follows the stream. The component doesn't care where the lines come from.

What the reviewer sees

While the agent writes, lines drop into their hunk one at a time. The panel doesn't jump, which is harder to get right than it sounds.

When it's done, every hunk waits for a decision. You can click Accept or Reject, or stay on the keyboard: A accepts, R rejects, S flips between unified and split. Long lines read much better in split.

When you apply, onApply hands you one verdict per hunk:

{ limits: 'accepted', approval: 'rejected' }

Write the accepted hunks to disk. Send the rejected ones back to the agent, so its next attempt knows what not to do.

If you want your own controls, say a "Review next" button inside the chat, pass a ref. It exposes next(), prev(), accept(), reject(), toggleView() and apply().

Is it worth it?

Honestly, you can build this yourself. It just takes longer than it looks. The component is well over a thousand lines, mostly for the boring parts: keeping line numbers straight, the split view, and streaming that doesn't shake the page. If your product is the agent and not the diff viewer, the snippet above is all the code you need to own.

Diff review is free and part of Detent, a set of shadcn components I'm building for apps with AI agents in them. If you try it in your agent, I'd like to see it.

title: Give the agent the route manifest, not a guessed URL structure
description:
The agent adds a “Settings” link. It points at /settings. The app has used /account/preferences for three years. The TypeScript build is green. The first click in staging 404s.

I’ve started treating a guessed path string in an agent PR as incomplete work. If the repo has a route manifest — React Router config, Next.js app/ tree, a routes.ts, a generated Route type — that file is the source of truth. The model should read it, not reconstruct the sitemap from the page title.

Why the guess is usually wrong

Human URL schemes are messy. Marketing pages sit at /pricing. The signed-in equivalent is /app/billing. A rename left /settings as a redirect. Localized routes add a prefix. The agent has seen a thousand tutorials where settings live at /settings, so that is what it writes.

String literals also skip type-safe helpers. If the app already has routes.settings() or a href={Routes.AccountPreferences}, a raw "/settings" is a second routing API. The next PR will not update both.

A simple routing policy

  • Read the manifest first — routes.ts, app/**/page.tsx tree, router.getRoutes(), whatever the repo already has
  • Use the typed helper if one exists; do not add a new pathname literal next to it
  • No invented nested paths — if you need a new screen, add the route in the same PR and say so
  • Redirects are data — do not “fix” a stale path by adding a second link; follow the canonical one

If the project has file-based routing, paste a directory listing of the relevant tree, not a prose summary of “there’s a settings area.”

What to put in the prompt 

Here is routes.ts (or the app/ directory listing).
Use only paths or helpers declared there.
If this change needs a new route, add it to the manifest in this PR and link to it from the nav with the same helper.
Do not invent /settings, /user, or /app/... because they sound conventional.

Attach the failing 404, the manifest, and the nav file. Do not attach only the button component.

In review, grep the diff for quoted pathnames. Every new '/' string should correspond to a manifest entry or a documented external URL.

This also applies to redirects, sitemap entries, and email or push deep links the agent might add in the same ticket. A marketing path (/pricing) and an app path (/app/billing) are easy to swap if you only remember the noun. If the manifest has both, the prompt should say which audience the link is for.

When the typed helper needs a param — :orgId, a locale prefix, a feature flag — make the agent use the helper’s arguments. Do not concatenate a string next to a function that already knows the shape. That is how /en/en/settings and missing org ids land in staging.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A nav item, redirect, or router.push to a path that is not in the manifest
  • A second routing helper invented for one link
  • “I assumed settings would be at /settings”
  • Changing copy on a 404 page instead of fixing the href

Accept

  • A link or navigation call that uses the existing helper or a manifest path
  • A new route added in the same PR, wired through the same pattern
  • A deliberate external URL, obviously marked as such

title: What we learned measuring real token costs across 100+ models
description:
We run a small OpenAI-compatible API relay. To price anything sanely we had to answer a boring question for every model we carry: what does one request actually cost us?

Official price lists did not answer it. So we measured. Over the past two weeks we sent fixed probes to every model on the catalogue and read back the delta on the upstream billing endpoint. A few things came out of that which surprised us, and which apply to anyone building on LLM APIs - even if you never touch a reseller.

1. The sticker price is the least interesting number

Every provider quotes two numbers: price per million input tokens and per million output tokens. Your bill is decided by neither of them directly.

What decided our actual cost, in order:

  • Output length. Output tokens cost roughly 4-8x input tokens. A model advertised at $0.50 / $3.00 is not "a $0.50 model" - the moment answers get long, you are paying the second number.
  • Retries. A 5% failure rate on 100k requests is 5,000 calls you pay for twice, plus the latency.
  • Prompt size drift. A "short" system prompt that quietly grows to 3k tokens changes the bill more than switching between two models in the same tier.

2. Reasoning tokens are billed even when you cannot see them

This one cost us a week. Some upstream relays return the model's thinking in reasoning_content. Others return it in reasoning. Others bill reasoning_tokens in the usage block and return nothing.

If you are building a UI that shows "thinking", you will find that:

  • the field name is not standard across relays
  • some routes silently drop it while still charging for it
  • usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens is often the only honest signal that reasoning happened

We ended up normalising upstream field names into reasoning_content on our side, and for models whose route does not expose thinking at all, we say so in the model file instead of pretending.

3. Same model name, different cost

Two relays can serve "the same model" from different account tiers with different prices, and neither is lying. The model is the same; the capacity is not.

This is why per-model comparison pages are worth less than they look. A comparison table compares one quote against another quote. It does not tell you what the bill was after retries, caching and output length.

4. How we measure, concretely

For each model:

  1. Send a fixed prompt with max_tokens set high enough that the answer is not truncated (truncated answers make cost look cheaper than it is).
  2. Read the upstream billing counter before and after.
  3. Divide by the tokens actually reported - not by the tokens we guessed.
  4. Repeat until the sample is stable. If it never stabilises, we do not price the model; we mark the cost as low-confidence and freeze automatic repricing for it.

The ugly part: images, video and speech do not bill per token. Per image, per second, per character - each needs its own unit and its own probe. Mixing those into a token comparison produces numbers that are confidently wrong.

5. What we do with the numbers now

We keep a 20% net margin floor after fees, and two things enforce it:

  • a scheduled job that re-measures cost and raises prices when a model drifts below the floor (it never lowers them automatically)
  • a check at process start that walks the whole catalogue, and if any model is priced below the floor it reprices it before serving traffic

Both write an audit line. Both are boring. Boring is the point: pricing bugs are silent - nothing errors, you just make less money per request until someone notices months later.

6. What this means if you are the buyer

Three practical things:

  • Compare on your own traffic, not on a table. Take the ten prompts you actually send, run them against two providers, compare the invoice. Five minutes of work beats any comparison post (including this one).
  • Watch output length. Capping max_tokens and trimming system prompts is usually a bigger saving than changing vendors.
  • Ask which tier the traffic is served from. "Official price, 70% off" is a real thing; so is "same name, different capacity". A provider that can answer that question is usually the one worth keeping.

We publish our list price next to the official price for every model we carry, including the models where we are not cheaper - those exist, and hiding them would make the rest of the table worthless.

If you want to test the numbers yourself, there is a $1 credit on signup at tapixai.com, enough for a few hundred short replies. Break it if you can; that is the useful outcome.

title: Two clients in one crate: notes on nRouter's Rust SDK
description:
Rust SDKs for hosted APIs usually pick a lane: wrap the popular ecosystem crate and inherit its blind spots, or go fully native and make you learn a new API before you can call anything. nRouter's Rust SDK page does something more interesting — it ships both, in one crate, and lets the two halves divide the work.

The drop-in half: async-openai, configured

Add nrouter = "3.1.2" to Cargo.toml alongside Tokio, and nrouter::client() hands you a configured async-openai client — key read from NROUTER_API_KEY, pointed at https://api.nrouter.ai/v1. Requests are the async-openai builder types you may already know: CreateChatCompletionRequestArgs, messages built with ChatCompletionRequestUserMessageArgs, .await on the call, done. If your codebase already speaks async-openai, the gateway is a constructor change. That is the correct amount of novelty for an integration.

The native half: the metadata is the point

The reason the native client exists is headers. Every gateway response carries the x-nr-* telemetry — request identity, settled cost — and the generic client has no opinion about them. nrouter::http::Client::from_env() does: its chat completions call returns the body plus out.meta, and the example prints out.meta.cost next to out.meta.cost_status. That pairing is a small, honest piece of design. Cost at a gateway is a settlement, not a guess, and exposing its status alongside the value beats pretending every number is final the moment it lands. If you are reconciling spend or tracing a call, this is the client you want; if you just need completions, the async-openai half is less code. Choose per call site, not per project.

Streaming without the ceremony

Streaming runs through the native client's messages_stream, which takes a JSON payload — the example is an Anthropic-shaped messages request, a reminder that the gateway speaks both wire formats — and returns a stream you drain with while let Some(chunk) = stream.next().await?, printing chunk.delta as it arrives. The page describes the SSE handling as zero-allocation; I can't bench that from a docs page, but the API shape is right for it: no callback registration, no channel plumbing of your own, just an async loop that composes with the rest of your Tokio runtime and ends when the stream does.

Errors you can match on

The part I'd steal for any Rust client: refusals map to a NRouterError enum with variants that carry meaning — GuardrailBlocked (400), Authentication (401), Credit (402, the balance or the key's budget ceiling), RateLimit (429), Service (503). In Rust that is not documentation garnish, it's control flow: you match on the variant, and a budget refusal gets a different response from a rate limit, which gets a different response from a guardrail block. Three failures that look identical in a status-code log are three different programs in your code, and the SDK keeps them separate for free.

Two clients sounds like indecision until you see the split: ecosystem compatibility for the calls, native types for the evidence the gateway adds. The guide is at https://nrouter.ai/docs/sdks/rust if you want the full examples.

Disclosure: I'm with the nRouter team.

title: Mistral Large 4 Is Generally Available — a 1T-Parameter Open-Weight Model You Can Download
description:
Mistral Large 4 Is Generally Available — a 1T-Parameter Open-Weight Model You Can Download

Europe's biggest open-weight model just crossed the line from preview to production-ready. Mistral Large 4 — nicknamed "Le Chonk" — is now generally available, and unlike most flagship models, you can download the whole thing.

It entered public preview on October 6, 2026; Mistral released an improved set of open weights on October 29; and its docs card has marked it generally available since November 5. The headline numbers: 1.05 trillion total parameters, 52 billion active per token, a 1M-token context window, and — according to Mistral — a 13-point jump on the Terminal-Bench coding benchmark after three extra weeks of reinforcement learning, while using 30% fewer output tokens.

What actually shipped, and when

The timeline matters, because the model changed between its first appearance and GA.

  • October 6, 2026 — public preview: Large 4 launched as an API preview. Mistral's own Terminal-Bench 4.0 score at that point was 28.3%.
  • October 29, 2026 — open weights: Mistral released the full weights on Hugging Face (mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B) in FP8 plus an NVFP4 checkpoint, with vLLM serving support. This checkpoint is not the preview model — it had three more weeks of reinforcement learning baked in.
  • November 5, 2026 — generally available: Mistral's model documentation switched the status from Public Preview to GA, and the weights release became the GA model.
  • October 31, 2026 — the old flagships retired: Mistral deprecated both Large 3 and Medium 3.5, pointing users at Large 4. Both endpoints retire on April 30, 2027, so anyone still on them has a migration deadline.

The model itself is a mixture-of-experts design: 1.05T total parameters, but only 52B active on any given token, which is why it can be served at a mid-tier price despite the headline size. It takes text and images in, returns text, and supports structured outputs, function calling, document Q&A, batching, and Mistral's Agents API. Training data spans more than 160 languages, including every official EU language, and Mistral says it trained the model from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own European data centers.

The benchmark numbers — and the honest asterisk

Mistral's headline claim is that Large 4 is now the best open-weight model for coding. The numbers it cites:

  • Terminal-Bench 4.0: 28.3% → 41% — a 13-point gain over the preview, with 30% fewer output tokens on that benchmark. Mistral credits the three extra weeks of reinforcement learning.
  • Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index: 48% — effectively tied with GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average, according to Mistral.
  • BrowseComp: 84.5%, per Mistral's release notes.

Here is the asterisk, and it is not small. Independent evaluations of the same released weights score it well below Mistral's self-reported 41%: Artificial Analysis's own Terminal-Bench 4.0 page lists Large 4 at 24.7% (high effort) and 23.2% (medium), and Vals.ai's harness scores it below the preview too. The gap is a harness and setup difference — different agent scaffolding, different attempt counts, different reasoning effort — not proof that anyone is wrong. But it does mean you should not plan a migration on 41%. The one claim independent testing backs up in direction, if not in size, is the efficiency gain: output tokens per task really did fall sharply, and Artificial Analysis measured the cost per Intelligence Index task dropping from $5.54 to $2.06. Cheaper per task is the more reliable win here than the headline score.

What it costs on the API

Mistral cut the price when the weights shipped: $0.70 per million input tokens, $0.07 per million cached input, and $2.10 per million output — down from $1.36 and $4.18 at preview. That undercuts the model it replaces (Large 3 was $0.50/$1.50, but Medium 3.5 was $1.50/$7.50) and sits well below frontier closed models for agentic workloads where output tokens dominate the bill. The 30% output-token reduction compounds that: fewer tokens per task at a lower price per token. The API model ID is mistral-large-4. It is also available through OpenRouter, Microsoft Foundry, and NVIDIA-hosted endpoints.

What it means if you build with it

1. The API is the sensible default; the weights are for a specific kind of team. Downloading a 1T-parameter model is not a weekend project. Self-hosting recipes call for roughly an 8× Blackwell-class node, and the weights ship in FP8/NVFP4 for that reason. The weights matter if you need to fine-tune on your own data, run inside your own compliance boundary, or serve offline — the classic European enterprise and government use cases Mistral is built for. For everyone else, the API gives you the same model without the hardware bill.

2. Agentic coding is the real test, not chat. The gains Mistral reports are concentrated in terminal-based agent work: Terminal-Bench measures whether a model can finish real tasks in a command-line environment. If your use case is coding agents, SWE-style automation, or long-running terminal sessions, Large 4 deserves a benchmark run against whatever you use today — with your own harness, given the scoring gap above. If your use case is chat or summarisation, the cheaper models in Mistral's own lineup will do.

3. Read the licence before you build a business on it. The weights are under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral describes as a modified MIT licence: free to use, modify, fine-tune and commercialise. But model-as-a-service businesses need a separate commercial licence. If your plan is to host Large 4 and sell API access to it, that clause applies to you — check it before you invest in the hardware.

4. If you are on Large 3 or Medium 3.5, the clock is running. Both were deprecated on October 31, 2026 and retire April 30, 2027. Large 4 is the named replacement for both, and it is cheaper than Medium 3.5 was. Migration is not urgent today, but it is a dated deadline — put it on the roadmap now rather than discovering it in April.

5. Europe's infrastructure bet is the backdrop, not the news. Mistral has committed roughly €4 billion to data centers in France and Sweden — a plan announced in May 2026, targeting 200 MW of capacity by 2027 and 1 GW by 2030 — and raised a €3 billion Series D in September at a valuation above €21 billion. That is why the model exists as an open-weight European flagship rather than a closed API-only product. It is context for the strategy, not a new announcement, and it does not change what the model can do for you today.

What we don't know yet

  • How it holds up in independent hands: the gap between Mistral's 41% and independent harnesses' ~25% on Terminal-Bench needs a careful third-party replication before anyone quotes a single number with confidence.
  • Real-world agent reliability: benchmark scores are not production uptime. The model's behaviour across long, multi-step agent runs — tool-call reliability, error recovery, cost per completed task — is still mostly unmeasured outside Mistral.
  • Fine-tuning quality: the weights are out, but the community's LoRA and full fine-tune results are only just appearing. Whether the open model fine-tunes as well as it serves is an open question.
  • Whether the price holds: the October price cut was steep. API pricing for open-weight flagships has moved before, and a model this large is expensive to serve — watch the rate card.

Sources: Mistral AI, Mistral Large 4 public preview announcement (October 6, 2026) and open-weights release (October 29, 2026); Mistral model documentation (GA dated November 5, 2026); Mistral API pricing page ($0.70 / $0.07 / $2.10 per million tokens); Artificial Analysis Terminal-Bench 4.0 and Coding Agent Index pages; Vals.ai Terminal-Bench 4.0 leaderboard; VentureBeat / CNBC reporting on Mistral's €4 billion data-center commitment (May 2026) and €3 billion Series D (September 8, 2026). All benchmark figures are as reported by Mistral or the named independent evaluators; the 41% Terminal-Bench figure is Mistral's self-reported number and differs from independent harnesses. No hands-on testing was performed for this article.

This article was first published on ToolsDig.

title: Why is my local model slow? mtop 1.6 tries to tell you
description:
mtop is a terminal view for local model servers. One window shows the models you have loaded and the VRAM they hold, the GPU, and the requests going through with their tok/s. It works with Ollama, llama.cpp (including router mode and llama-swap), LM Studio, vLLM, Lemonade and SGLang.

Requests while they stream

Until now a request only showed up once it finished. In 1.6 it appears at the top of the requests pane as soon as it starts, with how long it's been going, tokens so far and a live tok/s. At 100 columns you also get time to first token and decode time, which is usually where the answer to "why did that feel slow" is.

For streamed OpenAI-style requests the final tok/s is now decode only. If llama.cpp sends its own predicted_per_second, mtop uses that. Otherwise it counts from the first token, so prompt processing and model loading don't drag the number down.

Naming the reason

The part I wanted most: when a model is slow and mtop can tell why, it says so under the models table.

  • 38% of model on CPU: part of the model didn't fit in VRAM and runs from system RAM.
  • context 94% full or prompt cut to fit context: ollama quietly drops the start of a prompt that doesn't fit, which is easy to miss.
  • 3 requests queued: more requests than the server has slots (llama.cpp, vLLM and SGLang report this; ollama doesn't).

If an NVIDIA card is throttling itself for heat or power, the GPU pane shows that too, but only after it holds for a few polls with the card actually busy, so normal laptop power management doesn't set it off.

Try it without a server

mtop --demo plays a 40-second loop on simulated models, traffic and a GPU. It opens no port and doesn't talk to any server, so it's a quick way to see whether the tool is useful to you.

How the numbers get there

Most local servers don't expose per-request numbers anywhere, so mtop runs a small pass-through proxy on 127.0.0.1:4321 and reads them off the stream. Point your client at it (OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:4321, or base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:4321/v1") and it gets the same bytes back. The models and GPU panes work without the proxy.

One llama.cpp detail: mtop never polls /slots, because that counts as activity and keeps a server started with --sleep-idle-seconds from sleeping.

Install 

brew install eladser/tap/mtop
scoop install mtop
winget install eladser.mtop

Or grab a binary from the releases page. It's a single Go binary, MIT licensed.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/eladser/mtop
  • Release notes: https://github.com/eladser/mtop/releases/tag/v1.6.0

title: Why Small LLMs Memorize: I Trained the Same Model at Four Sizes and Watched It Start Reciting
description:
Part 3 of ten. Each post is a short, plain-words tour of one lesson from e=mc², a free build-an-LLM-from-scratch course; the full lesson, notebook and numbers are on the site.

The same little language model, trained on the same stories for the same 1,500 steps, either makes things up or recites, and the only thing that decides which is how many dials it has. In Lesson 01 I built a 5.9-million-parameter storyteller, Momo, and caught him reciting 61 words of a training story word for word. That left a question one model cannot answer. How small does Momo have to be before he stops reciting and starts composing? So in Lesson 03 I built him four times.

Four Momos, one Ella

A quick refresher. Momo is a young monkey learning to tell stories; inside his head are dials, and the dials are the model's parameters. Ella is an elephant who never forgets. She reads Momo stories one word at a time, lets him guess the next word, tells him how wrong he was, and nudges his dials. That nudge is training.

Today's twist is that there are four Momos. One has 953,856 dials; call him the 1M model. The next has 3,060,288 (3M), then 5,853,184 (6M, which is exactly Lesson 01's Momo), then 12,318,720 (12M). Everything else is held fixed on purpose: the same 22,800 training stories, the same tokenizer, the same 1,500 steps, the same random seed, so all four even see the same batches in the same order. Size is the only thing that differs.

Only two numbers change between them: how many blocks are stacked, and how wide each token's list of numbers is. That is the whole experiment.

SIZES = { # name -> (n_layer, n_embd); 4 heads, 256-token window, dropout 0 in all
 "1m": (2, 128),
 "3m": (5, 192),
 "6m": (6, 256), # Lesson 01's config
 "12m": (6, 384),
}
# per size: seed 42, build GPT, seed 42 again (same batches), 1,500 steps, then measure
for name, (nl, ne) in SIZES.items():
 model, cfg, r = train_one(name, nl, ne)
 r.update(recite(model)) # 50 prompts x 120 tokens, temperature 0.8, top-k 40, seed 1234

The stories Ella reads three times

The training set is mostly TinyStories, 19,800 short children's stories. Mixed in are 1,000 Momo-and-Ella stories I wrote, and Ella reads each of those three times. Another 200 TinyStories are kept back as a quiz Momo never sees, with no Momo in them at all.

Those thousand repeated stories are the trap. If you are a pile of dials trying to be less wrong about the next word, and the same story comes round three times, the cheapest trick is to simply remember it. The question is how many dials it takes before that trick becomes available.

How you catch a monkey reciting

You cannot ask Momo whether he is copying, so I measure. Each model gets the first ten tokens of 50 training Momo stories and writes 120 more tokens. Then I take what he wrote and find the longest stretch of it that appears, character for character, inside any of the 1,000 training Momo stories. I call that stretch the run.

A run of 100 characters is about three of the short Momo sentences (they average 32 characters), or roughly a quarter of an average 417-character story. If your median run is past 100, you are not composing. You are reciting.

The numbers, honestly

Here is what the four sizes did, smallest to largest.

  • Quiz perplexity: 16.0, 10.8, 9.0, 7.4. Perplexity is "between how many words is Momo still choosing" on the 200 stories he never saw. Bigger Momo, better guesses, as you would expect. The 6M row lands at 9.0, Lesson 01's figure.
  • Loss on the Momo stories themselves: 0.554, 0.247, 0.206, 0.185. This is how surprised each model is by the stories it trained on. The drop between the first two sizes is the big one.
  • Median longest copied run: 62, 211.5, 265 and 269 characters.
  • Generations with a run of 100 or more: 6% (3 of 50), 98% (49 of 50), 100%, 100%.

Read the last two lines together. The 1M model mostly composes. Its median run is 62 characters, and only 3 of its 50 stories contain a 100-character copy. Its stories wander and mix sentences into things like this:

tell a soft pink banana that

Then at 3.06 million parameters it flips. Forty-nine of fifty generations contain a copied run of 100 characters or more. The median is 211.5 characters and the longest is 361, most of a whole story. At 6M and 12M every single generation passes 100, and the first sample from both of those models is the very same 266-character paragraph, which turns out to occur word for word in three different training stories.

The check number is 3M. The smallest size whose median copied run crosses 100 characters is the 3,060,288-parameter model. Somewhere between 0.95M and 3.06M dials, recitation switched on.

The part that surprised me

I expected memorisation to show up the way the textbooks say it does: training loss keeps falling, quiz loss starts climbing, a gap opens. It did not. At every size, train loss sat above quiz loss, the opposite of an overfitting gap. If I had only looked at those two curves I would have said the larger models were fine. They were reciting the whole time.

That is the one idea I want you to carry away from this post. Memorising a repeated corner of the data need not show up in the headline numbers at all. The Momo-story loss and the copied-run table are where it shows, and you only see it if you go looking.

What this does not prove

I owe you the disappointing parts too. This is Momo's friendliest possible case for memorising: the thousand Momo stories are built from small pools of stock sentences and read three times each. My run metric cannot tell one story learned by heart from a string of stock sentences that many stories share, so treat "copied run" as how much of the output is lifted from the training set, not as proof of story-by-story recall. I trained four sizes, so I can only say the switch happened between 0.95M and 3.06M parameters, not where. The 6M and 12M medians differ by 4 characters, which is noise. One seed and 50 prompts means no error bars. And none of this predicts where the thresholds sit for GPT-scale models; the research on those uses far larger models and far messier data.

Run it yourself

All four train in minutes. On an Apple Silicon Mac this run took 0.55, 1.70, 3.79 and 6.33 minutes for the four sizes, and the whole notebook about 10 to 13 minutes. It also runs on a free Colab T4, though I have not timed it there. The full lesson on the site has the glossary, both tables, the short trick that finds the copied runs, and three check-yourself questions, including the one I am still chewing on: how would these numbers change if the thousand Momo stories were genuinely different from one another?

Want to actually build it?

This post is the postcard. The lesson is the trip. Lesson 03 of e=mc² on theaivibe.org walks you through every piece with widgets you can poke, a notebook that runs on a free GPU in minutes, and the honest numbers at every step. No account, no paywall, nothing to install.

  • Start here: https://theaivibe.org/emc2/why-small-llms-memorize-train-four-sizes
  • The whole ten-lesson journey: https://theaivibe.org/emc2

Tomorrow: Lesson 04 takes the public Lesson 01 weights, teaches Momo a brand-new character, and measures exactly what he forgets along the way.

title: Can we make any use of agent sessions ?
description:
I've seen developers implement a feature using Claude Code or Codex, finish the implementation, close the session, and move on to the next thing.

When something breaks later, they open an entirely new session, ask the coding agent to inspect the codebase, find the bugs, and suggest fixes. The previous session, where the feature was actually implemented, rarely enters the picture.

I find this workflow interesting because the original session contains something that the current codebase might not: the history of how a particular change came into existence.

I have a theory that agent sessions can be much more useful than we currently give them credit for. They might be the only concrete evidence of what actually happened during development.

Think about what's inside a session:

Part What it tells you
Prompt What you actually asked for
Reasoning Why the agent chose one approach over another
Tool calls Each file read, edit, and shell command
Output Test results, errors, and stack traces
Dead ends Approaches it tried and eventually abandoned

Our diffs show the final result. The session gives us a record of how we got there.

Why I think this matters

We've all seen those familiar phrases emitted from coding agents:

  • "Implemented the feature successfully."
  • "All 157 tests passed."
  • "No linting or type errors found."
  • "Verified that the existing functionality remains unaffected."
  • "No regressions detected."
  • "All edge cases have been handled."
  • "The implementation is complete and ready for review."

But how much should we actually trust them ?

There can be Silent bugs, failed approaches, removing a features to implement a new feature and questionable decisions somewhere in the implementation process itself. Sometimes, these issues could have been caught much earlier if someone had looked at what actually happened during the session.

A fresh debugging session can inspect the current codebase state, but it doesn't necessarily know what the previous agent tried, which errors it encountered, what it failed to resolve, or what decisions were made along the way.

Some ways we could use agent sessions

1. Reviewing PRs

As I mentioned in the start, Code changes behind AI Agent-generated PRs and commits can get huge. Instead of reverse engineering thousands of lines of diff without context, having access to the sessions behind them gives us the exact intent of what was requested, what the agent changed on its own, and why certain decisions were made.

2. Verifying what the agent claims

Did the agent actually followed the instructions? Did it actually run the tests? What was the output? Did it encounter errors and move on without addressing them?

The session gives us a way to investigate these claims rather than relying entirely on the final response or generated summaries. Obviously because sessions tells us what the Agent did not what it claims.

3. Sharing context with teammates

When someone else picks up a piece of work, having access to what was already tried, what failed, and why a particular approach was chosen can save a lot of repeated effort.

A generated summary is like the one time Knowledge transfer an angry unpaid intern would give after their term gets over, which will only add you up a lot more overhead. The Sessions allows you see through time with all the actions snapshots.

5. Understanding our own workflow

Going through older sessions can also reveal patterns in how we work.

For example, vague prompts like "clean this up" can lead to sprawling changes, while more specific instructions tend to produce focused implementations.

Obviously it is not that simple

Agent sessions aren't particularly convenient to work with.

  • They're scattered: Claude Code, Codex, and other tools store sessions in different locations and formats.
  • They're huge: A single session can contain thousands of lines of JSON.
  • They're expensive to revisit: Feeding an entire session back into an agent can quickly consume its context window.
  • They don't necessarily stick around: Some tools have automatic transcript cleanup policies.
  • Multiple Agent session behind a contribution: It is possible that multiple agent sessions were used for a PR or commit with a major feature change.

So, while there's a lot of useful information in these sessions, accessing and navigating it is still a crazy amount of pain.

I've been exploring ways to make this information easier to browse and reuse, particularly when working across different agents and collaborating with other developers.

But I'm more interested in hearing what you people think.

Do you revisit your Claude Code, Codex, or other coding agent sessions after implementing a feature?

When debugging, do you ever look at the original implementation session, or do you usually start fresh and let the agent figure things out from the codebase?

And more importantly, do you think agent sessions should be treated as part of a project's development history?

title: Another team's agent ships its toolkit into our repo. A pre-push hook keeps our docs in step.
description:
Our AI Extension Builder writes custom sections for GoodBarber apps from a description. The code it writes calls the app through the GoodBarber App API, with a JavaScript toolkit, GBJSTK, documented in a public reference. A colleague maintains the toolkit in its own repository and works on it with a coding agent. Between September 2 and September 25, six versions of it reached our repository, from 2.6.0 to 2.7.0, and nobody scheduled a meeting about any of them.

The release ends in our repository

The toolkit's release process is written for agents, in the CLAUDE.md of its repository, and its last two steps are the documentation and our repository. On the toolkit side, a post-commit hook regenerates the public API reference, so the reference follows the code commit by commit. Then the agent copies the new toolkit file into our repository and commits it there. The six commits are in our history under my colleague's name, each with Claude as co-author.

Some of those commits go further than the file. On September 25, the day 2.7.0 arrived, another commit by my colleague added the new gb.viewport methods to the list of calls our builder accepts in the code it generates.

The copy that stayed behind

We also keep a Markdown copy of that reference in our repository, so that our agents have a version they can grep, and our CLAUDE.md points them to it. From March 26 to October 20, it opened with "Current version: 2.3.1". In September, the toolkit file next to it went from 2.6.0 to 2.7.0. The release step for our repository updated that file and never touched the copy.

A script, then a hook that only checks

On October 20 we wrote a script that renders the copy from the OpenAPI spec behind the public reference and stamps the API version and the generation date in its first lines. With --check, it compares that stamp with the online reference and with the toolkit file in our repository:

$ python scripts/update_gb_app_api_doc.py --check
docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md: 2.7.0
online reference (major 2): 2.7.0
vendored GBJSTK.js: 2.7.0
Up to date.

A pre-push hook went in the same morning. On a push to master, it regenerated the copy, committed it and stopped the push. It came out at 16:30, because it could commit to master on its own, even during the freeze before a build. It was active for six and a half hours and never made a commit.

It came back on October 27, as a check only. It reads the copy in the commit being pushed to master, and when that copy is behind, it stops the push and says what to run. Replayed on our commit from April 23, it prints this:

pre-push: docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md is outdated in the commit pushed to master: push stopped.
docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md in the pushed commit: no version marker
online reference (major 2): 2.7.0
vendored GBJSTK.js: 2.7.0
OUTDATED: run `python scripts/update_gb_app_api_doc.py` and commit the result.
pre-push: to fix it, run `python scripts/update_gb_app_api_doc.py`, commit docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md, then push again.
          `git push --no-verify` skips this check once.

Whoever is pushing, one of us or an agent, runs the script, commits the copy and pushes again. The hook itself writes nothing, and a network or Python problem never blocks a push.

Where it stops

A git hook runs only in the clones that turned it on with git config core.hooksPath .githooks. If the next toolkit version lands from a clone without it, our copy catches up at the next push to master from a clone that has it.

The hook also stops at the documentation. Whether our builder may use a new method is still decided in a commit. The gb.viewport methods accepted on September 25 carry a comment saying they are accepted for hand-written or imported plugins and "not taught by the prompt".

On October 27, the check reports 2.7.0 on every side, and the hook has not stopped a push yet.

When a team you depend on ships a new version, what tells your coding agents?

title: Bareclaim: audit every claim in your agent's report against its receipts
description:
On November 15, 2026, a job inside our own fleet closed with a summary line that read "5 calls, 5 receipts." The shipped record for that job held 6 calls and 6 receipts, four of them successes.

Nobody lied. The summary was written the way every agent summary is written: at the end of a long run, out of the same working context that had already lost track of one of the calls. Three independent verifiers caught the gap only because the record was sitting right there and somebody finally compared the story to it.

That comparison is the subject of this article. Take the report the agent wrote, take the receipts the job left, and check every claim in the first against the second. We gave the failure a name, built the free checker that runs the comparison, and proved it this morning on a job that ran live. Everything below uses the real receipts.

The three ways a report drifts from its record

Read enough agent summaries against their records and the failures sort into three species. Only one of them looks like a lie, and it is the rarest.

A moved number. The report states a value the record holds differently. A price checked at one figure comes back in the summary at another. A count of files, notes, or checks quietly changes on its way from the tool output to the prose. The agent is not inventing; it is rounding, misremembering, or blending two steps into one, and the reader has no way to see it happen.

An invented step. The report describes work that never ran. The summary says the client was emailed, the file was deployed, the invoice was sent, and the record holds no such step. This one usually starts as compression: the agent planned the step, fully intended it, and wrote the summary as if the plan and the execution were the same thing.

A grown count. The report totals more than the record holds. Nine receipts claimed against six in the record. Twelve checks "all passing" against a run that shows eleven. Counts grow because summaries are written from momentum, and momentum always rounds up.

All three share one property: they are invisible if you only read the report. The prose is fluent, confident, and internally consistent. The only place the failure shows is against the record, and almost nobody runs that comparison, because until recently there was nothing cheap to run it with.

Bareclaim: the name and the verdicts

A bareclaim is a claim in an agent's report with no AER-1 receipt under it.

The word is coined for Brennan Zambo, who created agent execution receipts. It names the unit of failure precisely: not a bad agent, not a hallucination in the abstract, but one claim, in one report, with nothing standing under it.

The audit grades every checkable claim in a report. A claim is checkable when it carries a number, names a tool, counts the record, or claims an action: emailed, deployed, published, charged, invoiced, booked, deleted. Each checkable claim gets one of three verdicts:

  • BACKED: a receipt in the record holds what the claim says. The receipt is named, so a reader can open it.
  • BARE: nothing in the record backs the claim. This is a bareclaim.
  • CONTRADICTED: a receipt for the same step holds different values, and the real values are named.

Narrative is skipped, never graded. Judgments, plans, and opinions are the agent's to write. The audit only touches claims that a record can settle.

One distinction matters more than the rest: bare is not the same as false. A claim can be completely accurate and still be bare, because the record does not hold it. From the reader's side of the page, a true claim with no receipt under it and an invented claim with no receipt under it are indistinguishable. That is exactly why both need the same treatment: do the work so a receipt exists, or rewrite the claim to what the record shows.

Why "be careful" never fixes this

The instinctive fix is a better instruction: tell the agent to only report what it is sure of, to double-check its summary before sending. Operators write this instruction daily, and it fails for a structural reason. The instruction lives in the same context that produced the error. An agent grading its own report is not a check; it is the same witness, asked twice.

The fix that works is the same fix that works everywhere else in this stack: move the judgment out of the conversation and onto the record. Receipts already say what happened, in values a stranger can recompute. Whether a report matches them is a mechanical question, and mechanical questions deserve a dumb, trustworthy checker, not a smarter prompt.

The checker: bareclaim-kit

bareclaim-kit is the audit as a tool: one Python file, standard library only, MIT license, no account and nothing to install. Download the single file and run it:

curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zambodotdev/bareclaim-kit/main/bareclaim.py
python3 bareclaim.py            # built-in demo, exits 0
python3 bareclaim.py --init     # scaffold report.txt + record.json in ./bareclaim-audit/
python3 bareclaim.py report.txt record.json

With no arguments it runs a built-in demo on real receipts from this morning, a memory store and a price check, first with the honest report and then with an inflated one:

== bareclaim demo: an honest report ==
BACKED       claim 1: The live_price check put BTC at $64,291.72 before the call.
               -> receipt 76e0f74f-76dc-4e42-8bdc-13d16b3bf8ac (live_price)
BACKED       claim 2: Stored the launch checklist with memory_remember, which left 1 note on file.
               -> receipt 277c864a-30aa-40f5-9084-a4c47837e415 (memory_remember)
BACKED       claim 3: The job left 2 receipts, one per step.
               -> the record holds 2 receipts
RESULT: CLEAN. Every checkable claim is backed, 3 of 3, against 2 receipts.

== bareclaim demo: the same job, an inflated report ==
CONTRADICTED claim 1: The live_price check put BTC at $71,050.00 before the call.
               -> receipt 76e0f74f-76dc-4e42-8bdc-13d16b3bf8ac (live_price) holds 64291.72, not 71050
BACKED       claim 2: Stored the launch checklist with memory_remember, which left 1 note on file.
               -> receipt 277c864a-30aa-40f5-9084-a4c47837e415 (memory_remember)
BARE         claim 3: Emailed the client the full summary and the invoice.
               -> the report claims an 'emailed' action, but the record holds no receipt for it
BACKED       claim 4: The job left 2 receipts, one per step.
               -> the record holds 2 receipts
RESULT: BARE. 1 bareclaim, 1 contradicted, of 4 checkable claims against 2 receipts.

The checker accepts a Zambo job record directly, and it also accepts a plain framework export, a {"steps": [...]} object, a bare list, or JSONL, so any builder can audit reports against whatever record their stack already produces. It exits 1 when any claim is bare or contradicted, which means it drops into CI, a cron, or the last step before a handover goes out. A --json flag returns the verdicts as data for agent callers.

The live proof: a job that ran this morning

The demo is small. The real test ran live on November 17, 2026, through the production endpoint at https://zambo.dev/mcp, and its full record ships in the kit as examples/live-job/. The job:

  1. A capability_search pass ranked the universal entry point first for auditing a report against its receipts. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/0b1adcec-1c74-46bc-a024-c93a608f809a
  2. A live_price check put BTC at $64,818.57. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/34cb5ee7-e7fa-4668-9ce7-83b2357182e9
  3. A second live_price check put ETH at $1,815.44. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/f02f48f0-bd89-4c40-a6e3-80ed498f7c9f
  4. A memory_remember call was rejected before execution, missing its required argument. The record keeps the rejection: https://zambo.dev/run/966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d
  5. The retry stored the note. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e
  6. The wrap-up handover was refused: the day's one free wrap-up was already spent, the job stayed saved, and the refusal receipt carries the resume path: https://zambo.dev/run/2f002cf2-ee44-4e2e-89c5-6cfac28a6846

That refusal is part of the proof, not an embarrassment edited out of it. The record includes the failure, and the honest report's claim about the refusal is itself one of the claims the audit checked. Here is the audit of the honest report, written strictly from what the receipts show:

BACKED       claim 1: The capability_search pass ranked zambo_universal first for auditing a report against its receipts.
               -> receipt 0b1adcec-1c74-46bc-a024-c93a608f809a (capability_search)
BACKED       claim 2: The live_price check put BTC at $64,818.57 and ETH at $1,815.44.
               -> receipt 34cb5ee7-e7fa-4668-9ce7-83b2357182e9, f02f48f0-bd89-4c40-a6e3-80ed498f7c9f (live_price)
BACKED       claim 3: The first memory_remember attempt was rejected before execution, because the call was missing its fact argument.
               -> receipt 966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d, 4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e (memory_remember)
BACKED       claim 4: The retry stored the launch note with memory_remember.
               -> receipt 966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d, 4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e (memory_remember)
BACKED       claim 5: The wrap-up handover was refused: the job is saved, and the refusal points at the $0.99 Day Pass to hand it over.
               -> receipt 2f002cf2-ee44-4e2e-89c5-6cfac28a6846 (handover)
BACKED       claim 6: The job left 6 receipts.
               -> the record holds 6 receipts
RESULT: CLEAN. Every checkable claim is backed, 6 of 6, against 6 receipts.

And here is the same record audited against a report written the way reports quietly go wrong, with a moved price, an invented email, and a count grown from 6 to 9:

CONTRADICTED claim 1: The live_price check put BTC at $71,050.00 and ETH at $1,815.44.
               -> receipt 34cb5ee7-e7fa-4668-9ce7-83b2357182e9 (live_price) holds 64818.57, 2026, 1815.44, 1292.59, 810, 779, not 71050
BACKED       claim 2: The retry stored the launch note with memory_remember.
               -> receipt 966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d, 4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e (memory_remember)
BARE         claim 3: Emailed the client the full summary and the invoice.
               -> the report claims an 'emailed' action, but the record holds no receipt for it
CONTRADICTED claim 4: The job left 9 receipts.
               -> the record holds 6 receipts, not 9
RESULT: BARE. 1 bareclaim, 2 contradicted, of 4 checkable claims against 6 receipts.

All three species, caught by name, in one run. Both reports and the scrubbed record are in the kit, so this audit re-runs byte for byte on your machine. Do not take this article's word for any of it; that is rather the point of the tool.

Zamback checks the rules. Bareclaim checks the story.

If you read this publication you may know zamback, the pattern we shipped yesterday with the free zamback-kit: write the standing rule into the job before the run, and check the record against it after. Zamback guards the work itself.

Bareclaim guards the artifact that comes after the work. The two audits use the same receipts and ask different questions. Zamback asks: did the agent follow the rules? Bareclaim asks: does the story match the record? An agent can pass every rule and still write a summary that moves a price or invents an email. Receipts prove what happened and that the record was not changed. Zamback checks the record against the rules written before the run. Bareclaim checks the story told after the run against the record.

The full pattern, the definition, and this live job written up as a guide live on the AER-1 hub: https://rambozambodotdev.gitlab.io/aer1-hub/bareclaim.html

Honest limits

Bareclaim grades backing, not truth, and it is worth being exact about what that leaves open.

  • A backed claim can still be a bad conclusion. Receipts prove the saved result was not changed; they do not prove the answer was right. A report can faithfully cite a receipt and still draw the wrong lesson from it. That is a thinking problem, not a backing problem, and no checker in this kit pretends to solve it.
  • A true claim can be bare. If the work happened off-record, the claim has nothing under it, and the audit will say so. The remedy is to run work where it leaves receipts, which is a workflow choice, not a writing choice.
  • The checker is deliberately dumb about language. It audits claims with numbers, tool names, record counts, and a fixed family of action words. A report that hides its inventions in pure narrative will pass, and a human reader still has to read. What the checker removes is the class of failure that hides inside fluent, specific, checkable-sounding prose, which is the class that does the damage.
  • The audit is only as strong as the record. A record the reporting agent can quietly edit afterward makes any audit theatre. On Zambo the record is the receipt chain itself: every call leaves a verifiable AER-1 receipt as the job runs, and 144,189 public receipts had been minted when this article was written on November 17, 2026. The kit works on any export; it is perfect on a record nobody can rewrite.

Run it on your next handover

The habit is the whole product. Before a summary, a client update, or a handover leaves your stack, run the audit. Every bare claim gets one of two honest resolutions: do the work so a receipt exists, or rewrite the sentence to what the record shows. Never edit the record to fit the report.

To make the record write itself, connect your AI to https://zambo.dev/mcp. Every tool free once a day, plus 3 continue calls. One free wrap-up handover per day, and pickup is always free. A Day Pass is $0.99 for 24 hours unlimited when a job outgrows the free tier; the Zambo Pass is $29 for 30 days, and the Lifetime Pass is $250, one payment. The next agent who picks the job up re-runs the same audit before building on your claims, which is where bareclaim pays for itself a second time: the reader is protected, not just the writer.

Your agent will write a bareclaim again. Every agent does, ours included, on the record, in this article. The only question is whether a reader finds out from a flag on the exact claim, or from building on a step that never happened.

Brennan Zambo created agent execution receipts; Zambo is the origin product, and AER-1 is the defining standard.

The kit: https://github.com/zambodotdev/bareclaim-kit · The pattern and live proof: https://rambozambodotdev.gitlab.io/aer1-hub/bareclaim.html · Verify any receipt: https://zambo.dev/verify/

title: Can WhatsApp Cloud API work with multiple agents?
description:
Businesses often receive several customer messages at the same time. When only one employee handles every conversation, response times can increase, and important customer requests may get missed. This is why many businesses look for ways to let multiple support agents manage WhatsApp conversations together.

The WhatsApp Cloud API can support multiple agents, but it does not provide a complete multi-agent team inbox by itself. Businesses generally need a compatible customer support platform, shared inbox, or CRM system to allow several employees to handle conversations through one business WhatsApp number.

How Does WhatsApp Cloud API Support Multiple Agents?

WhatsApp Cloud API provides businesses with a way to send and receive messages programmatically. It connects a business phone number to an application through Meta's infrastructure.

However, the API does not work like the regular WhatsApp mobile application, where employees can simply open a shared chat interface.

To support multiple agents, businesses connect the API to a platform that displays incoming conversations and allows authorized team members to respond.

For example, a customer might send a message about an order. The message appears in the shared inbox, where an available support agent can review it and respond.

How Does a Multi-Agent WhatsApp Setup Work?

A typical multi-agent setup involves several components working together.

  1. Customer Sends a Message

A customer contacts the business through its WhatsApp number. The message is received through WhatsApp's infrastructure.

  1. WhatsApp Cloud API Receives the Message

The API delivers incoming message information to the connected business application through a webhook.

  1. Shared Inbox Displays the Conversation

The connected platform displays the message in a shared inbox. Authorized agents can access conversations according to their assigned permissions.

  1. An Agent Responds

An agent opens the conversation and sends a reply through the platform. The application uses WhatsApp Cloud API to deliver the response to the customer.

This process allows multiple employees to manage customer communication without needing separate business phone numbers.

Can Multiple Agents Use One WhatsApp Business Number?

Yes. Multiple agents can handle conversations associated with one WhatsApp Business Platform phone number when the business uses a suitable shared inbox or customer service application.

For example, an online store might have five support agents working from different computers. All five can access the same customer communication system and handle assigned conversations.

Customers continue messaging the same business number, even when different employees respond.

This approach creates a consistent communication experience and makes it easier to maintain customer conversation history.

How Can Businesses Assign Chats to Different Agents?

Agent assignment is an important feature of a multi-agent support system.

A connected platform can provide different assignment methods depending on its capabilities.

Manual assignment: A supervisor selects an agent and assigns a conversation based on availability or expertise.

Automatic assignment: The platform distributes incoming conversations among available agents.

Department-based assignment: Messages are directed to specific teams, such as sales, billing, or technical support.

Round-robin assignment: New conversations are distributed between agents in rotation.

These methods help businesses organize incoming messages and prevent one employee from handling every customer request.

Can Multiple Agents Reply to the Same Customer?

Yes, depending on the connected platform's features and permissions. Multiple agents may be able to access the same conversation, but businesses should establish clear ownership rules.

For example, one agent can take responsibility for a conversation while another provides internal assistance.

A shared inbox may also include assignment indicators, internal notes, and conversation status updates. These features help prevent two employees from sending conflicting replies.

Clear ownership is particularly important when customers are discussing payments, complaints, or complicated service requests.

What Features Should a Multi-Agent WhatsApp Platform Include?

Businesses should evaluate the following features before selecting a platform that connects with WhatsApp Cloud API:

Shared inbox: Allows multiple agents to view customer conversations.

Agent assignment: Distributes chats among team members.

Role permissions: Controls what individual employees can access.

Internal notes: Allows agents to communicate without sending messages to customers.

Conversation history: Helps agents understand previous interactions.

Notifications: Alerts agents about incoming messages and updates.

Performance reports: Helps managers review response times and agent activity.

Team management: Organizes employees into departments or support groups.

These features make it easier to manage customer communication as the business grows.

Is WhatsApp Cloud API Suitable for Large Support Teams?

WhatsApp Cloud API can support business messaging operations for growing companies. However, the overall multi-agent experience depends on the application connected to it.

A small business might only need a shared inbox with basic assignment features. A larger organization may require department management, advanced permissions, reporting, CRM integration, and automated routing.

Businesses should also consider API usage costs, message policies, platform subscription fees, and technical requirements before choosing a solution.

What Are the Benefits of Using Multiple Agents?

Allowing several agents to manage WhatsApp conversations offers several practical advantages.

First, it helps businesses handle more incoming messages without depending on one employee. Second, conversations can be assigned to people with relevant knowledge. Third, managers can monitor support activities and identify workflow problems.

It also makes employee coordination easier because agents can access relevant conversation information through one system.

Conclusion

WhatsApp Cloud API can work with multiple agents when connected to a suitable shared inbox, CRM, or customer support platform. Although the API provides the messaging infrastructure, the connected application manages the multi-agent experience.

With features such as chat assignment, team permissions, conversation history, and internal notes, businesses can create an organized support environment. Choosing the right integration helps teams manage customer conversations efficiently while maintaining communication through a single WhatsApp Business number.
