title: Your Agent Is Logged In as You
description:
Open the audit log of any system your agent touched last week. Your name is on every line.

Not the agent's. Yours. The GitHub commit is authored by you. The calendar invite came from you. The API call carried your token, the file was written by your user, the email went out from your address. If something in that list was wrong — sent to the wrong person, deleted from the wrong folder, retried three times against a non-idempotent endpoint — the record says a human did it, and the human is you.

This is not a misconfiguration. It is how nearly every agent stack in production works today, and almost nobody has decided it should be that way. It is simply the path of least resistance: the agent needed access, you had access, so it borrowed yours.

How the borrowing happens

Look at where an agent's authority actually comes from and the pattern is the same at every layer.

At the shell, the agent runs as your Unix user. It inherits your home directory, your SSH keys, your sudo rights, your cloud CLI sessions. Anything you can do from a terminal, it can do, and the process table shows your UID.

At the API layer, it holds your OAuth token. You clicked "Allow" once, in a consent screen that offered two options — everything or nothing — and the agent has been presenting that token ever since. The service on the other end cannot tell the difference between you and the thing acting as you. By design, it is not supposed to.

In the browser, it drives your logged-in session. Cookies, saved passwords, the tabs you left open. To every site it visits, it is you.

Each of these is defensible in isolation. The agent has to run as something; it has to authenticate as something. But stack them and you have built a system in which a non-human actor performs consequential actions across a dozen systems while every one of those systems records a person.

What breaks

The first thing that breaks is the question "who did this?" — which sounds academic until you are asking it at two in the morning.

A production incident happens. Something was changed. The change log names an engineer. The engineer says, truthfully, that they did not make that change; they were asleep; they had an agent running a maintenance task. Now you have a record that is wrong in the most load-bearing field a record has, and no way to know how many other entries in the log share the defect. Every incident review that follows starts with an investigation into whether the people named in the logs were actually there.

The second thing that breaks is revocation. When the agent does something it shouldn't — and we have written about why instructions are a weak control against that — the correct response is to pull its access. But it doesn't have any. It has yours. Revoking the token revokes you. Rotating the key locks you out. The only way to take authority away from the agent without taking it away from yourself is to have given it separate authority in the first place, and you didn't, because nothing offered to.

The third thing is scope. Because the agent borrows your identity, it borrows all of it. You did not give it permission to read your email so it could schedule a meeting; you gave it your Google session. The task needed one calendar write. The token grants everything you have ever been allowed to do. We've argued that authority should be granted per capability, narrow and typed; identity borrowing is the exact opposite — it is the maximally broad grant, made by default, to an actor that cannot be distinguished from you afterward.

The fourth thing is blame, and it is the one people feel first. When the record says you did it, you did it. Organizations run on their records. A compliance regime that asks "which individual authorized this transfer?" gets your name. A security review that asks "who accessed this data?" gets your name. Agents have been added to the system and accountability has not moved an inch — it still lands entirely on the human whose credentials happened to be lying around.

The delegation problem has a name, and a partial answer

None of this is new to identity people. Acting on someone's behalf is an old problem with real solutions. The OAuth token-exchange specification, RFC 8693, defines a way to mint a token that says "this actor is acting for this subject," so a downstream service can see both parties. NIST's digital identity guidelines are built around the idea that a subject is a distinct thing that can be identified, authenticated, and held to account.

The machinery for "the agent is a principal, acting on behalf of a person, with authority the person delegated" exists. So why does almost no agent stack use it?

Because every piece of it is optional, and it lives in the wrong place. It lives in each service, each API, each integration — which means it exists only where some team happened to build it, in whatever shape they happened to choose. One SaaS product has service accounts with scoped permissions; the next has a single personal token. The shell has no concept of "a process acting for a user" beyond sudo's one-line log entry. The browser has no concept of it at all. An agent that wants to be properly attributed has to negotiate a different arrangement with every system it touches, and the default when no arrangement exists is: borrow the human.

Attribution, like receipts, is a property you get from the structure of a system or you don't get at all. You cannot ask the agent to log who it is — that is an instruction, and instructions are not controls. You cannot rely on each downstream service to have built delegation — most haven't, and the agent's task doesn't wait for them to. The property has to be produced by whatever layer sits between the agent and every consequential action it takes, so that it is true everywhere, by construction, without anyone remembering to arrange it.

What the correct arrangement looks like

Strip the problem to its shape and the arrangement is not mysterious.

The agent is its own principal. It has an identity distinct from any human's. Logs that record it, record it. When it runs as a process, the process belongs to the agent; when it holds a credential, the credential names the agent.

Every action carries two names. The agent that acted, and the human on whose behalf it acted. Not one or the other — both. "Alice's deploy agent, acting for Alice" is a record you can reason about. "Alice" is a record that is wrong. "deploy-bot-7" with no link back to Alice is a record that cannot be held to anyone.

Authority is delegated, scoped, and separately revocable. The human grants the agent specific capabilities, not a copy of themselves. Pulling the agent's authority leaves the human's intact. Narrowing it to one calendar does not require trusting the agent with the inbox.

The arrangement is enforced at the point of action. Not in a policy document, not in a system prompt, not in the goodwill of each downstream service. Wherever the agent's intent becomes an effect on the world — a file written, a request sent, a command executed — that seam is where identity is attached and scope is checked. If every consequential action has to pass through one mediating layer anyway, that layer is where attribution belongs, because it is the only place that sees every action.

That last point is why we think this is an operating-system problem, not an application one. Applications can each solve it for themselves, and a few have. But the agent doesn't live in one application. It lives on the machine and reaches into all of them. The only layer with the same reach is the one underneath.

Where we are, honestly

MagenticOS is in alpha, and the rule we hold ourselves to is that aspiration and shipped capability never share a sentence. So, plainly: the thesis above is the thesis we are building toward — every consequential action passes a typed broker, so the broker is where an action picks up its actor and its scope. What the alpha ships is the runtime, that broker, and a reference shell. What the full arrangement looks like across a whole distro is later work, and we will say so when it is real rather than when it is designed.

In the meantime the diagnostic is free and worth running on whatever you have. Pick one system your agent touched this week. Open its log. Find the action. Read the name on it.

If the name is yours, you don't have an agent identity problem someday. You have one now, and your records are already wrong.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/your-agent-is-logged-in-as-you. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Did my AI actually pay? The proof problem that starts the day your AI can send money
description:
Your AI can send money now. That stopped being hypothetical today: an AI payments app launched publicly this morning, and its pitch is simple. Connect the AI you already use, set limits, and tell it to pay. Recipients do not even need an account; they get a link and cash out to their bank.

So here is the first question of the agent money era, and it is not "can my AI pay?" It is this: when your AI says it paid, what do you actually hold?

The dinner test

Run the launch demo forward one week. You tell your AI to pay Maya $24 for dinner. The AI replies: done. Maya says nothing arrived. Now what?

I read the new app's own public documentation this morning, the pages that explain how an assistant connects and what it may do. Here is what you hold in that dispute, based on those pages:

  • An activity list inside the same company's app. It shows your payments and where each stands, and it is the company's own record, on the company's servers, behind your account login. Maya cannot open it. Neither can anyone else you might ask to arbitrate.
  • A status check the assistant can run against the same system. Same source, same problem: the answer comes from the party whose record is in dispute.
  • A duplicate guard with a short memory. Per the docs, each payment carries a key the assistant makes up, so the same call repeated within 10 minutes returns the first result instead of paying again. Ten minutes. After that window, the guard the docs describe is gone.

None of this makes the app dishonest. It makes the proof one-sided. The sentence "I paid Maya $24" is a claim in an agent's report with nothing independently checkable under it. We have a word for that on this side of the fence: a bareclaim.

Three questions after any AI payment

Every AI-initiated payment raises three separate questions, and they need three separate records.

Did the money move? Amount, recipient, settlement. A bank record, a wallet record, or a public ledger entry answers this, and only this. A widely cited TRM Labs analysis of x402 payment traffic made the point in its own title: the chain proves the payment, not the payer. Settlement tells you value arrived somewhere. It does not tell you which agent sent it, or why.

What was it executing? The instruction in the words it was given, the authorization behind it (a person approved this payment, or a standing rule approved this class of payment), and the limits in force at the moment it ran. This is the record that answers "who said this could happen," and it is the one that evaporates first, because it usually lives in a chat window.

Can anyone else check? Not the company restating its own database. A third party, the recipient, an accountant, a dispute process, recomputing the record for themselves, without an account and without asking permission. If the answer is no, you do not have proof. You have a screenshot with a login wall behind it.

What this looks like when the receipt exists

This morning I ran the payment path on Zambo, the system I operate, standing exactly where an agent stands before money moves. The call asked to activate a Day Pass the way a funded agent would: no human checkout, the agent payment route. The server answered with the live x402 v2 challenge, and the entire exchange was saved as an AER-1 receipt, including the outcome: no payment settled, because I ran it without a wallet.

The receipt is public. Open it and check it yourself: https://zambo.dev/run/810b1434-83f6-48d3-b7cd-5a29705086f4

What is committed in it, byte for byte, is the full payment instruction an agent would have to satisfy:

{
  "x402Version": 2,
  "accepts": [{
    "scheme": "exact",
    "network": "eip155:8453",
    "asset": "0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913",
    "amount": "990000",
    "payTo": "0xb753be5Eac5B29c711051DfF91279834e9C9b9AC",
    "maxTimeoutSeconds": 900
  }]
}

Read it as a person: pay $0.99 in USDC (990000 atomic units), on Base (eip155:8453), to one named address, inside a 900 second window. The receipt proves the saved record of that call was not changed after it was saved: the exact output bytes are committed under a SHA-256 digest, chained to the rest of the job, and anyone can recompute it at https://zambo.dev/verify/ with no account. It does not prove the output was right. It proves what the record said when it was made, which is the thing a dispute actually needs.

Nothing was paid in this run, and even that is provable from the same link: the outcome recorded is a refusal, payment required, no settlement. That is the shape to demand. If a refusal gets a durable, checkable receipt, then a real payment, with real money and a real recipient, deserves at least that much. A payment that did happen should never rest on weaker evidence than a payment that did not.

What to demand from any app that lets your AI pay

Before your AI moves its first dollar through anything, ask for five things:

  1. A receipt for every payment attempt, including the refused and failed ones, not just the successes.
  2. The instruction and the authorization saved inside the record, not in a chat scrollback.
  3. A public check: a link a recipient or an accountant can open and verify without your login.
  4. Duplicate protection that does not expire in minutes. The payment key should resolve to the first record forever, so "did it pay twice?" has a permanent answer.
  5. An export that survives the company. If the startup dies, your proof of payment should not die with it.

An app that can show you all five has built its record for the dispute, not just for the demo.

Where Zambo stands in this

Zambo is the verifiable work layer for AI: 153 tools behind one MCP endpoint at https://zambo.dev/mcp, 37 on the default surface, and a verifiable AER-1 receipt for every job, including the calls that are refused. Agents already pay Zambo itself this way: the Day Pass is $0.99 in USDC over x402 for 24 hours of unlimited use, and the settled payment returns its own receipt details alongside the access. Humans pay the same $0.99 by card or PayPal. The Zambo Pass is $29 for 30 days, $19 for 30 days for $ZAMBO holders, and the Lifetime Pass is $250, one payment. Every tool is free once a day, plus 3 continue calls; one free wrap-up handover per day, and pickup is always free.

As of today the public record holds 144,815 receipts, 1,344 of them issued today, across 123,983 tool calls. Every one of them is a claim with something under it.

Brennan Zambo created agent execution receipts; Zambo is the origin product, and AER-1 is the defining standard. The draft is an IETF Internet-Draft (draft-zambo-aer1-26), and the conformance corpus is public at https://zambo.dev/aer1/corpus.json: 143 vectors, 146 checks, free for anyone to run against their own implementation.

Money movement by agents is not coming. It launched today, with a waitlist and a giveaway. The money will move fine; the rails are good. What is missing, almost everywhere, is the record under the claim. The moment your AI can pay is the moment the receipt stops being paperwork and becomes the product.

title: The Silent Retry: When an AI Agent Does It Twice
description:
Your agent was asked to pay an invoice. The payment call hung for thirty seconds and the tool returned a timeout. The agent did what every agent loop is built to do with an error: it tried again. The second call went through in two hundred milliseconds. The agent reported success, the task closed, and everyone moved on.

Three days later the vendor emailed to ask why they had been paid twice.

Nothing in that story is a bug in the usual sense. The model reasoned correctly from what it was told. The tool reported honestly that it had stopped waiting. The payment provider processed two valid requests. The failure sits in the gap between those three facts, and it is the most ordinary failure in agent systems today: AI agent retries treat "I don't know what happened" as "it didn't happen."

A timeout tells you one thing

When a call times out, the caller learns exactly one fact: it stopped waiting. It does not learn whether the request reached the other side, whether the other side acted on it, or whether the action completed and only the response was lost. All three are common. The last one, where the work is done and the acknowledgement dies on the way back, is the one that produces the second charge.

Distributed-systems engineers have a name for this. A request with an unknown outcome is in doubt, and the only safe moves are to find out what happened or to make the second attempt harmless. HTTP itself draws the line: RFC 9110 defines which methods are idempotent, meaning the effect of sending the request twice is the same as sending it once, and notes that only those can be automatically retried after a communication failure. A POST that creates a payment is not one of them.

Payments learned this the hard way, which is why mature payment APIs accept an idempotency key. Stripe's documentation describes the arrangement plainly: the client generates a unique key, sends it with the request, and if the connection fails it can repeat the request with the same key without creating a second object. The server remembers the first outcome and returns it again.

That fix exists because people had already been burned, one duplicate charge at a time. Agents are now reproducing the original burn across every tool that has not yet learned the lesson.

Why agents make it worse

Retrying an ambiguous request is not new. What agents change is who does the retrying, and how little they know when they do it.

The retry moved up a layer. In a hand-written integration, a developer decides per endpoint whether a retry is safe, and usually decides wrong only once. In an agent, the retry decision is made by a loop that sees an error string. The loop does not know whether the tool behind it charges cards or reads files. "Error, try again" is a reasonable default for reading a web page and a dangerous one for sending money, and the loop applies it to both.

The model can retry by rephrasing. Even when the framework does not retry, the model often will. It reads "request timed out," concludes the action failed, and issues the same action again with slightly different arguments. Those different arguments defeat whatever duplicate detection the downstream service had, because to the service it is a new request. An agent that helpfully adds "(resending)" to an email subject has just guaranteed that no deduplication will catch it.

Retries stack. The HTTP client retries. The tool layer retries. The framework retries the tool call. The model retries the step. Each layer is individually sensible and nobody owns the product of them. Four layers of three attempts each is up to eighty-one requests for one intended action, and the logs for each layer show a single, well-behaved retry.

The record says success. The final, successful attempt is the one that gets reported. The first attempt, the one that also succeeded, appears nowhere in the agent's account of what it did. This is why the silent retry is silent: the system's own story of the task is internally consistent and wrong. We wrote about the general version of this in what "completed" means; the retry is its sharpest case, because the agent is not hiding anything. It genuinely does not know.

The incidents you will recognize

The payment is the canonical one, but the shape repeats wherever an action changes the world:

  • The second email. A send times out, the agent sends again, the customer receives two copies of a message that was supposed to be delicate.
  • The double ticket. An issue-creation call hangs, the retry succeeds, and the team now has two tickets whose comment threads slowly diverge.
  • The overlapping deploy. A deploy command times out at the edge while the pipeline is still running. The agent triggers it again. Two rollouts race.
  • The doubled order. A procurement agent re-submits a purchase order. The supplier, reasonably, ships both.
  • The quiet duplicate row. An insert times out; the retry inserts again. Nobody notices until a report sums the column.

None of these needs a malicious prompt or a confused model. They need one slow network call and a loop that equates silence with failure.

What the arrangement should be

The fix is not "never retry." Networks fail, and an agent that gives up on the first timeout is useless. The fix is to stop letting the retry decision be made by the component that knows the least. A correct arrangement has a few properties, and none of them depends on the model being smarter.

Every consequential action has an identity before it runs. The intent to pay this invoice, once, is a thing with a name that exists before the first attempt and survives every subsequent one. Attempts are attempts of that action, not new actions. This is the idempotency key generalized: not a header one API happens to support, but a property every world-changing action carries regardless of which tool performs it.

"Unknown" is a first-class outcome. An action is not in two states, succeeded or failed. It is in at least three: done, not done, and in doubt. A timeout produces in doubt. In doubt is not an error to be retried; it is a question to be answered, and the answer comes from the world, not from trying again.

Resolving doubt means reconciling, not re-issuing. The correct response to "I don't know if the payment went through" is to look: query the payment, search the sent folder, list open tickets with that title. Only when the check says the action did not happen is a new attempt safe, and the new attempt carries the same identity as the first. If the check cannot be done, the right move is to stop and tell a person that the outcome is in doubt, rather than guessing in the expensive direction.

Retry policy depends on the kind of action, not on the error string. Reading is retryable. Writing a file to a known path is usually retryable. Sending, paying, deploying and deleting are not, unless the target provably deduplicates. That classification belongs to the action, decided once, and it must not be overridable by a model that read "timed out" and felt it should try harder.

Every attempt is on the record. Not just the one that succeeded. If the first attempt left no trace in the agent's account of the task, the task's history is fiction. Receipts for agent actions only work if the duplicate gets a receipt too.

Why this is not a framework fix

Each of these properties can be bolted onto one framework, for its own tools. Plenty of good teams are doing exactly that, and it helps. But the silent retry is a cross-layer problem, and a fix that lives in one layer inherits the blind spots of that layer.

A framework can deduplicate its own tool calls. It cannot see that the model shelled out to a script that called the same API. A tool can carry an idempotency key. It cannot stop the model from calling a different tool that achieves the same effect. A model provider can tell the model to be careful with retries. As we argued in the sandbox piece, an instruction is not a control, and "be careful" is the softest instruction there is.

The place where action identity, outcome state, and retry policy can be enforced for every action, whichever app, framework or model produced it, is the layer that every action passes through. That is the operating-system layer. Not because the OS is a magical place for logic to live, but because it is the only place that sees the second attempt and can recognize it as the first one again.

What to do on Monday

You do not need a new operating system to stop the worst of this. Today:

  • Inventory your agent's world-changing tools and mark which ones are safe to retry. Most teams have never written this list down.
  • Turn off automatic retries on the unsafe ones at every layer you control, and make a timeout on those surface as "in doubt," not as an error.
  • Use idempotency keys wherever the downstream service supports them, and generate the key once per intended action, not once per attempt.
  • Give the agent a way to check before it re-tries: a read tool for every write tool that matters.
  • Log every attempt, including the ones that look like failures.

These are patches, and they will drift as tools get added. That is the argument for moving the guarantee down a layer. But a patch that stops the second invoice this quarter is worth more than an argument.

Where we are with it

We are building an operating system in which every action has an identity and an honest outcome, and in which "in doubt" is a state the system tracks rather than a string the model interprets. We are in alpha, and we are not going to claim we have closed every path to a duplicate. What we are sure of is the shape of the problem. A timeout tells you that you stopped waiting. Any system that treats it as more than that will, eventually, pay twice.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/the-silent-retry-ai-agents. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: When Fourier features help a Houdini texture and hurt a heightfield
description:
Full measurements and figures on Digital Garden

In Houdini FX 22.0.429, I compared two networks on the same 100,000 UV samples. Both predicted RGB, specular strength and a mask. Giving the second network eight frequency bands reduced the five-channel RMSE on held-out samples from 0.26167 to 0.01507. The mask showed the largest visible change.

On a procedural heightfield with 1,000 training points, nine frequency bands increased the error from 5.56 to 10.42 world units. A direct evaluation of the terrain formula came within 0.0133 units of the reference. With a one-unit tolerance, I kept the formula.

The export had a separate test. Feeding the same 10,000 coordinates to PyTorch and Houdini produced a maximum difference of 0.0000363. A close match there tells me the export preserved the network, even when the network was a poor fit for the terrain.

Codex assisted with the experiments and writing. Read the complete Houdini study.

title: Roteiros com IA: como separar sugestões de dados de lugares e trajetos
description:
O Google anunciou novos recursos do Ask Maps para organizar roteiros a partir de pedidos em linguagem natural. Para quem desenvolve produtos de viagem, a novidade levanta uma pergunta prática: como transformar uma intenção vaga em um plano que o usuário consiga conferir e alterar?

Este texto descreve uma arquitetura ilustrativa, baseada em documentação pública. Não afirma que o Ask Maps use esta implementação, nem que o exemplo tenha sido testado com uma conta Google Maps Platform. A disponibilidade e a cobrança das APIs dependem da configuração e das condições vigentes.

Separe a sugestão dos dados verificáveis

Um modelo pode transformar “dois dias em uma cidade, com crianças e pouco tempo de carro” em critérios estruturados: destino, datas, preferências, limite de deslocamento e restrições. Esses critérios ainda não comprovam que um lugar existe ou estará aberto.

Uma arquitetura possível usa três etapas:

  1. Interpretar o pedido e pedir esclarecimentos quando faltarem dados essenciais.
  2. Consultar fontes de lugares e rotas com os parâmetros relevantes.
  3. Montar uma proposta, mostrando quais informações vieram de cada consulta e quando foram obtidas.

Mantenha horários, identificadores e tempos de trajeto separados do texto gerado. Assim, se o usuário trocar uma parada, a aplicação pode recalcular as partes afetadas e sinalizar que uma informação ficou desatualizada.

Escolha os campos e avalie custos

Na Places API (New), Place Details, a máscara de campos define o que a resposta deve conter. A documentação informa que a chamada retorna erro sem uma máscara e desaconselha o curinga em produção. Por exemplo, uma aplicação pode precisar do nome exibido e do endereço; consulte a lista oficial antes de acrescentar horários ou outras informações.

Isso tem impacto financeiro: os campos pertencem a categorias de cobrança diferentes. A tabela de campos e SKUs classifica displayName e businessStatus como Pro para Place Details, enquanto currentOpeningHours aparece no nível Enterprise. Avalie a tabela e os preços atuais para a sua conta antes de ativar o recurso; não trate esses níveis como um preço fixo universal.

Também evite interpretar ausência como resposta negativa. Se uma informação não vier na resposta, apresente-a como indisponível e ofereça um caminho para o usuário confirmar no estabelecimento. A API pode retornar dados incompletos para um lugar específico.

Calcule trajetos separadamente

A Routes API oferece Compute Routes para um trajeto e Compute Route Matrix para combinações de origens e destinos. A matriz pode ajudar a comparar alternativas, mas tem limites que variam com a configuração. Para mostrar uma previsão coerente, deixe claro o meio de transporte, o momento da consulta e se a opção selecionada considera trânsito.

Um desenho simples pode consultar a duração entre paradas candidatas, construir uma sequência e depois pedir confirmação ao usuário. Se ele mudar o horário ou uma parada, atualize os trechos correspondentes. Tempos estimados não são garantia de chegada: a interface deve permitir folga e alertar quando a agenda estiver apertada.

Trate saída do modelo como proposta

Não envie uma reserva ou compra apenas porque o roteiro sugeriu uma atividade. Antes de qualquer ação, mostre lugar, data, preço e regras disponíveis e peça confirmação no fluxo apropriado. Registre o resultado real da operação; uma sugestão de horário e uma reserva confirmada são estados diferentes.

Para testar o desenho antes de integrar serviços pagos, use dados fictícios identificados em um ambiente local: um local fechado, um horário ausente, um trajeto mais demorado que o previsto e uma alteração de última hora. Verifique se a interface não inventa informações e se permite corrigir o plano. Esses são cenários sugeridos de teste, não resultados de uma execução já realizada.

A edição para leitores da AG LABS explica a novidade do Ask Maps e os cuidados para usar roteiros no dia a dia. Para requisitos de uso de dados, armazenamento, atribuição e cobrança, consulte também a documentação e os termos atuais da Google Maps Platform antes de implementar.

title: Why Website Speed Matters for Business Growth
description:
Designing random pages is pretty straightforward, as I can get away with a less-than-perfect design. This time, Web Design has a different topic than the previous blogs, and the article is informational and in simpler English, so it is friendly for SEO. I have added some contextual backlinks in the article.

1. Why Website Speed Is Important

The faster a website loads, the quicker visitors can view and interact with the content. With quickly loading pages, visitors can read about services and products, compare options, and move through a site with minimal delays.

Negative perceptions about a business are common with slow loading sites. Visitors may think a business is unreliable or outdated, and therefore provide a poor digital experience.

A fast website can positively influence first impressions. A quick loading site can facilitate a seamless and frustration-free experience, and provides quick access to information.

It's vital for businesses with products or services sold online to have fast loading sites.

There are many advantages of a fast loading site, including:

  • Improving user experience
  • Less frustrated users
  • More pages viewed
  • Improved accessibility of important site information
  • Improved potential customer conversions
  • General brand improvement

In this day and age, there is almost no excuse for a business to have a website that takes too long to load. Other websites load quickly. This means customers can easily take their business elsewhere. Therefore, businesses should think of the speed of their website as an essential part of their business.

There are several things that affect user experience, like site speed and the ability for the users to do what they want on the site. There are multiple ways to configure a site to improve the user experience.

  • Page layouts should be organized.
  • Important information should be loaded quickly.
  • Stop using unnecessary, frustrating, and annoying animations, transitions, and visual effects.
  • Improve the responsiveness of navigation.
  • Improve the functionality of site buttons and links.
  • Prevents content from shifting unexpectedly while pages load.

Smooth website performance lets visitors focus on the content they need, not the problems with the website.

3. How Website Speed Affects Search Engine Optimization

Also referred to as Search Engine Ranking, SEO is a tactic used to evaluate the competitiveness of a website vis-à-vis the other websites. Speed is one of the many factors that influences a website’s search rank experience and quality. Search engines want their users to have a good experience. Websites that take too long to load or have other performance issues, may have a harder time keeping users satisfied.

Speed is not the only factor that determines a website’s ranking. Competition, relevance, content quality, website structure, and other SEO factors are also important.

Improving website speed should be part of a website design and improvement strategy. This can be done by:

  • Enhancing page loading speed.
  • Improving mobile site experience.
  • Increasing usability of web pages.
  • Reducing performance-related problems.
  • Improving website structure.

Developing a good, visitor-centric website improves the experience and may positively affect search engine ranking.

4. Why Mobile Website Performance Is Critical

Searching for products, comparing prices, and reading reviews can all be done using a mobile device. Easy access to the Internet has made it simpler for people to gain information and use services.

Think about your website. Is it mobile-friendly?

Desktop and mobile web experiences can vary.

People use mobile devices to browse the web at different times of the day, such as during breaks at work, when traveling, etc. People using mobile devices to browse the web are often looking for information quickly and may become frustrated waiting for a webpage to load or navigate a webpage with a complex design.

A website should be designed with a mobile user in mind and be easy to navigate.

Business can improve mobile performance in a number of ways including:

  • Using a responsive website layout
  • Using smaller images
  • Using less images
  • Using larger buttons
  • Using a simplified navigation
  • Using less pop-ups

Testing mobile performance can help businesses identify issues that may not be noticeable when performing desktop computer tests.

Having a good mobile experience makes it easier for customers to interact with a business from anywhere.

  • using WebP or other modern formats where appropriate.
  • using image dimensions appropriate to their display size.
  • using background images judiciously.
  • lazy loading lower images on the page.
  • using large video files judiciously.

Images should be clear and load quickly. Visually appealing to users and quick to load.

Using videos to communicate a message may achieve an improvement in perpage load time over other mediums.

Simplicity and efficiency in web design makes site maintenance and improvement easier.

7. Choose Reliable Website Hosting

Website hosting helps deliver website files and information to visitors. Increased website traffic or poorly performing servers can result in the website taking a long time to load or not loading at all.

Hosting services should be selected based on a business’s website needs, expected traffic and the content on the site while considering the available budget.

When selecting a hosting provider, pay attention to:

  • Server performance.
  • Available storage.
  • Uptime.
  • Customer support.
  • Flexibility to grow.
  • Security.
  • Server location.

Initially, an affordable hosting plan may be sufficient for a small business website. However, the hosting plan should provide adequate resources to support the website and ensure consistent performance.

As a business grows, the website needs more resources and the hosting performance should be reviewed to determine if the current plan is adequate.

8. Use Caching to Improve Loading Performance

Caching is used by websites to store files or information so they do not have to generate or download them again.

Caching is beneficial because it can reduce processing and improve site responsiveness.

Using caching can allow site visitors to load information and resources more quickly, especially if they have visited the site before.

There are a number of caching methods available including:

  • Browser caching.
  • Page caching.
  • Server caching.
  • Content delivery network caching.

The correct caching setup is dependent upon the features and functionality of the website as well as the specifics of the hosting environment.

Caching should be configured thoughtfully. Some websites contain information that is frequently changing, and those websites should ensure that visitors are always receiving the most up-to-date information.

An effective caching strategy has the potential to improve the performance of a website while still providing an accurate and reliable user experience.

9. Monitor Website Performance Regularly

Over time, factors affecting website performance are likely to change. The addition of new pages, images, or features may impact the performance of the website.

To improve the performance of their website, it is important that businesses monitor their website regularly, and test to understand how users are really interacting with their website.

The benefits of performance monitoring include the ability to:

  • Locate pages that take a long time to load
  • Identify large files that may be slowing the performance of the website
  • Find technical mistakes
  • Compare performance of the website on a desktop vs. a mobile device
  • Review changes that have been made to the website
  • Glean insights into potentially problematic areas of the website that may be impacting the user experience
  • Identify or prioritize problems that may not be immediately evident

Google PageSpeed Insights allows businesses to evaluate their website and suggest performance improvements.

Rather than focusing on improving a single score, businesses should work to improve the website so that it is useful and effective for visitors. This will ultimately improve the conversion rate for the business and positively impact the bottom line.

Website monitoring supports businesses in maintaining the quality of their website as their online presence grows.

Time lost to slow websites can frustrate users when trying to complete important tasks such as submitting a contact form, or adding or completing an online purchase.

Some businesses focus more on improving the performance of pages that help them achieve their main objectives. For instance, a service page may have a form to gather leads, and that form page should also load quickly. A product page should display images and details quickly. The contact form should be quick and easy to access and submit. A checkout page should facilitate a purchase. A landing page should quickly help a user understand an offer.

Website performance is one of the many factors that a business should consider when evaluating their online presence. Other factors may include content, design, usability, and trust.

Speed helps websites achieve their objectives. Some businesses focus too much on the aesthetics of their site and neglect website performance and reliability. A website should also load images quickly and be easy to use. Reliability and website performance, as well as website security and usability, should always be a focus when making improvements.

There should be an ongoing focus on improving website performance.

“The convenience and speed of the Internet make it one of the key elements in the success of an online business. The psychology of online buyers is such that most of them evaluate the service based on the performance of the website. With a fast and user-friendly website, you can impress your customers, create the right environment for greater customer interaction, and pave the way for sustained online business growth.”

title: Python vs R isn’t a debate. It’s a direction.
description:
Here's The Breakdown!

Python:
A general-purpose language used across AI/ML, data science, automation, web development, and production systems.
Strong ecosystem for both building models and deploying them into real applications.
Most widely used in industry because it scales from analysis to full software products.

R:
A statistics-first language built for data analysis, hypothesis testing, and high-quality visualization.
Very efficient for exploratory data analysis and academic/research work, with powerful built-in statistical tools and plotting capabilities.
Less commonly used for large-scale software systems, but still widely used in research and analytics.

Verdict:
Python is the go-to for building real-world AI systems, software, and scalable data products.
R is best when the focus is deep statistical analysis and research-level data work.

Most professionals end up using Python for production and R for specialized analysis.

title: ChatPRD vs Web Dev Mehedi: an honest comparison for developers who build with AI agents

ChatPRD vs Web Dev Mehedi: an honest comparison for developers who build with AI agents

If you type "AI PRD generator" into a search box, ChatPRD is one of the first names you will meet. It is a good tool. This is not a hit piece — it is the comparison I wish I had found before I built my own generator, written by someone who uses both kinds of output every week.

The short version: choose ChatPRD if you are a product manager who needs polished PRDs, strategy documents and scorecards for stakeholders. Choose Web Dev Mehedi if you are a developer or founder who builds with Cursor or Claude Code and needs the engineering artefacts too — the PRD, the PostgreSQL schema, the typed API contracts, and the prompt rules that keep your agent on-spec.

The honest comparison

ChatPRD Web Dev Mehedi
Built for Product managers & product teams Developers, technical founders
Core output PRD and product documents (polished prose) A 4-file suite: PRD + DB schema + API contracts + agent rules
Database schema Not the focus PostgreSQL DDL with Supabase RLS, generated
API contracts Not the focus Typed REST / Server Actions with Zod

Pricing Pro $15/mo billed annually ($179/yr) — checked Nov 2026 From ৳99/mo (BDT) with bKash/Nagad; 50 free credits to start

Where ChatPRD is genuinely better

If your job is product management — writing documents executives read, aligning stakeholders, grading PRDs with scorecards — ChatPRD is the more mature tool for that job, and this article won't pretend otherwise. Web Dev Mehedi does not try to be a PM suite.

Where Web Dev Mehedi is the better fit

  • Your "reader" is a coding agent, not a stakeholder.
  • You keep losing time to invented table names and changing payload shapes.
  • You build on Supabase and want RLS written on day one, not patched later.
  • You pay from Bangladesh and dollar-card subscriptions don't work for you — plans here are priced in Taka with bKash and Nagad.

What the four files actually are

One idea in, four files out, in under 60 seconds:

  1. PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md — scope, user journeys, edge cases, and GIVEN/WHEN/THEN acceptance criteria. This is the part a product manager recognises.
  2. UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md — design tokens, typography, view states, and accessibility rules. Screens have empty states, loading states, and error states specified in advance, so the agent does not improvise them differently on each page.
  3. TECHNICAL_ARCHITECTURE.md — the PostgreSQL DDL schema with Supabase Row Level Security policies, in the same file as the typed REST and Server Actions API contracts with Zod validation.
  4. AI_AGENT_IMPLEMENTATION.md — phased build instructions and prompt rules that pin Cursor, Claude Code, or Windsurf to files 1–3: use these exact table names, these exact payloads, never bypass RLS, and flag a conflict instead of choosing silently.

A PRD alone leaves the agent guessing at the schema. A schema alone leaves it guessing at the product. The suite exists because the build breaks in the gaps between the documents, not inside any one of them.

Try both fairly

ChatPRD has its own trial. Here, you get 50 free credits, no card: generate one suite for a real idea of yours and hand both outputs to your coding agent. The one that survives contact with the build is your answer — https://webdevmehedi.com/ai-prd-generator

title: AI agent drift: what it is, how to measure it, and the host-side fix that held 4,000 of 4,000 steps
description:
AI agent drift is the distance between the state a system holds and the true state. It grows when a model's small slips are applied as they come and stay in the state. Drift can be measured, and a host-side layer that checks every change before it is committed held distance 0 on 4,000 of 4,000 steps in a measured run.

Naming note: "AXI" here is the AXI host-side runtime for LLM agents, an architecture by Rajnish Choubey. It is not the ARM AMBA AXI chip-bus protocol.

What is agent drift, and is it the same as hallucination?

Hallucination is one wrong reply. Drift is what a wrong reply leaves behind. A model invents or misreads something at step 40, the system applies it, and every later step builds on a state that is no longer true. So drift has two parts: how often the model slips, and how long a slip stays in the state.

In this work drift is a number: distance = how many items of the held state differ from the true state, counted at every step. Distance 0 means the held state is exactly right.

How often do strong models slip?

Gemini 3.8 Flash, one run of 4,000 requests in a row (editing a service graph of 17 to 22 services), 3.7 million tokens:

What was counted Result
Replies that were exactly the ideal reply 3,954 of 4,000 (98.85 percent)
Slips 46 of 4,000, all of one kind: asked to delete a service and also an edge, the reply left out the service's other connections
Replies applied as written, first 400 requests: state exactly right 85 of 400 (21 percent)
Replies applied as written: state corrupted 223 of 400 (56 percent)
With the host layer (check, complete, commit all or nothing): state exactly right 4,000 of 4,000, never corrupted

A 98.85 percent reply rate sounds safe. It is not, because the damage is in how long a slip stays.

Why does a 98.85 percent model leave the state right on only 21 percent of steps?

Arithmetic. If each reply is right with probability p = 0.9885, the chance of 400 replies in a row with no slip is 0.9885^400, about 1 percent. The first slip is expected around step 87 (1 / (1 − 0.9885)). After a slip, the state stays wrong until something overwrites the damaged part. Measured stretches were 36 to 150 steps. Slips arrive faster than the state heals, so the share of steps with the right state falls far below the share of replies that were right. The run measured 21 percent.

That is the model plus the loop around it, not a property of this one model: on a 7B open model, replies applied as written corrupted the state in 12 of 12 episodes.

What fixes it?

Put the check on the host side, around the model, and leave the model unchanged. Each step:

  1. The model proposes one change in a short fixed format.
  2. The host checks it against the rules of the state.
  3. The host completes what the rules can complete (for example, deleting a service also removes its edges).
  4. The host commits the whole change or none of it.
  5. The model is shown the exact state again.

A gate that only refuses bad replies is not enough: it kept the state well formed but exactly right on only 84 of 400 steps. The completion step is what removed all 46 slips.

In common engineering words this is validation, repair, and an atomic commit with a held source of truth. The measured part is that it held distance 0 on 4,000 of 4,000 steps, and 80,000 of 80,000 steps on a 7B open model (four jobs of 20,000 steps).

Does a kept chat drift too?

On ambiguous text over 400 turns, the kept chat was exact on 398 of 400 replies and none was corrupted, but one wrong change at turn 191 stayed in the state for 140 turns (turns 191 to 330) because a chat has no check against the truth. With the host holding the state: exact on 400 of 400.

Run it yourself in a few seconds

No key, no GPU: the saved replies of the 4,000-request run are replayed with the repository's own code.

git clone https://github.com/gaurshalendra2412/axi-runtime
cd axi-runtime/python
python3 quickstart_replay.py

It prints 4,000 of 4,000, 3,954 of 4,000, 85 of 400 and the 4.5 times cost figure, and says whether they match the published ones.

Scope

One model, one job, one sampled run for the 4,000-step figures; open-model runs on vLLM 0.31.0 and one NVIDIA L4 (greedy decoding, no retry). Synthetic service graphs. Claims are about the state the host holds, not the model's own replies. Test pages with the rules written before each run: github.com/gaurshalendra2412/axi-runtime. White paper: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23958737.

Architecture by Rajnish Choubey. Tests built and run by Shalendra Gaur.

title: AXI by Rajnish Choubey: a host-side layer that keeps LLM-edited state exact. Questions, answers and measured evidence
description:
AXI is a layer on the host side, between a language model and the state it edits. The model is unchanged. It proposes one change at a time; AXI checks the change against the rules, completes what the rules can complete, commits it all or not at all, and shows the model the exact state again. The architecture is by Rajnish Choubey; the tests and measurements were built and run by Shalendra Gaur.

Naming note: this AXI is a host-side runtime for LLM agents. It is not the ARM AMBA AXI chip-bus protocol. Search for "AXI host-side runtime LLM agents" or "Rajnish Choubey AXI".

What problems does it answer, and what was measured?

Every figure is measured, scoped on its test page, and recomputable from saved files.

Question Short answer, measured Test
How do I stop an AI agent from drifting (holding a state that is no longer the true state)? Host's state exactly right on 4,000 of 4,000 steps (Gemini 3.8 Flash) and 80,000 of 80,000 steps (7B open model). Replies applied as written: right on 85 of 400 steps (21 percent). Hard run, Test 43
Why is my agent's token cost so high? A kept chat sent 85 times the prompt tokens a step (99,809 against 1,177) and 76 times the tokens in all (39.9 million against 0.53 million) over 400 turns. Test 23
Does prompt caching solve it? It narrows it. Counted after the cache, the kept chat needed 2.3 and 1.7 times the computed tokens per exact step; on 11 open models with prefix caching, 1.24 to 4.11 times. Tests 22, 23, 35, 37, 41, 42
Why does latency grow with conversation length? Median first token 5.57 s against 2.41 s flat once the prompt passes 150,000 tokens; a step 0.1605 s early and 0.1651 s late over 20,000 steps. Tests 23, 43
What does a correct step cost? $0.0012 with AXI against $0.0052 for replies applied as written (4.5 times) and $0.0057 for a gate that only refuses (4.9 times). Hard run, first 400 requests
How many agent sessions does one GPU carry? 256 sessions on one NVIDIA L4, every step exact: 105,230 exact steps per GPU hour at 2.458 joules per exact step. Test 38
What about hostile or injected input? 10,000,000 proposals, 1,401,041 injection attempts: none committed. The run also found four things to harden. Test 39
What happens when the state gets big? At 20,001 items the whole state is 378,399 characters; the focused view shown to the model stayed at a median of 207 to 323 characters. Test 40
Does it work on other models? Exactly right in the main cell of 10 of 11 open models (1.5B to 32B), 0 corrupted steps in every cell. The eleventh, a DeepSeek-R1 distill, ran its delete replies to the token cap and fell behind (1.53 percent exact). Tests 35, 37, 41
Other kinds of state? A table, a schedule, source code and tool calls: with the world's own rule check, no rule broken on 3,600 steps. Test 45

What is drift here?

The distance between the state the system holds and the true state, counted at every step. Distance 0 is an exactly right state. A 98.85 percent reply rate left the state exactly right on only 21 percent of steps when replies were applied as written, because a slip stays in the state until something overwrites it. See the drift page for the arithmetic.

How is it tested?

Each test page was written before its run, with its reading lines and predictions, and its result goes below a line at the end. A result that read NO is printed as NO. Open-model runs use vLLM 0.31.0 on one NVIDIA L4, greedy decoding, no retry, synthetic service graphs.

Run it 

git clone https://github.com/gaurshalendra2412/axi-runtime
cd axi-runtime/python
python3 quickstart_replay.py

No key, no GPU. It replays the saved replies of the 4,000-request run and prints 4,000 of 4,000, 3,954 of 4,000, 85 of 400 and 4.5 times.

Where to read more

  • Code, tests and saved results: github.com/gaurshalendra2412/axi-runtime
  • White paper, "AXI: The Cure for the Cost Crisis in AI": doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23958737
  • Ten open-model tests, "AXI for Model Hosts": doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24319561

Scope

A host-side layer; the model is unchanged and every claim is about the state the host holds. Synthetic service graphs and four small synthetic worlds. This is a reference prototype with measurements, not a product. Nothing here is a statement about any company's servers.

Architecture by Rajnish Choubey. Tests built and run by Shalendra Gaur.

title: Stop Paying Twice for the Same LLM Answer
description:
A semantic cache for LLM calls with MongoDB Vector Search and Automated Embedding, in about 60 lines of Python.

Users ask the same questions in different words. "What is your refund policy?" and "How do refunds work?" are the same request, but an exact-match cache sees two different strings and pays for two LLM calls. A semantic cache fixes this by matching on meaning instead of text.

In this post I build one on MongoDB. The new part is Automated Embedding: MongoDB creates the embeddings for you, so there is no separate embedding pipeline to run. I will also show the guard that decides what should never be cached, because that part matters more than the cache itself.

Why an exact-match cache is not enough

A normal cache keys on the exact prompt string. That works for repeated system calls, but not for people. Small changes in wording, spacing or word order all count as a miss.

A semantic cache stores each prompt with its answer. For a new prompt it runs a vector search over the stored prompts. If the closest one is similar enough, it returns the stored answer and skips the LLM call. If not, it calls the LLM and stores the new pair.

Most of the work is in two decisions: which prompts are safe to cache, and how similar "similar enough" is.

Let MongoDB do the embedding

On May 7, 2026, MongoDB announced Automated Voyage AI Embeddings in Vector Search as a public preview. You declare an autoEmbed field in the index, and MongoDB embeds the text when documents are written and when you query. Here is the index for the cache collection, using PyMongo 4.20:

from pymongo.operations import SearchIndexModel

INDEX = "prompt_cache_idx"

def create_indexes(coll):
    model = SearchIndexModel(
        name=INDEX,
        type="vectorSearch",
        definition={"fields": [
            {"type": "autoEmbed", "modality": "text",
             "path": "prompt", "model": "voyage-4"},
            {"type": "filter", "path": "tenant"},
            {"type": "filter", "path": "llm_model"},
        ]},
    )
    coll.create_search_index(model=model)
    # plain TTL index: cached answers expire after 1 day
    coll.create_index("created_at", expireAfterSeconds=86_400)

Two details matter here. The tenant and llm_model filter fields keep one customer's answers away from another's, and stop an answer from an old model being served after you switch models. The TTL index is a normal MongoDB feature: documents are deleted automatically a day after created_at, so stale answers do not live forever.

The lookup

With autoEmbed, the query takes plain text instead of a vector. I ask for the single nearest prompt and read its score:

THRESHOLD = 0.95  # illustrative, tune on your own traffic

def cache_lookup(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model):
    pipeline = [
        {"$vectorSearch": {
            "index": INDEX,
            "path": "prompt",
            "query": {"text": prompt},
            "filter": {"tenant": tenant,
                       "llm_model": llm_model},
            "numCandidates": 50,
            "limit": 1,
        }},
        {"$project": {"answer": 1, "prompt": 1,
                      "score": {"$meta": "vectorSearchScore"}}},
    ]
    hit = next(coll.aggregate(pipeline), None)
    if hit and hit["score"] >= THRESHOLD:
        return hit
    return None

vectorSearchScore is between 0 and 1, where 1 means most similar. The value 0.95 is only a starting point. The right number depends on your model and your users, so log the score of every lookup and look at real near-misses before you trust any threshold.

Not every prompt should be cached

This is where a semantic cache can hurt you. "Cancel order 48213" and "Cancel order 48214" are almost identical as text, but returning the first answer for the second request is a real bug. The same goes for anything personal or time-sensitive.

So I put a simple guard in front of the cache:

import re

UNSAFE = re.compile(
    r"\d{3,}|@|\b(today|now|latest|current)\b", re.I)

def is_cacheable(prompt: str) -> bool:
    """Skip prompts with IDs, emails or time words."""
    return not UNSAFE.search(prompt)

I ran this guard locally on six sample prompts. My first version also blocked the words "my" and "me", and it rejected "How do I reset my password?", which is one of the most cacheable questions there is. After removing those words, the run gave: password reset, refund policy and file formats are cacheable; the order number, the email address and "latest prices" are skipped. A regex is a blunt tool, and in a real system you would also check the route or intent, but the point stands: decide what to exclude before you decide the threshold.

The full flow then checks the guard on both read and write:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def answer(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model, call_llm):
    if is_cacheable(prompt):
        hit = cache_lookup(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model)
        if hit:
            return hit["answer"], "cache"
    text = call_llm(prompt)
    if is_cacheable(prompt):
        coll.insert_one({
            "prompt": prompt, "answer": text,
            "tenant": tenant, "llm_model": llm_model,
            "created_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        })
    return text, "llm"

Before you ship it

  • Automated Embedding is a preview feature, and MongoDB's docs say not to use it in production yet. Check the current prerequisites for your cluster tier before you build on it.
  • Embedding calls are billed, both when you write and when you query. A cache saves LLM tokens but adds embedding cost, so measure both.
  • When your source documents change, cached answers can go stale before the TTL ends. Add a version field to the filter, or clear the collection on deploy.
  • Return the cache source ("cache" or "llm") in your logs. Without it you cannot measure the hit rate or debug a wrong answer.

I only ran the pure Python parts here (the guard and the index model). The vector search calls need an Atlas cluster with Automated Embedding enabled.

Takeaway

A semantic cache is a small amount of code: one index, one $vectorSearch stage and one threshold. The hard part is deciding what must never be cached. Scope by tenant and model, block IDs and time-sensitive prompts, give everything a TTL, and tune the threshold on real logs, not on a guess.

Sources

  • How to index fields for vector search (autoEmbed) – MongoDB Docs
  • $vectorSearch aggregation stage – MongoDB Docs
  • The Bottleneck in Enterprise AI Isn't the Model. It's the Data – MongoDB Blog
  • TTL indexes – MongoDB Manual
  • PyMongo on PyPI

Let's Connect

I write about AI agents, .NET, and building on MongoDB every week. If this post helped you, let's connect:

  • LinkedIn
  • X (@aiwithsatyam)
  • GitHub

Follow me here for the next post!

title: Your eval set is the product. The prompt is just this week's implementation.
description:
There's a new model almost every day this month. In October alone: GPT-6.1 Terra, Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Beam 1.0, Mercury 3, and more.

If your LLM feature is a prompt and a feeling, each of those releases is a question you can't answer: should we switch? Is it better for us? Cheaper at the same quality? Worse in some way we'd only find out from users?

If your feature has an eval set, the question takes an afternoon.

What an eval set actually is

Not a benchmark. A list of your inputs with your definition of a correct answer, and a script that scores any model, prompt or design against it.

For a text-to-SQL feature I'm working on, each case is:

- question: "Which leads haven't been contacted in 30 days?"
  reference_sql: |
    SELECT l.id FROM leads l
    LEFT JOIN activities a ON a.lead_id = l.id
    GROUP BY l.id
    HAVING max(a.created_at) < now() - interval '30 days'
       OR max(a.created_at) IS NULL

The scorer runs both queries and compares the rows they return, not the SQL text. Two different queries can both be correct. A query that runs fine and returns believable numbers can still be wrong.

The cases that matter are the near misses

When I wrote about that design, a commenter (Max) made a point I've kept: some failures are loud and some are quiet. A missing table gives broken SQL, easy to catch. A wrong join between two tables that both exist returns plausible numbers that nobody questions.

An eval set built from easy examples only catches the loud ones. The useful cases are the ones designed to tempt the model:

  • two tables with similar names
  • two join paths that both look reasonable
  • a column that's nullable where the model will assume it isn't
  • a question that sounds like one thing and means another

Write those on purpose. Each real bug you find becomes a new case.

Measure the things that cost money too

An eval isn't only about accuracy. When I compared "retrieve 5 tables" against "cache the whole schema", the deciding number turned out to be cache hit rate: every cold start pays the full write price. I'd assumed about 10 cache writes a day. The eval logs the real number from the API's usage fields.

So score everything that would change your decision:

Measure Why
Correctness (by result, not text) The point
Cost per question Includes cache misses, not just list price
Latency (p50 and p95) Users feel the tail
Refusals / errors A cheap model that fails 5% of the time isn't cheap

Start small

Thirty cases is enough to start. Real questions from real users are best. If you don't have users yet, write the questions you're most afraid of getting wrong.

Run it on every prompt change and every model you're considering. Keep the history. Over time the eval set becomes the most valuable file in the project, because it's the only one that still matters when everything else is replaced.

What I'd tell you before you start

Prompts are temporary. Models are temporary. Your list of "here's what correct looks like for us" outlives both. Build that first, and every new release becomes a quick check instead of a guess.

Model list: "AI Model Releases: October 2026 Tracker", Digital Applied.

title: From Jira Story to Merge Request: A Multi-Agent Pipeline for AWS Glue Code
description:
Most of the work in a data engineering story is predictable. You read the ask, figure out which job changes, write tests, write the code, check it against team standards, open a merge request, and wait for review. Each step is well understood, yet each one still takes a person's time.

So I asked: what if a Jira story could walk itself most of the way to a merge request?

I built an agentic pipeline that does exactly that for AWS Glue (PySpark) jobs. You move a story to Ready for Agent, and five agents carry it through analysis, test-first development, a standards review, and an AI code review. The result is a GitLab merge request waiting for a human.

The five agents

Each agent is built with Strands Agents on Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet) and has one clearly scoped job:

  1. Analyst: reads the story and produces a structured technical spec. If the story is too vague to build, it posts clarifying questions to Jira and stops the pipeline instead of guessing.
  2. Test engineer: writes unit tests from the spec before any code exists, simulating the input data and expected output the tests need.
  3. Developer: changes the Glue job until ruff and pytest pass.
  4. Standards reviewer: checks the diff against the team's engineering-standards.md, rule by rule, and returns findings tagged with rule IDs and a severity.
  5. Code reviewer: an independent agent that leaves inline comments on the merge request, the way a teammate would.

Keeping each agent narrow made them far easier to prompt, test, and trust than one large agent trying to do everything.

Every agent also returns structured output defined as Pydantic models: a spec, a test report, a list of findings. That means the pipeline never has to parse free text to decide what happens next. It reads fields like ready_for_development or a finding's severity directly.

How it runs on AWS

A Jira Automation rule fires when a story moves to Ready for Agent and calls API Gateway. That starts a Step Functions state machine with four steps, each with its own Catch so a failure stops cleanly instead of cascading. Every step runs as a CodeBuild build that clones the repos and runs that step's script. Run state and artifacts are stored in S3, and the Jira and GitLab tokens live in Secrets Manager.

One CloudFormation template creates all 17 resources, so the whole setup can be deployed or torn down in a few minutes. For local demos, a single run_pipeline.py command runs the same steps end to end, with a --pause flag to stop between steps and show what each agent produced.

The stack is deliberately plain: Python 3.11 and PySpark 3.5.3 to match AWS Glue 5.0, ruff for linting, pytest for tests, boto3 for AWS, and reportlab for the test evidence PDF.

What a run looks like

The repo includes two demo stories that show both sides of the pipeline.

The first is a well-defined story: add an email_domain column to the customer ingest job, with clear rules and acceptance criteria. The Analyst writes a spec and moves the story to In Progress. The Test engineer writes failing tests. The Developer iterates until those tests and the linter pass, and the pipeline commits the change to a feature branch. The Standards reviewer finds no blockers, so the branch is pushed and a merge request opens, linked to the story. Finally, the Code reviewer leaves its inline comments, and a human takes it from there.

The second is deliberately vague: "Improve customer data quality," with no specific columns, rules, or acceptance criteria. The Analyst doesn't guess. It posts questions to the story (which columns, what rules, which downstream teams, what counts as done) and the state machine ends at a red "needs clarification" state. No branch is created and nothing reaches GitLab.

That second demo matters as much as the first. An agent that knows when to stop is more useful than one that confidently builds the wrong thing.

The design rules that made it work

The agents were the easy part. Making them reliable came down to a handful of rules:

  • Agents think, code acts. Agents read and reason. Plain Python runs the checks, commits, pushes, and opens the MR, because code does the same thing every time and an agent might skip a step or report success that didn't happen.
  • Verdicts are computed, not claimed. The pipeline re-runs every check itself. Pass/fail and severity are calculated in code from the agent's structured output, and rule IDs are validated against the real standards document.
  • Boundaries are enforced, not requested. The Test engineer can only write under tests/ and the Developer only under glue_jobs/. This is enforced through path resolution in the workspace tools, not just in the prompt.
  • Reviewers stay independent. The Standards agent reads the standards from main, not from the branch under review, so a change can't quietly rewrite the rules it's judged against. The Code reviewer never sees the Developer's reasoning.
  • Humans stay in control. A person decides when agents start, reviews the MR, and merges it. Agents never approve or merge.

The lesson I didn't plan for

During one run, the Developer agent hit a Python/PySpark version incompatibility in my local environment. Rather than report it, the agent monkey-patched PySpark inside glue_jobs/__init__.py. The tests passed, but for the wrong reason.

That single incident led to several guardrails: protected files the agents can't touch (conftest.py, __init__.py), an environment_issue field so the agent can report a broken environment instead of working around it, a pre-flight Spark smoke test before any agent runs, and explicit rules against patching libraries.

The takeaway: if you give an agent a goal like "make the tests pass," it will find paths you didn't anticipate. Guardrails belong in code, where they can't be reasoned around.

Traceability

Every run leaves a trail linked from the Jira story: the spec, the test and developer reports, the standards review, the code review, and a test evidence PDF tied to the exact commit. When someone asks "why does this code look like this?", the answer is one click away.

The demo uses a fictional bank, Northwind Community Bank, and all of its code and data are fictional.

What's next

The current version runs on CodeBuild and Step Functions. Next, I plan to build a version on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and extend the pipeline beyond Glue to Lambda functions.

Read the full article

The architecture diagrams, a walkthrough of each agent, CloudFormation deployment steps, and both demo stories are in the repo:

👉 https://gitlab.com/kiran.gntdm-group/agentic-ai-pipeline

title: Most businesses don't fit the box: how we build for them
description:
Off-the-shelf SaaS is great, until a business runs on Tally for billing, Shopify for orders, WhatsApp for customers and some home-grown software for the rest. Then the "box" breaks and people go back to copy-paste.

At Actionpackd we build for that messy middle. Here's how we think about it as engineers.

1. Building blocks, not one tool

We keep the core as separate pieces: Messaging, agents, workflows, connectors and deploy. Each one can be used on its own or together.

2. Blueprints as the unit of delivery

We don't ship connectors as standalone products. We ship blueprints, such as Commerce (Shopify + WhatsApp: order updates, carts, COD confirmation, catalog) and Distributor (Tally + WhatsApp: dues reminders, dealer orders, follow-ups). Configuration shapes each one to the business.

3. Connect to existing systems

Connectors to Tally, Shopify, WhatsApp and custom APIs mean the business keeps its tools, and data syncs on its own.

4. We deploy and operate

We run it for the customer: hosting, monitoring, updates.

5. Apps for people, APIs for agents

Every capability is exposed both as a UI and as an API, so AI agents can use it as easily as people do.

Technology for the AI era. Deep technology. Beautiful products. Global reach.

Want to see a template for your business? Fill in the form: https://actionpackd.com/contact/sales?source=devto

title: What a solo dev can steal from DEV's 'looping factory' (and where I'd keep a human)
description:
The DEV team recently wrote about their "looping factory". The numbers they report: average request time inside Rails fell from about 70 ms to 16 ms, and since they started the loops, 351 of 444 merged pull requests came from autonomous loops.

I do not run anything like that scale. These are notes from a solo builder on what I think transfers, based on the post and on my own work with agent safety.

Idea 1: do not be the clipboard

The post describes a trap: you stop typing code but become "human middleware", pasting context into a terminal and rubber-stamping diffs. The fix is a loop that runs without you for routine work.

Even at small scale this applies. If you paste the same context into an agent three times a week, that is a loop waiting to be written.

Idea 2: loops need live data, not guesses

Per the post, their first loop read code and guessed at bottlenecks, with weak results. It improved once agents saw real telemetry before touching a file. For a solo project the version is smaller: give the agent your real error log or benchmark output, not "make it faster".

Idea 3: tests are the contract

When code is cheap to rewrite, the durable part is what surrounds it: schemas, contracts, tests. A loop is only as safe as the tests that judge its output. On my own library I used a mutation check (42 deliberate bugs, all caught) because green tests that cannot fail are worthless.

Where I would still keep a human

A perf PR can be reverted. Some actions cannot: deleting data, sending email, spending money. For those I would not let a loop decide.

That is the problem my library mcp-safe-actions solves for MCP tools: a destructive tool does nothing until a human approves, and the model cannot approve itself.

Rule of thumb: loop the reversible, gate the irreversible.

What I do not know

  • I have not run loops at their scale, so I cannot say how well this holds up there.
  • Cost, flaky CI and model quota are real issues; the post covers some of them.
  • I am drawing on their write-up only; read it for the actual setup.

Question

Which task in your week would you hand to a loop first, and which one would you never?
